author: AfricanFeminism
title: Naming the Violence: FGM Survivors Take Their Fight for Justice Online
content:
I was just 17 years old, in a WhatsApp group with peers discussing sexual and gender-based violence when I first heard that Female Genital Mutilation (FGM) was violence. I remember being agitated by the turn the discussion took. Though much of that conversation is murky now, I remember repeating the same lines: ‘

FGM is culture; if we can advocate for abortion, then surely we could allow others to practise their culture in peace

’. A colleague then insinuated that such statements were why more girls and women were being harmed – that I was, in fact, supporting violence against women and girls.


Teenage me had just started her activism journey, but carried the authority of someone who thought she knew it all. For her, FGM was a normal part of existence. My mother, aunties, cousins and almost every woman I knew had gone through it. I had heard stories of older women travelling for days to be cut. Being cut was an honour. Families paid the woman who performed the cutting. There was no way, teenage me would think, that love and violence could coexist. So being called a perpetrator on that platform did not sit well with her.


I left pressed to prove someone wrong. I decided to learn more about FGM, hoping to win the next argument. I dove into its history, beyond what I had absorbed socially.


Why were women cut? How had it become part of our history? As I travelled from one district to another, I heard stories about female chiefs, hints from the Sunnah, and other explanations. Whatever argument I would make next had to be concise. It had to convince others – and, by this point, myself – that FGM was not violence. 


But the more I learned and met the women in different locations, the more my need to prove a point faded. The research kept returning me to the same message: FGM is violence. Teenage me found stories of women discovering they had been cut as children. Older sisters fighting to protect younger sisters. Communities and countries organising against the practice. Women whose genitalia had been sewn together until marriage. Girls being forced into marriages, with FGM part of a much larger system of control over their bodies and futures.


And somewhere in that search, she had to confront a question she had never thought to ask: what if something could be culture and still be violent? The more she learnt, the more she was shattered by the harm done to her own body, and to the bodies of millions of girls before her. 


A woman during a march against FGM in Sierra Leone. Photo by

Massah Brockarie.


 


Facing the fear of naming as a survivor


FGM was the first issue I was ever truly scared to write about. There have always been stories of women being kidnapped, physically assaulted, and even killed for advocating against FGM. And the women who sold dresses, the men who sponsored the cutting, these were people I had loved and admired all my life. Talking negatively about a practice they held dear felt like a betrayal of their trust. And, to be honest, I also thought ”I am okay for now. So, what I experienced was not great harm, right?”


Then one day, on a trip travelling back from Waterloo, eastern…Sierra Leone, I saw girls as young as six walking along the streets. Something shifted in me. Suddenly, this was no longer a debate about culture, history or what I had been taught to believe. These were children. Girls who, like me, had yet to understand the lifelong implications of what could be done to their bodies. If I remained silent, this violence would continue to be meted out upon young girls and women across the country. 


I went straight to Facebook and wrote, “

I’m a cut woman; I once believed that this was an African thing. It never was”, and there I named

t the

harm that FGM is.

 I was surprised by how many people agreed with me. Of course, some people told me to stop. Was it the first time to publicly say that? And really, to look at this as a personal experience that connected to millions of other girls and women, and it needed to be named. Not faceless statistics. 


Since then, I have kept writing. I kept sharing my

 story

 and other advocacy work across social media platforms. The first post opened a conversation with my cousin, who had also been cut. We talked about the harm and absurdity of it and promised that our daughters, if we had them, would not be subjected to the same harm.


The bravery to speak about FGM online, and the conversations it sparked, has stayed with me, and it has …

author: William Shoki
title: Brazil’s racket society
content:
Brazil’s presidential election is headed for a runoff. In the first round on October 4, far-right Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former president Jair Bolsonaro, edged out President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva 47 percent to 45 percent. The right also consolidated its hold on Congress, with Bolsonaro’s Liberal Party now the largest bloc in the Senate. The result came despite Flávio’s thin record, his documented ties to Rio de Janeiro’s militias, and his father’s 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election.

As Latin America’s largest economy and its most populous democracy, Brazil has long served as a bellwether for the region, and increasingly for the world. Analysts of neoliberalism have used “Brazilianization” to describe a future of informal work, fortified elites, and hollowed-out states that they see arriving in the global North. The outcome of the runoff will help decide whether Brazil holds out against a regional turn toward Trump-aligned strongmen, a wave that has already swept Argentina, Ecuador, and, most recently, Colombia.

The stakes are high. Lula’s third term delivered growth, rising wages, and record-low unemployment, but it was hemmed in by a hostile Congress, and household debt and the cost of living kept climbing. Meanwhile, the Trump administration has intervened with unusual openness. It has imposed punitive tariffs and sanctioned a Supreme Court justice, and it has designated Brazil’s two largest criminal factions as terrorist organizations. As Benjamin Fogel

wrote in


Jacobin

 before the vote, “something deeper and more paradigmatic is going on” than ordinary frustration with an incumbent.

In this conversation, editor William Shoki speaks with Fogel, a historian of Brazil and contributing editor at

Jacobin

 and an alumnus of

Africa Is a Country

, to unpack the first-round results, the coalition of interests behind Flávio, and the political economy that makes it cohere. They discuss why Brazilian capital has made its peace with predation, why anti-corruption politics so often breeds cynicism, how “security slop” became the right’s signature policy, and what Brazil and South Africa reveal about everyone else’s future.

William Shoki

For readers who haven’t followed Brazil since Lula came to power for his third term in 2022, what happened on October 4?

Benjamin Fogel

To give a little background: Lula won the election in 2022, but at the same time, what people were calling the most right-wing Congress ever was elected. So if Bolsonaro was defeated at the polls, Bolsonarismo — and we can get into what that is later — was still very much alive.

That election was contested. Apart from all sorts of maneuvers before the vote — trying to discredit it through disinformation channels, trying to buy votes, voter intimidation, and obstruction by the Federal Highway Police on the day — there was an attempted coup, which led into the events of January 8, 2023. That bore some resemblance to January 6, in that you had a bunch of fanatical Bolsonaro supporters storm Congress and trash the place. But Brazil, unlike the United States, has a history of military coups, and it was touch and go whether the military would back it. There were other aspects to this, such as a plot to assassinate Lula, his vice president, and the Supreme Court justice who was overseeing the elections.

So it was defeated, and some people had thought this would discredit the right. It certainly weakened them for a while. But having a right-wing Congress made it really difficult for the Lula government to govern. In terms of the macroeconomic agenda, there were some successes. We’re not talking about anything dramatic, but the economy was growing at three or four percent, and the minimum wage increased. Overall, people were slightly better off than when Lula started, but there wasn’t a massive shift in wealth, and there were other factors we should get into later.

Bolsonarismo persisted. Then last year, Bolsonaro was successfully prosecuted for the failed coup, along with a bunch of his allies — the first time anybody has ever been successfully prosecuted for one. He was in prison and then placed under house arrest for health reasons — as people like to say, he’s permanently ill. What that meant is that the throne of the Brazilian right was up for grabs, and there were a number of pretenders. These included the governor of São Paulo, Tarcísio de Freitas, who’s just been reelected by a huge …

author: Kalundi Serumaga
title: As Long as You Don’t Say Nothing, You Can Say Anything at All
content:
In Uganda, censorship is a reality, and in fact, a governance necessity. Once those governing us came to the realization that they cannot give the population what it needs, either because they don’t want to, or because they are not able, then they have got to try to stop the conversation about governing. Why permit or encourage talk about something you know is not going to change? Why raise hope?


That becomes step one, the usual result of which is to then see the discourse migrate to creative spaces, where it operates in a much more multi-layered and subliminal way. This requires a different kind of management of that arts scene, as step two.


With political censorship, matters have been very clear for some time now. Vocal activists who say things that those in power find offensive now have a standard playbook against them. They get barred from as many media outlets as they can. In extreme cases, landlords can be persuaded to evict them from their homes and business premises. Media houses themselves can be banned, or their troublesome journalists harassed or dismissed. There have been reports of even the tax authorities being sent after the records of businesses owned by such critics. Social media influencers are brought on board to cast the predictable aspersions.


Social media platforms themselves can be shut down as a whole. During the contentious 2021 general election, there was a shutdown across the board. Up to today, Facebook remains banned. Then there are the abductions.


This is not to say it comes easy. The human is designed to see, reflect and speak. So political censorship has it challenges. Recently, some laws seeking to make digital democracy more punishable were thwarted. But in the end, it gets done. Of late, there has been a steady stream of convictions of simple users of X (formerly Twitter) for making posts critical of important government figures. The longest sentence has been six years for the offence of insulting the president via TikTok.


The arts are a different kind of problem, requiring a different set of tools. Art is nebulous. It defies time and form. The key thing to understand is that there is a difference between freedom of speech, and freedom of expression. The Uganda arts sector has suffered over a two decades of deliberate sabotage in my view, and this is why I argue that arts censorship has thus been historically approached in a structural way.


In terms of practical implementation of immediate measures, the lines between politics, art, media and morality are very blurred. Many personalities wear more than one hat, with prominent journalists also being politicians, musicians being opinion leaders, and politicians becoming entertainers.


So the goal has been to create an entirely plastic and artificial practice of noisy, energetic, colourful, but ultimately very hollow forms of “African” expression.


This is actually the best form of arts censorship; creative voices must be monitored, and then led astray.


The transformation of the singer Bobi Wine into the major opposition politician known as Robert Kyagulanyi was not the origin of this process, but became the occasion for its intensification.


There had been other political musicians, like Ronald Mayinja whose themes had become a source of quiet nervousness among the authorities. Various theories exist as to how he vanished from prominence, amid a flurry of mixed messaging.


The closest analogy I can think of is the analyses I have seen by and about certain pioneers of old-school Hip Hop in the United States, such as Wise Intelligent, KRS-One, Chuck D and others, who say that the art form was hijacked.


Citing examples from original rap groups such as Roc Nation, they argue that the wider American power structure and society became worried about the political impact of rap music due to its articulation of Black political concerns about racism, imperialism, and poverty. 


They say that the strategic response to this was to encourage the emergence of a new kind of Hip Hop practice, which was mainstreamed and made the dominant and more accessible kind. This was done through the manipulation and encouragement of entertainers more concerned with hedonistic themes in the way those in charge of the major recording companies signed up, curated, distributed and marketed them. The result is largely what became known as “Gangsta Rap”. 


They argue that this process was aimed at depoliticizing, or corrupting a valid art form …

author: Ibrahima Diallo
title: Drongo Company: Can Washington’s new PSYOP unit win back African trust?
content:
In mid-July, the US Army activated

Delta Company

 of the 7th Psychological Operations (PSYOP) Battalion under 3rd Special Forces Group. The unit has taken on the informal name ‘Drongo’, a nod to an African bird known for its ability to vocally mimic other species to drive off competitors. Its declared purpose is to support US Africa Command’s (AFRICOM) influence and information operations across the continent, though it is not technically an AFRICOM unit as it belongs to Army special operations and executes missions in AFRICOM’s area of responsibility.


Drongo’s existence says less about African security dynamics than about Washington’s shrinking appetite and capacity for direct military engagement on the continent. AFRICOM

 told Congress

 earlier this year that the command’s regional posture has declined by roughly three-quarters over the past decade,

 degrading intelligence collection and security cooperation

 even as terrorism, near-peer competition, and economic rivalry intensify. That decline reflects both access lost to successive coups and a deliberate shift toward a lighter footprint through partner-nation capacity-building, selective drawdowns, and standoff tools such as airpower, visible in the Command’s

 intensified strikes in Somalia

. Read in that context, standing up a unit to project influence through phones, broadcasts, and local intermediaries is a rational, inexpensive way to maintain relevance where Washington can no longer sustain a physical presence. The question is not whether it should exist, but whether it can do the job it was built for.


The Department of Defense

defines

 psychological operations or PSYOPs as influencing the emotions, motives, reasoning and, ultimately, the behavior of foreign audiences. In practice it spans two very different objectives. The first is narrow and behavioural, e.g., persuading fighters to defect, villagers to report roadside bombs, or communities to disregard specific rumours. These objectives do not require audiences to like or trust Washington. The second is what might be called strategic persuasion, i.e., getting audiences to accept an account of US intentions that competes with rival narratives. That depends almost entirely on the credibility of the sender. Drongo’s stated purpose, operating

across contested environments

 where strategic rivals are shaping foreign opinion, places it in the second category. Countering adversarial narratives about the US is, by definition, a contest over what Africans believe about American intentions. The credibility deficit is therefore not a hedge on the unit’s prospects, but the terrain it operates in.


That deficit and animosity toward the West is due largely by France. Paris’s post-colonial legacy and persistent failure to deliver mutually beneficial economic and security arrangements eroded its credibility on the continent long before

Opération Barkhane

 wound down. Additionally,

Françafrique’s

 one-sided extractive models persisting from the colonial era ran their course, and a military presence once justified as counterterrorism assistance came to be seen as another means through which Paris preserved its regional influence. The result was a surge in

anti-French sentiment

, mass protests and, between 2022 and 2025, the

departure of French forces

 from the region: forced in the Sahel, negotiated on the coast. By failing to distinguish its own approach, Washington has been pooled into the same category of actors some Africans view as exploitative. And while adversarial messaging often casts

the West as one bloc

, the US has built a record of its own.


In September 2021, then-Colonel Mamadi Doumbouya’s special forces overthrew then-Guinean President Alpha Condé, who had grown increasingly dubious of Western, and particularly French, motives. Doumbouya is a former French Foreign Legionnaire who had

trained

 in Israel, Senegal, Gabon, and at l’École de Guerre in Paris. He has also participated in US-led exercises, and his coup took place while US Green Berets were in-country training his units. Washington

condemned the takeover

, suspended training, and denied foreknowledge, and no evidence of American involvement has surfaced. However, the optics fueled uncorroborated suspicions and reinforced the belief that Western powers manipulate African politics to suit their strategic interests. In January 2026, Doumbouya was sworn in as president with a

US delegation in attendance

, and …

author: Mada Masr
title: Prosecution says journalists’ testimony indicates Matsda2sh was ‘Brotherhood media cell,’ EIPR says statement unproven position
content:
The Public Prosecution issued a

statement

 on Wednesday regarding the investigations into the six Matsda2sh fact-checking platform’s journalists, stating that one of them admitted that all the defendants — as well as others — had joined a media committee affiliated with the Muslim Brotherhood.

 


It said they had been tasked with carrying out “media plans” based on spreading and broadcasting rumors and false news about state institutions, exclusively highlighting the shortcomings of those institutions, disparaging the roles and performance of their officials and overblowing issues related to select groups, as well as fabricating and exaggerating events related to them. 


From its side, the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, whose lawyers are leading the defense counsel representing the journalists, repeated its demands for their release, for the charges against them to be dropped and for the case to be closed.


In

response

 to the prosecution’s statement, EIPR said that its media statements published on social media hold no evidentiary value in law and amount only to a summary of the prosecution’s case, none of which has been presented before a court, while none of its claims has been proven.

 


The organization pointed out the prosecution’s failure to address the fact that the six journalists did not appear before the prosecution until five days after their arrest, during which time they were denied contact with their families and lawyers, in violation of the law, despite relatives and lawyers filing 18 complaints with the prosecution during that period.


The prosecution’s statement also failed to mention that the order to hold the journalists in custody is issued by investigating authorities under the exceptional provisions of the counterterrorism law, which only permit the measure “when there is a threat of terrorist crimes and when such measure is required to confront that threat,” according to EIPR.

 


Yet the prosecution’s claims, based on the security investigations, accuse the journalists only of publishing rumors or “false” reports, without identifying “the imminent terrorist threat that required depriving the six journalists of their right to appear before a judicial authority within 24 hours of their arrest, during which documented violations were committed against them.”  


The six journalists appeared before the prosecutions five days after their forced disappearance following their arrest, during which they were held at National Security Agency premises. 


None were brought before prosecutors until the first of the six was presented to the Supreme State Security Prosecution on Saturday, with the other five interrogated on the following day. The prosecution ordered that one of the six be brought for forensic medical examination, after some of the defendants complained of being subjected to torture and maltreatment at the NSA premises, with lawyers calling for officers responsible for those premises to be investigated.


The prosecution stated that the first journalist who was investigated admitted that the defendants received “monthly funding of sums in foreign currencies,” via bank transfers from a company owned by a “fugitive member of the Muslim Brotherhood” in a foreign country.


The prosecution also said it found communication groups on a secure messaging app on his phone, connecting him and the other detainees with the “fugitive member,” as well as emails from the latter to them. All but one admitted to regularly receiving sums of money in US dollars, transferred from a foreign country.


After the statement’s publication, EIPR director, Hossam Bahgat, told Mada Masr that the prosecution is pointing to the procedural steps Matsda2sh took to regularize as though it were incriminating evidence.

Bahgat noted that following the “

Zambia plane crisis

,” the company that owns the platform registered employment contracts for its staff, which were presented to Egyptian banks in order for accounts to be opened through which the journalists would receive their salaries.

 


Authorities previously

arrested

 a former member of the Matsda2sh team in 2023, after the platform published a series of investigations about a private jet carrying cash, counterfeit gold and weapons, that was taken into custody in Zambia with a number of Egyptian nationals on board, some of whom had alleged military and police backgrounds.

statement

author: Mzi Velapi
title: Memorial service held for victims of the Strand mass shooting
content:
In the early hours of Sunday morning, 27 September, gunmen opened fire on patrons at a shisanyama in Lwandle, near Cape Town, killing ten people. “Five individuals died on the scene while five others succumbed to injuries sustained after being transported to medical facilities. Eleven others are receiving medical treatment for injuries sustained. Lwandle police have opened murder and attempted murder cases,” said the police. The community believes the mass shooting is related to the extortion racket that is ravaging Cape Town townships.


One of the victims, Khululekani Ndlovu, will be laid to rest this weekend. The nine other people killed will be buried next weekend in the Eastern Cape. The Nomzamo Community Hall in Strand, south east of Cape Town, was packed with mourners and members of political parties for the memorial service.


Speaking to

Elitsha

, the chairperson of the police board in South Africa, Francina Lukas, said that extortion and business rivalry and lack of opportunities for young people are some of the factors contributing to high crime rates in the townships of Cape Town. She said that the lack of trust the community has in the police contributes to high crime rate.


“The police need to do much more than what they are doing in terms of compliance to make sure that businesses in the township comply with their licenses and bylaws. But the issue of trust is still a burning issue in our communities. So we need to overcome that issue to see that trust in the police is restored,” she said.


Families of the Strand 10


Speaking on behalf of the Sikweza family who lost their daughter, Avuyile, her uncle, Luyanda Macokeni, said she had plans to return to school next year. The 20-year-old passed her matric in 2024. She applied to continue her education next year and had just received responses from two universities offering her a place to study. She was expected to make a choice between the two. “Avuyile is supposed to the one burying us as elders but we are the ones burying her. It’s not God’s will that we are here today, it is because of someone’s will,” he said.


Siyathemba Jilaji was one of the victims who died on his way to the hospital, according to his friend. “He said he was going to change in the car so when the shooting began, I thought he was still in the car. A bullet grazed me under my arm. After the shooting, I went to the car to check for him. But, I didn’t know that he was amongst the bodies that were lying next to the entrance that I ran past,” she said.


Sivenathi Manxiwa’s father, Lubabalo Ndamane, said that he is not going to forgive the person who murdered his son. “I also don’t want to know who they are. Even if they can be arrested, I would not go to court. I leave everything to God and God will deal with him. I want to know what drove him to shoot at the young people who were out enjoying themselves,” he said.


The 10 people who died during the mass shooting in Strand last weekend

.

Photo from Facebook

.


The police said that the investigation into the mass murder is still ongoing.

author: Caleb Okereke
title: Matthew Blaise wants to be your friend and neighbor
content:
Matthew Blaise and I must have been in our mid teens when we first met. I don’t remember the exact year, but I remember that it was on Facebook. It did not take long for that online connection to become a real friendship, and it is one that has persisted despite life carrying us in different directions.   


When we sit down for this conversation in September, I am in Philadelphia and Matthew is in Brazil. He is preparing for

Friends and Neighbors

, a new art and literary festival in Lagos built around a deceptively simple question: What responsibility do we have to the people we call our friends and our neighbors?


It is a question that makes our own friendship an interesting place from which to begin. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 


Caleb:

 Something I find provocative about the title “Friends and Neighbors” is that you also seem to be making a statement about the ways queerness shows up in the ordinary. I’m thinking about this song, “Your driver could be LGBT, your friend could be LGBT, your neighbour could be LGBT.” Was that part of the conceptual framing?


Matthew:

 Actually, that’s another way to see it. When I thought of this concept, I thought of proximity within our community. A trip from Lagos to Europe is cheaper than a trip from Lagos to Abidjan, which is a neighboring country. For me, that’s a metaphor for what a lot of friendship within the African continent, especially around queerness, has been due to bad policy, homophobia and criminalization.


Queer people within Africa are not so familiar with themselves. And in that sense, we really haven’t constructed what queer Africanness is because we are still not so close to ourselves. But I find it interesting that you also see it from the point of everyday life, where people you come in contact with could be of this community or could possess these identities without you knowing.


Caleb:

 That’s what immediately came to my attention. Even when you say, “Hello, friends. Hello, neighbors,” you’re talking to all of us, right? It’s not “queer friends and neighbors.” The implicit read is that even if you’re straight, queer people are all around you. They’re your friends. They’re your neighbors. They might not tell you that they’re queer, but they’re there.


Matthew:

 From the perspective of bell hooks, societies should be built on love and friendship. This very important foundation of love has been taken away from queer people, or we’ve not been given that due to our queerness. Governmental policies and criminalization also make us live our lives in isolation. What it means to be friends right now is also very transactional, especially for queer people.


Caleb:

 One thing that has defined our friendship, at least for me, is honesty. There are things I can tell you that I can’t tell anybody else, obviously, so a sort of radical honesty. And as you were talking about transactional relationships, it made me think, what is the place of honesty in friendship, especially in a context where being honest about yourself can carry consequences?


Matthew:

 I think you don’t owe everyone that truth about yourself. For those who I truly trust, I owe them that responsibility of truth. And I do believe, for every friendship, there has to be that investment in honesty.


Caleb:

 But friendship in and of itself is a risk. I don’t think we realize that, but every friendship is a risk.


Matthew:

 Yeah, friendship sometimes, I mean, it’s not a constant state of feeling a certain way. It’s a roller coaster of emotions. It’s a journey. It’s an adventure. So you encounter a lot of things on the way.


You stretch your hand to someone and they actually bite your hand, then you know they are not really having that good intention towards you. So you can decide to stretch your hand again or push them away. But for me, I think it’s important that we’re able to stretch our hands and bring people together and do the work of educating them until we just know they’re irredeemable.


Caleb:

 Yeah…


Matthew:

 What responsibility do you think you owe me as your friend?


Caleb:

 You are now the one asking me questions. But no, I mean, I think you owe your friend loyalty. That’s one of the things that I’m non-negotiable on. I mean, there are many other things you owe your friend.


Matthew:

 You owe them honesty also?


Caleb:

 You owe them honesty. You also owe your friends grace. I give grace a lot. Maybe it’s not even grace. I’m also like, oh …

author: WoMin
title: Women on the frontlines: Organise, Educate, Liberate, Celebrate!
content:
Across social justice movements, both in the Present and in the Past, education has been a central piece binding theory and praxis. It is from this understanding that, from the 17

th

 to the 18

th

 of September, the

Afro-International Feminist Organising School (AFRO-IFOS),

 a movement building space that uses popular education to strengthen our collective knowledge, share our experiences, and grow our international movement, hosted a School of Facilitators in Nairobi, Kenya, to support the deepening of a Decolonial Feminist Popular Education praxis across the more than 30 countries and territories represented, from Africa and the Americas.


There is power in naming the inequalities and wounds we carry as peoples who have been dispossessed of land, livelihoods, cultures and Knowledge. However, our greatest challenge is creating spaces that encourage us to dream of a world beyond the limits of colonial imagination.


Popular education has been a powerful practice for creating such spaces. Rooted in the knowledge and lived experiences of the people, it invites us to learn not only from books and institutions, but from one another.


Education is a political commitment


In the 1971 BBC film “

Behind the lines

”, Maria, a Mozambican guerrilla fighter explains that education was at the heart of why she decided to join the liberation struggle. In her experience

“If a girl reached a certain class [The colonialists] said that is enough for us, Africans.”


(Literacy Campaign, Guerrilla warfare in Angola, 1968. Photo: Augusta Conchiglia)


Our feminist

herstories

 across Africa and beyond have been deeply shaped by anti-colonial struggles. It was within the liberation movements that many women and men encountered education as a practice of freedom, in learning to question colonial power, reclaiming their histories and wisdom, fighting to protect their sovereignty and imagining forms of collective life beyond the impositions of heteropatriarchal, capitalist, colonial systems.


As feminist ancestor Nawal El Saadawi reminds us

“good education means creating dissatisfaction and disobedience.”

 Her wordsspeak to the transformative power of education to nurture the critical consciousness needed to both understand the conditions that constrain us and to connect them to our personal experiences, which is fundamental to organise collectively towards liberation.


But liberation cannot be achieved by a few, full liberation requires all of us. Our political project must be sustained by an intentional educational project that deepens our proposals and equips us to build the worlds we envision.


The educator is a pollinator


Through processes of learning, unlearning, relearning and imagining together, we become both teachers and students in our movements. This is one of the many ways in which decolonial feminist popular education inspires us to cultivate relational ways of working together that are grounded in mutual learning, listening, solidarity and care.


Instead of positioning the educator as the one who holds all the answers, popular educators create spaces where all can collectively formulate the questions that emerge from our struggles and where all can develop the knowledge needed to respond.


“Vou aprender a ler

 /

Para ensinar minhas camaradas

 /

I will learn how to read

 /

To teach my comrades”


Brazilian struggle song


The same way bees are essential for healthy environments, popular educators are an important part of feminist movements infrastructure. Popular educators nurture the power that already exists within movements.


Like the flower, each individual carries something that can nourish the collective. Learning is never only for ourselves. What we learn becomes a good we carry around our movements, to share, to exchange, to teach and to transform. Knowledge moves between us, allowing new ideas, possibilities and material actions to be activated. It is through this circulation of knowledge that we can produce the sweet taste of hope needed to build different futures.


Organising and liberating as we educate


“The beast is too big, and we need a political project that inspires us to build something every day and not just to fight and destroy the world as we know it.” –


Sandra, Guatemala


A decolonial feminist popular education praxis can build bridges across our different struggles, experiences, beliefs and movements, creating the conditions to move beyond simply resisting what exists …

author: Abahlali_3
title: Record Fuel Price Increase: A Crisis for the Poor
content:
6 October 2026 Abahlali baseMjondolo Press Statement

Record Fuel Price Increase: A Crisis for the Poor

The record increase in the fuel price, which will take inland 95 petrol to R30.25 a litre from 7 October, will push poor people even deeper into suffering.

We are already living through a devastating social crisis. Around 13.1 million people are unemployed or have given up looking for work. There are around 5 million unemployed young people between the ages of 15 and 34, and the unemployment rate for this group is 47.4%. Among young people between 15 and 24, unemployment has reached 62.8%. Around 3.8 million young people aged 15 to 24 are not in employment, education or training. Around five million people continue to live in shack settlements, and there are around 3,400 shack settlements across the country.

Millions of people do not have sufficient access to healthy food. The Pietermaritzburg Economic Justice and Dignity group calculated that in September the average household food basket cost R5,488.06, while a basic nutritionally adequate food basket cost R6,655.29. The average cost of feeding one child was R970.27 a month, while the Child Support Grant is only R580 a month.

A worker earning the national minimum wage can work for the whole month and still not earn enough to buy a nutritionally adequate food basket for a household, even before paying rent, electricity, transport, school costs and other necessities.

Official statistics show that 14% of households have inadequate access to food and 8.2% have severely inadequate access to food. Almost one in four South African children under five are stunted.

The social devastation has plunged millions of people into deep suffering, and robbed millions, especially young people, of any hope for a viable future.

We cannot continue like this. Yet in this crisis a corrupt and morally depraved political elite, now organised across a number of political parties, continues to loot public funds. At the same time a deeply cynical business elite continues to make enormous profits from the labour and consumption of poor and working-class people. Supermarkets make massive profits while people go hungry. Executives earn millions while workers struggle to feed their families. Food has become a commodity from which large companies make profit while millions of people cannot afford enough to eat. This is simply immoral and it must be stopped.

The first thing that needs to be done is to stop cutting public spending to please business. Austerity must be immediately stopped and public money must be used for the public good. Social grants must be increased to protect people from hunger. Wages must be increased to give people enough to live on. Public transport must be safe and affordable. The social value of land must be put before its commercial value and land must be made available for housing, food production and recreation.

There can be no food security in a country where wealth and land are so unequally distributed. Hunger is not caused by a lack of food. It is caused by impoverishment, unemployment and inequality, and by a food system in which land, production and distribution are controlled for profit.

We need a massive project to build food sovereignty. Poor people cannot remain dependent on a food system controlled by a small number of large supermarket chains and food corporations. Urban land reform must make land available for people to grow food close to where they live. Municipalities must support community gardens, small farmers, street traders and local food producers, and establish public and community markets where healthy food can be sold directly and affordably.

It is critical that we break the control of the large supermarkets over the food system and build a food system organised around public need rather than private profit.

Food cannot continue to be treated as a commodity in a country where millions go hungry. Access to healthy food must be treated as a right.

In a social crisis of this extent the corrupt political elite, the state and capital have lost all moral and political credibility and we cannot continue to accept their authority while millions go hungry and millions of young people have no future.

Land must be occupied and put to democratically managed social purposes while we build the democratic power of the poor and the working class to put land, wealth and power in the hands of the people.

Thapelo Mohapi 084 576 5117 Snenhlanhla …

author: AfricanFeminism
title: Who Can Afford to Imagine Liberation?
content:
I recently had a conversation with an acquaintance who had applied for activist welfare support after the floods in Accra, Ghana this June destroyed much of what they owned. Their appliances, gadgets and other belongings were gone or damaged, rent was still due, and they had the very reasonable fear that the rains could return and the next flood could be worse. They work full-time with a grassroots organization, which can mean having a job without necessarily having the financial security to suddenly move house, replace their belongings and start again. They never received feedback on that application. Through the kind of backdoor follow-up that has become an unofficial administrative system of its own in social justice movements, they eventually learned that the welfare fund was specifically for activists who needed relocation, medical assistance, provisions and other forms of support as a result of their activism.


I understand why such a fund exists. People face threats, violence and displacement because of the politics of the work, and there should be resources when that happens. But I kept returning to the question of what counts as care in activism and what has to happen before suffering becomes recognizable as an activist emergency. A flooded home is an emergency. Losing almost everything you own is an emergency. Having rent due while trying to find somewhere safe to live is an emergency. You can spend your working life asking why the state has failed people, and still discover that the existing welfare responses want to know whether the state failed you because of your activism.


A friend recently underwent surgery and is carrying a substantial medical bill while continuing her work as the executive director of a Lesbian, Bisexual Queer organization. She cannot easily access her organization’s welfare fund because of her position, which would be a conflict of interest, and the external fund does not cover medical needs unrelated to activism.


Professionalization that overlooks precarity


Over time, we have professionalized the work of liberation, and a relatively small group of people now spends their working lives organising, documenting, researching, advocating, and building movements around questions that affect far more people than those on the payroll. Health, safety, dignity, discrimination, economic security and democratic participation remain enormous public questions, while the labour of pursuing them has become professional work. 


If we have decided that social change requires people to do this work as their jobs, what have we built around the people whose working lives now carry it?                                   


Philanthropy has made much of this professionalization possible. The work may be funded while the people doing it remain precarious. This is especially visible among grassroots activists, organisers, mobilisers and younger groups working around social justice, many of whom move from one short contract, stipend or grant period to the next. They are still living ordinary lives around the work: paying rent, taking public transport, dealing with medical expenses, supporting family and trying to meet the everyday costs of being alive. Stipends are often treated as wages for full-time work while covering very little of what a life actually costs. 


This work is also happening amid growing political hostility toward the very questions activists are organising around. Across the continent, gender and sexuality have become an increasingly contested political terrain, with governments and political actors advancing laws and policies that restrict the lives of women, girls and LGBTQIA people, while broader civic spaces are being narrowed through arrests, restrictions of protest, expression and association. In many places, the consequences of being associated with this work can include surveillance, intimidation, detention or violence. Activists are working amid growing militarism and political repression, while being expected to organise, support communities and keep these questions in the public eye. To do this work, therefore, is to work within the consequences of the politics one is trying to change. 


Professional security would mean earning a salary that sustains a life, having insurance and healthcare when things go wrong, and having some form of welfare that can absorb the ordinary shocks of being alive. Without those things, working in a nonprofit can feel almost synonymous …

author: Folashade Roberts
title: Old Nollywood 2.0
content:
Scroll to the comments under the movie

Love in Every Word

 on YouTube, and you will find viewers from Lagos to London, Accra, Houston, and beyond, tagging sisters to “come and watch this.” Even though the movie had no cinema release and no streaming deal, it reached 15 million views within a week of its March 2025 release on the Omoni Oboli TV YouTube channel. It reached roughly 30 million by year’s end. Actress and filmmaker Omoni Oboli and her business partner, Tomi Adeoye, launched Omoni Oboli TV in December 2023. Since then, the channel has gained more than two million subscribers. The success of

Love in Every Word

 and its sequel pushed their YouTube television channel past 182 million total views across 550 videos, and it was named YouTube Nigeria’s Top Creator Channel of 2025.

The story and style of

Love in Every Word

 are typical of Nollywood cinema, but there is something about the success of its format that raises questions. Is it an example of a new paradigm for how we understand the present-day movie industry in Nigeria? Or is it marking a return to the spirit of the original Nollywood? Does this format’s mix of “New Nollywood” and “Old Nollywood” betoken a new concept? Perhaps we could call it “Old Nollywood 2.0.”

Sometimes journalists and scholars like to divide film history into neat periods of succession. But looking at the history of Nollywood cinema, the reality is that there have been overlapping industrial formations. For the past three decades, the Nollywood phenomenon and its global impact have been described, analyzed, and debated, and the storyline goes something like this. Once upon a time, in the late 1980s, in the street markets of Onitsha and Lagos, movie theaters were declining because the cost of production and distribution of celluloid films was prohibitive. Independent producers were shooting television drama on video, working with Nigerian television networks, while the Yoruba traveling theater troupes were experimenting with video. Alongside this development, traders and marketers, who were already distributing imported and pirated Hollywood and Bollywood films, began to make and market their own cheaply produced melodrama on VHS.

Before Nollywood, there was a politically Pan-Africanist movie industry across Africa into which the recently liberated postcolonial nation-states enthusiastically invested. In the 1970s, the Nigerian government expanded its involvement in film and cultural production when it hosted FESTAC ’77 and repositioned the existing Nigerian Film Unit (formerly Colonial Film Unit) into the Nigerian Film Corporation, with a mandate to broaden its responsibilities and foster development of the national film industry. Filmmakers such as Ola Balogun and Adamu Halilu made artistically stunning films, sometimes collaborating with Black artists from across the world.

With the onset of structural adjustment policies imposed by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), alongside the devastation of civil wars and repressive regimes, the state’s investment in a liberated media crumbled. What some consider the “golden age” of artistically brilliant, politically progressive Nigerian cinema was diminished. Into the void stepped entrepreneurial, commercially minded filmmakers who took advantage of the straight-to-video format and what economists call the “informal market” of the street. The new “video-films” (first made on VHS and then on VCD and DVD) were quite popular for a multitude of genres, from crime (

Issakaba

, 2001), domestic melodrama (

Violated

, 1996), and family drama (

Rattlesnake

, 1995), to religion (

Agony of a Mother

, 2002), romance (

Keeping Faith: Is That Love

?, 2002), slapstick comedy (

Osuofia in London

, 2003), social mobility (

Glamour Girls

, 1994), urban aspiration (

Domitilla

, 1996), and occult and supernatural narratives (

Living in Bondage

, 1992, and

Nneka the Pretty Serpent

, 1994). The rapid success of these movies far exceeded expectations.

Nollywood’s enormous local and global popularity attracted new investors and renewed interest in theatrical exhibition. The opening of new multiplexes from 2004 created another route to audiences and encouraged a strand of filmmaking characterized by larger budgets, improved production values, and theatrical premieres. The transformation did not stop at the cinema. The South African company MultiChoice/Africa Magic expanded its investment in Nigerian content, while digital …

author: Emma Honeybun
title: First Nations oppose proposed ‘one-project, one-year’ bill following its first vote
content:
Several First Nations assemblies located across the country are rejecting the Building Canada Strong Act, according to a joint announcement issued Thursday afternoon.


It came on the same day the proposed law passed its first vote in the House of Commons, and moved on to be studied by a special committee.


Bill C-39 would expand on the government’s “one-project, one-review, within one-year approach to major infrastructure projects.”


While Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre called the bill “watered down,” opting to make an amendment to speed up the process even further — to between six months and a year — First Nations are saying the original proposal is already not enough time.


The Chiefs of Ontario

(COO)

, the Assembly of First Nations Quebec-Labrador

(AFNQL)

, the British Columbia Assembly of First Nations

(BCAFN)

 and Nishnawbe Aski Nation

(NAN)

 stated the proposed bill “weaponizes the parliamentary process,” and “overrides the inherent, Treaty and constitutionally protected rights of First Nations.”


“If Canada wants to fast-track major projects, it must first fast-track the respect, protection and implementation of First Nations rights,” said AFNQL Regional Chief Francis Verreault-Paul. “True certainty is built through partnership and respect, not by bypassing the very rights that create the conditions for lasting economic development.”


The proposed Bill C-39 works similarly to Bill C-5,

the Building Canada Act

, which gives ministers the authority to fast-track projects, such as the Pacific Link pipeline, if they are labeled in the national interest.


According to Ottawa, there are five criteria for meeting national interest. The project must “strengthen Canada’s autonomy, resilience, and security”; “provide economic or other benefits”; have “a high likelihood of successful execution”; “advance the interests of Indigenous Peoples”; and “contribute to clean growth and to meeting Canada’s climate change objectives.”


Projects of national interest are given the authority to fast-track through the assessment and consultation process, potentially exempting them from certain laws, such as the Species at Risk Act, which would slow down the period from approval to construction.


Bill C-39 introduced the concept of regions of national interest, zones which allow projects within its jurisdiction to be deemed in the national interest based on location.


This is because consultation and environmental assessment will be done to the region as a whole, rather than individual projects, before it can be labeled as such.


After the vote in Parliament, Green Party Leader Elizabeth May called the proposed law an “omnibus of omnibuses.”


Read more:


‘An incredible animal’: B.C. port expansion could drive southern resident killer whales to extinction, advocates warn


The First Nation groups shared concerns about the implications fast-tracking project consultation and assessment would have for Treaty rights, as well as environmental safeguards, “stripping away” the ability to “influence decisions affecting their territories.


“Accelerating project approvals cannot mean weakening the safeguards intended to protect them,” they wrote.


In the statement, the groups also brought attention to an imposed “one-year project timeline” that changes federal impact assessments and regulatory process so that regions labeled under the national interest can be “designated for accelerated development.


According to Ottawa, the one-year timeline serves as a 365-day countdown, and ministers must outline a reason for delay if it takes longer.


The groups wrote that First Nations must have “sufficient time, information and capacity” to understand potential impacts to traditional territories, as well as make decisions according to their own laws or governance.


“Free, prior, and informed consent cannot be squeezed into a predetermined federal project timeline. If meaningful consultation and accommodation require additional time, the timeline must be adjusted,” the statement continued.


According to Section 35 of

the Constitution Act,

 if any changes are to be made to First Nations rights or freedoms, the government must consult with leadership, as well as invite them to be part of the discussion overall.


But NAN Grand Chief Alvin Fiddler said that First Nations are no longer at the table.


“That is not reconciliation – it is a continuation of the same pattern our people have fought against for generations. Our …

author: Daron Letts
title: Crosswalk crash stalls Iqaluit traffic
content:
A downed crosswalk pole on Niaqungusiariaq Rd., across from Iqaluit’s Qikiqtani General Hospital clinic entrance, slowed traffic for 90 minutes, following a two-car collision at around noon on Thursday.


“Everyone was checked at the scene, and one person went to the hospital on their own afterwards for further assessment,” said city spokesperson Geoff Byrne in an email.


The city warned drivers of the traffic disruption in a public service announcement issued shortly after 12 p.m.


Two RCMP vehicles blocked Niaqungusiariaq Rd. about two hundred metres past the Sailijaaqvik boarding home at the southeast corner of the intersection. An RCMP truck also blocked Queen Elizabeth Way about 100 metres from the entrance to Astro Hill.


Traffic was backed up on Niaqungusiariaq Road all the way up to Joamie School for approximately 90 minutes while city workers removed the pole, broken in two places, with heavy equipment. The crew also filled-in the hole left behind.


The intersection is the site of Iqaluit’s first controlled

crosswalk

, which was installed in fall 2024.

author: Alison Avigayil Ramer
title: After October 7, I learned that movements need grief spaces
content:
This article

After October 7, I learned that movements need grief spaces

 was originally published by

Waging Nonviolence

.


Since the massacres on Oct. 7, now three years ago, the news has brought a steady stream of horror and broken promises. The ceasefire in Gaza has been broken thousands of times; the ceasefire with Iran only holds until the next strike. Many of us have responded by going numb or turning away. Over these three years, I’ve come to believe that collective mourning can help movements build sturdier organizing infrastructure, move through paralysis and numbness, and get back to the long-term work of creating systemic change.


I’ve spent nearly two decades living and working as a human rights defender, mostly in Palestine and Israel. For years, I responded to atrocities the way much of the dominant organizing culture did at the time: strategically. I prepared statements, launched campaigns and mobilized our base. I worked through several wars and the ongoing ethnic cleansing and genocide. Even though my colleagues and I were often physically together, we rarely had the opportunity to collectively mourn. In fact, mourning was often seen as something only the privileged could afford. As organizers and solidarity activists, we were the ones who needed to push past the pain and keep mobilizing.


And then, after each war, large swaths of colleagues and organizers would burn out, and our movement would suffer a setback. Movement researchers Paul Gorski and Cher Chen, studying U.S. human rights and social justice activists, found that an estimated 50 to 60 percent of organizers eventually walk away from movement work and never return, burned out by a culture that treats overwork and self-sacrifice as necessary. That culture also leaves no room to mourn and process the secondary trauma that accumulates, hastening burnout. These kinds of cycles make it especially hard for movements seeking systemic change to sustain themselves.


Sign Up for our Newsletter


We’ll send you a weekly email with the latest articles.


When Hamas attacked Israel in October 2023 and I was waiting in anticipation of the retaliation against Gaza, I knew I couldn’t respond with the same kind of organizing strategy that we usually use: preparation of advocacy statements, social media campaigns and fundraising appeals. I knew that while some people should and would continue that work, there also needed to be spaces for organizers and our base to mourn. And so, on Oct. 8, I opened a space for collective mourning online, sharing it in the many community, political and religious groups I was a part of, for anyone who needed somewhere to process what they were witnessing and feeling. Dozens of people joined: primarily my Jewish community at first, and then people from many faiths and chapters of my life, from Palestine to Palo Alto. 


As the assault on Gaza and the genocide continued, the room stayed open. More colleagues, including community organizers, artists, chaplains and psychologists, joined me in facilitating, and we held space for hundreds of people from across our communities to mourn together. We formed a collective called the

Social Change Sanctuary

 and developed a format that included facilitation and participation from attendees. Over time, we were invited to hold spaces for other communities in mourning. We’ve held spaces to grieve the ongoing genocide; climate catastrophes like the fires in Los Angeles; ICE raids, arrests and murders; and the war on Iran.


The Social Change Sanctuary hosts an Interdependence Day circle in 2025. (Alison Avigayil Ramer)


Participants repeatedly shared the difference it made in their lives to know they had a consistent space to mourn.


“In daily life, when something hurts, I turn away, I distract myself,” one participant told us. “But the collective mourning practice helped me move through the frozenness that constant news induced — helped me stop doomscrolling — and I’m able to return to my work.”


That participant went on to organize her community and raised $20,000 for refugees in Gaza. 


Another participant returned to their role as a chaplain, and extended her work to include “movement chaplaincy” holding one-on-one spaces for people doing solidarity work. 


Many participants also shared how witnessing the news with others enabled them to feel the emotions provoked by the headlines, leaving them feeling less isolated and more connected. That is co-regulation happening at …

author: Admin101
title: ATX Solidarity Network is Fighting Wage Theft, La Migra, and Apathy
content:
AK, a founding member of ATX Solidarity Network, discusses their experience organizing immigrant workers to confront wage theft and other issues in right-to-work Texas.


Increased ICE enforcement has raised fears about fighting back, turning many to seek services in a field dominated by


nonprofits. In this interview we explore the tensions organizing for direct action amid these conditions.


Black Rose/Rosa Negra (BRRN): We understand that you all in Austin, Texas have begun to build a solidarity network. What is that? How is it structured?


AK:

 A solidarity network is basically made up of workers and tenants from all over the city (or, in some cases, parts of a city) who have or may have issues with their bosses and landlords. Instead of organizing with our immediate coworkers or neighbors, we are individuals from different workplaces and living in different areas of town who fight for each other where we are at. Solidarity networks are meant to fill the void where workplace unions and tenant unions don’t exist. Since Texas is a “right to work” state, capital strategically undermines workers from building fighting organizations like unions. Solidarity networks are flexible enough to meet one or a few workers at one workplace or tenants at a complex, and temporarily bypass the immediate need for longstanding organizations.  


When you meet someone with a workplace or tenant issue, the whole solidarity network takes on the demands of the case, with those with the grievance–the issue(s) they want to fight around that directly affects them–being core organizers of their own campaign. We use direct action tactics, which means we don’t go through the courts or ask the cops or nonprofits to take care of the situation for us; we rely on just us to get the demand met by putting pressure on the boss or landlord until it becomes so unbearable they have no choice but to give in.


Like most solidarity networks there is a small group of core organizers who respond to the day- to-day needs of the organization. The people with the demands must be a part of this group. Then, there is a larger membership which is involved in many of the functions of the organization, but not all of its functions. They may pass out flyers with us, make phone calls, or research campaign targets, for example. Then there is a much larger network of people who will come out to actions when called on.


BRRN: Walk us through how you started it. Why this kind of organization, and what kinds of fights do you take on?


AK:

 Our specific solidarity network wanted to take on wage theft campaigns as our main, but not exclusive, area of struggle. We began working with another organization here that works in immigrant communities around stopping deportations. They were getting a lot of calls about wage theft, and helped us start the solidarity network to meet this need. Most of our initial calls came directly from them, and our first campaign came out of one of these calls. We also understand that the immigrant community, especially here in Texas, is very vulnerable to wage theft, and they often feel they do not have a lot of options for getting back stolen wages. We want to change that! Eventually, we want to create a citywide network of people who can respond to wage theft grievances, and other workplace and housing issues. We want to make bosses and landlords scared to even think about messing with us! 


In ATX, we have a small and unorganized left with a larger activist scene. A solidarity network is one form of organization that can work well under these conditions because you really only need a handful of core organizers and access to lots of people to show up to actions. We also see this form of organization being one in which committed leftists can develop relationships with other members of the working class. We see a lot of the left in ATX being very insular and removed from other everyday people. We feel it is important to be organizing in working-class communities since it is us as a class that are capable of transforming society. 


We also want to help normalize direct action tactics to push our collective ability to struggle even further. Ultimately, we would like to see more working-class organizations in our neighborhoods, workplaces, schools, and more. The solidarity network isn’t meant to be

the form

 of organization for widespread worker rebellion, but it is one form of organization that can respond to specific conditions that …

author: Valerie Anne
title: Horror Comedy ‘The Blood Countess’ Imagines Elizabeth Báthory as a Lesbian Vampire
content:
If I had a nickel for every piece of queer media about 17th century Hungarian countess Elizabeth Báthory released this year, I’d have two nickels. Which isn’t a lot, but it’s weird that it happened twice. After her strange appearance in Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, she also appears in the vampire horror comedy The Blood Countess directed and co-written by lesbian filmmaker Ulrike Ottinger. In the film, Báthory (played by Isabelle Huppert) wakes from a long slumber and finds herself in modern-day Vienna, searching for a book that could cure her vampirism.

I find two things interesting about the fact that the countess has appeared in two queer adaptations this year. The first is that Lizzie Borden actually never really portrayed her as a lesbian, even though she was set up parallel to Lizzie and lesbian serial killer Aileen Wuornos and was played by the same actress who played Lizzie’s lover. Before the much-later rumors that Elizabeth Báthory bathed in the blood of virgin girls, the crimes she was accused of were more along the lines of torture and cannibalism. So it’s interesting that was then interpreted as lesbianism. Then again, she was luring young women to her castle with three of her closest gal pals, so, who knows I guess. It is just fascinating to me that despite the fact that she has been in folklore for centuries, no new media has come out about her in years, and now these two instances pop up in the same year. Three, if you count the experimental film Báthory by Carlos Atanes. Something seems to be in the (bloody) water.

Unfortunately, it seems like perhaps The Blood Countess isn’t quite as gay as it could be. Then again, apparently Ottinger wrote the screenplay in 1998, almost 30 years ago, so that could potentially account for that. But still, I won’t say no to a lesbian vampire film so I’ll probably still check it out when it makes its North American theatrical release in spring 2027.

author: Taina Da Silva
title: Near Grassy Narrows, an Elder shows us how using the land also protects it
content:
Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich’s Land Back Garden on the outskirts of the Grassy Narrows First Nation. Photo by Taina Da Silva


I’m thinking about the power of my treaty rights as I drive to meet with Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich — Roberta Keesick — on a late summer day on the outskirts of Grassy Narrows.


Gwawich is an activist and trapper who has substantial experience of being on the land and creating land-based learning systems for our community. She grew up in our territory with a traditional Anishinaabek family, and she works to restore our traditional ways. 


As I pull into the site, Gwawich offers me some ripe vegetables — a squash, green beans and tomatoes — that she’s harvested from an extensive garden nearby. 


Gwawich and I are ten minutes outside of the reserve line of Grassy Narrows First Nation, a small and semi-remote community in northwestern Ontario. We sit at an off-grid campsite and community garden which Gwawich started by herself to host her Seven Grandfathers Teachings Program.


The Seven Grandfather Teachings — love, respect, bravery, truth, honesty, humility, and wisdom — are what Gwawich’s social program follows, and she hopes her program will impact Grassy in a way that will bring us Anishinaabek back to the land and culture. 


“Colonization has changed our ways of thinking,” she says. 


A lake in the traditional homelands of Grassy Narrows First Nation. Photo by Taina Da Silva


As the lake glistens in the background, Gwawich talks about how she is determined to decolonize our community from decades of learned behaviour — stemming from the reserve system that relocated people in our community, to the residential “school” system and

devastating mercury pollution

, which have all been an upheaval to our traditional ways.


Her campsite is available for any band members who want to get away from the reserve, and the garden is another free resource where members are often invited to pick fresh food.


“Land Back Garden” is painted on a wooden sign and it sits front-and-centre of the garden. Another sign near the campsite greets visitors to the “Seven Grandfather Teachings Program — Land Based Family Healing Initiative.”

This program is how families from Grassy are now able to access different opportunities designed to bring land based learning to the community, and it is what our aboriginal land title permits us to do in our territories. 


Anishinaabe Elder Gwawich’s program is helping Grassy Narrows members return to their traditional ways. Photo by Taina Da Silva


What started as a community-wide gardening initiative in 2020 has grown into the off-grid garden and campsite, a monthly food program in the community, and a small sewing building right in the reserve — all operating through outside funding.


Children from the reserve are able to experience what it might have been like for the older generations to gather traditionally, share food, and play games like the old days — and with some contemporary additions.


Today, there are community events with bungee trampolines, rock climbing, horse rides and even a zipline, Gwawich tells me with true pride. 


Gwawich speaks excitedly about a farmers’ market coming up, where she will be taking vegetables from the Land Back Garden to give away to Grassy families. 


She reminds me that “being out on the land makes our rights stronger,” and that running the site is a way to protect the land — and our rights under Treaty 3.


This is an area of land which I mistakenly used to associate as a settler hunting camp on so-called “Crown land,” before I learned about traditional land use areas and our history of ancient rock paintings, burial grounds and artifacts found across our territory. 


It takes community members like Gwawich to figure out ways to navigate the colonial systems that have been imposed on us, and decolonize our ways of thinking.


Gwawich remembers a time when the entirety of Grassy Narrows spoke our language and lived off trapping and fishing incomes when she was a child in the 1960s and 70s. 


“Even my siblings were helping with trapping and fishing when they were nine and ten years old,” she said, and we laughed at the idea of that happening now — because that is a lost tradition for Anishinaabek families.


Residential “schools” — an intentional violation of our human rights — and the resulting language and culture loss are not easily forgotten about in our communities. Repairing the losses and devastation is not a simple …

author: Chad Nelson
title: နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေရဲ့ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူတွေအပေါ် တိုက်ခိုက်မှုဟာ တကယ်တော့ အာရုံလွှဲတာပါပဲ
content:
Chad Nelson

.

The Political Class’s War on Immigrants is a Diversion

, January 30, 2015. Translated into Burmese by Hein Htet Kyaw.


ဂျန်နဝါရီ ၂၈ ရက်နေ့မှာ လော်ရက်တာ လင်းချ် (Loretta Lynch) ကို အစိုးရရှေ့နေချုပ် အဖြစ် ခန့်အပ်ဖို့ အမေရိကန် ဆီးနက်စစ်ဆေးမေးမြန်းခြင်း စတင်ချိန်မှာ၊ ရီပတ်ဘလစ်ကန်တွေဟာ အစိုးရက “တရားမဝင် ခိုးဝင်သူတွေ” လို့ သတ်မှတ်ထားတဲ့ လူတန်းစားအပေါ် သူမ ဘယ်လောက်အထိ အလိုက်သင့် ပေါင်းသင်းမလဲဆိုတာ မေးဖို့ အရမ်းစိတ်အားထက်သန်နေကြတာပါ။ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူတွေအပေါ် တင်းကြပ်တဲ့ ဂျက်ဖ် ဆက်ရှင်နိစ် (Jeff Sessions – R-AL) နဲ့ အပြန်အလှန် မေးမြန်းမှုတစ်ခုမှာ၊ ဆက်ရှင်နိစ်က အမေရိကမှာ အလုပ်လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့် ဘယ်သူ့မှာ ရှိလဲဆိုတာ လင်းချ် ဘယ်လိုယုံကြည်လဲ မေးခဲ့ပါတယ်။ သီးသန့်အနေနဲ့ပြောရရင်၊ “ဘယ်သူက ပိုပြီး လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့်ရှိသလဲ – တရားဝင်လာတဲ့ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူလား၊ နိုင်ငံသားလား၊ ဒါမှမဟုတ် တိုင်းပြည်ထဲ တရားမဝင် ဝင်လာတဲ့သူလား” လို့ သူက မေးခဲ့တာပါ။ လင်းချ်ကတော့ ဆက်ရှင်နိစ်ရဲ့ မေးခွန်းအတုအယောင်ကို လိမ္မာပါးနပ်စွာ ရှောင်လွှဲခဲ့ပြီး၊ လူတစ်ယောက်ဟာ ဒီမှာ တရားမဝင် ရှိနေရင်တောင် အမေရိကရဲ့ လုပ်သားအင်အားထဲမှာ ပါဝင်သူတစ်ယောက်အနေနဲ့ ရှိနေတာကိုပဲ ပိုသဘောကျတယ်လို့ ပြန်ဖြေခဲ့ပါတယ်။


ဆက်ရှင်နိစ်ရဲ့ မေးခွန်းထုတ်ပုံနည်းလမ်းနဲ့ သူလိုချင်နေတဲ့ အဖြေ ဟာ နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေရဲ့ လိမ်ညီနေတဲ့ အတွေးအခေါ်ကို အများကြီး ဖော်ပြနေပါတယ်။ ဝါရှင်တန်က နှစ်ပါတီစလုံးမှာပါတဲ့ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူတွေကို တိုက်ခိုက်တဲ့အုပ်စုက ရှယ်လ်ဒွန် ရစ်ချ်မန်း (Sheldon Richman) မှတ်ချက်ပြုသလိုပဲ “အလုပ်လုပ်ခွင့် ပေးပိုင်ခွင့်ဆိုတာ သူတို့ပေးမှ ရတာ” လို့ ယုံကြည်ထားကြတာပါ။ ဝမ်းနည်းစရာက အဲဒီယုံကြည်ချက်ဟာ ဒီတိုင်းပြည်ရဲ့ ဥပဒေဖြစ်နေတာပါပဲ။ ဒီနေ့ခေတ်မှာ ဘယ်သူအလုပ်လုပ်ခွင့်ရှိလဲဆိုတဲ့ မေးခွန်းကို ဝါရှင်တန်က ဗျူရိုကရက်တွေနဲ့ သူတို့ဆီကနေ လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့် လက်ဝါးကြီးအုပ်ခွင့် လာဝယ်နေတဲ့ အကျိုးစီးပွားကာကွယ်ရေး အုပ်စုတွေကပဲ အဓိက ဆုံးဖြတ်နေကြတာပါ။ မင်းအနေနဲ့ ကိုယ်ကြိုက်တဲ့ အလုပ်ကို လွတ်လပ်စွာ လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့်ရှိတယ်လို့ ထင်ချင်ထင်နေလိမ့်မယ်၊ ဒါပေမဲ့ အစိုးရက စည်းကမ်းချက်တွေ အမျိုးမျိုး ထုတ်ပြန်ပြီး မင်းရဲ့ ရွေးချယ်ခွင့်တွေကို အများကြီး ကျဉ်းမြောင်းအောင် လုပ်ပစ်လိုက်တာပါ။ အဲဒီအတားအဆီးတွေကို ကျော်လွှားနိုင်ခဲ့ရင်တောင် အစိုးရ သတ်မှတ်ထားတဲ့ စည်းမျဉ်းစည်းကမ်း နွံထဲမှာ ရုန်းကန်နေရတာနဲ့တင် မင်းရဲ့ ကျွမ်းကျင်မှုကို အပြည့်အဝ ထုတ်မသုံးနိုင်တော့ဘဲ ဖြစ်နေရပါတယ်။


နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေဟာ သူတို့ရဲ့ ပြည်သူတွေအပေါ် လွှမ်းမိုးချုပ်ကိုင်ထားနိုင်ဖို့ ဒီလိုမျိုး အရမ်းအရေးပါတဲ့ လုပ်ပိုင်ခွင့်ကို မှီခိုနေကြတာပါ။ ပြည်သူတွေကို အလုပ်လုပ်ခွင့် ပေးပိုင်ခွင့်ရှိနေတာ၊ နဲ့ အဲဒီခွင့်ပြုချက်နဲ့အတူ ပါလာတဲ့ စည်းကမ်းသတ်မှတ်ချက်တွေ အားလုံးက ကပ်ပါး နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေကို သူတို့အိတ်ကပ်ထဲ အထိရောက်ဆုံး နည်းလမ်းနဲ့ ပိုက်ဆံထည့်နိုင်အောင် ကူညီပေးထားပါတယ်။ အလုပ်တစ်ခုဟာ တရားမဝင် ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူရဲ့ အလုပ်ဖြစ်ဖြစ်၊ အမေရိကန် မှောင်ခိုဈေးကွက်က အလုပ်သမားရဲ့ အလုပ်ဖြစ်ဖြစ် စည်းမျဉ်းမရှိတဲ့ ဈေးကွက်တွေဆီ လမ်းကြောင်းပြောင်းသွားရင် နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေအနေနဲ့ အဲဒါကို စောင့်ကြည့်ဖို့နဲ့ ဆက်ကြေးတောင်းဖို့ ခက်သွားပါတယ်။ သူတို့ရဲ့ ရှုပ်ထွေးလှတဲ့ အခွန်၊ လုပ်အား၊ နဲ့ အုပ်ချုပ်ရေး ဥပဒေတွေကို မလိုက်နာရင်၊ သက်ဆိုင်ရာ အသက်မွေးဝမ်းကျောင်း လုပ်ငန်းတစ်ခုလုံးပေါ်မှာ လိုင်စင်စနစ်တွေ အထပ်ထပ် တင်ထားတာကို မလိုက်နာရင် မင်းရဲ့ အသက်မွေးဝမ်းကျောင်းလုပ်ငန်းပါ ရုတ်တရက် ဖျက်ဆီးခံရနိုင်ခြေ ရှိပါတယ်။ ဒီစနစ်တစ်ခုလုံးကို ထုတ်လုပ်သူတွေနဲ့ စားသုံးသူတွေကို ကာကွယ်ပေးနေပါတယ်ဆိုပြီး အတုအယောင် လိမ်ညာရောင်းချထားတာပါ။


တရားမဝင် ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချမှု သက်သက်က ဗျူရိုကရက်တွေကို ခြိမ်းခြောက်နေတာ မဟုတ်ပါဘူး။ သူတို့ အမှန်တကယ် ကြောက်တာက ထိန်းချုပ်မထားတဲ့ ရွှေ့ပြောင်းလုပ်သားတွေဆီကရတဲ့ ဝင်ငွေလမ်းကြောင်းတွေကို ချုပ်ကိုင်ခွင့် ဆုံးရှုံးသွားမှာကိုပါ။ ဆက်ရှင်နိစ်နဲ့ ကွန်ဂရက်ထဲက သူ့လို နယ်စပ်စောင့် စိစစ်ရေးသမားတွေဟာ သူတို့ကြောက်ရွံ့မှုကို “ငါတို့ နဲ့ သူတို့” ဆိုတဲ့ စကားလုံးတွေနဲ့ ဖုံးကွယ်ပြီး ရေးကြီးခွင်ကျယ် စကားလုံးအလှတွေ သုံးနေကြတာပါ၊ ဒါဟာ အရေးပါတဲ့ နိုင်ငံရေး ရည်ရွယ်ချက်အတွက် ပြုလုပ်ထားတဲ့ ပြဇာတ်တစ်ခုပါပဲ။ ဒီလို လှည့်ကွက်မျိုးနဲ့ နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေက မင်းတို့ကို လှည့်စားထားတာပါ။ သူတို့ ကြောက်နေတာဟာ အခွန်ဘဏ္ဍာ ဆုံးရှုံးမှာကို မဟုတ်ဘဲ၊ “မင်းတို့ရဲ့” အလုပ်တွေ၊ “မင်းတို့ရဲ့” ကျန်းမာရေးစောင့်ရှောက်ခွင့်တွေ၊ နဲ့ “မင်းတို့ရဲ့” လူမှုဖူလုံရေးတွေ ဆုံးရှုံးမှာကို ကြောက်နေရတာပါဆိုပြီး ယုံအောင် လှည့်စားထားတာပါ။ တရားဝင် ရှိနေပြီး အလုပ်လုပ်နေသူတွေ (အခွန်ဆောင်နေသူတွေ) ကိုတော့ မျိုးချစ်စိတ်ရှိသူတွေအဖြစ် သတ်မှတ်ပေးထားပါတယ်။ အစိုးရက သူတို့ရဲ့ လစာထဲက ဖြတ်တောက်ယူနေတာကို မုန်းတီးစရာလို့ မမြင်ဘဲ အားလုံးရဲ့ ကောင်းဖက်အတွက် အရေးပါတဲ့ ပါဝင်ဆောင်ရွက်မှုအဖြစ် ကြိုဆိုကြရပါတယ်။ ခွင့်ပြုချက်မရှိဘဲ အလုပ်လုပ်သူတွေကိုတော့ ရန်သူတွေ၊ တရားဝင် အလုပ်လုပ်နေသူတွေရဲ့ မွန်မြတ်တဲ့ အလုပ်ကို ဖျက်ဆီးနေသူတွေအဖြစ် ပုံဖော်ကြပါတယ်။ “မင်းတို့” က လူကောင်း၊ “သူတို့” က လူဆိုး ပေါ့။ နိုင်ငံရေးအရ အင်အားမရှိတဲ့ တရားမဝင် ရွှေ့ပြောင်းအခြေချသူတွေဟာ ဝါရှင်တန်အတွက် တိုက်ခိုက်ရ အလွယ်ဆုံး ပစ်မှတ်ဖြစ်နေပြီး နိုင်ငံရေးသမားတွေရဲ့ စိတ်ကူးယဉ် ပြဿနာရှာမှုတွေအတွက် လွယ်လွယ်ကူကူ …

author: Elizabeth Weill-Greenberg
title: Activists Are Pushing Cities and Companies to Cancel Parking Contracts With ICE
content:
The Trump administration’s abduction and deportation machine is multifaceted. There are clear-cut components — agents, shackles, and jails — and less obvious, although no less essential, ones — cars and parking spaces.


In an effort to impede the attacks on immigrants, mayors of some of the country’s largest cities, including

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani

,

Chicago Mayor Brandon Johnson

, and

Boston Mayor Michelle Wu

, have issued executive orders

banning Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)

 from using city-owned parking lots and properties.


But even in cities where mayors have banned ICE from using government-owned properties, ICE still has free reign to contract with private companies. After the federal agency

posted a notice

 seeking “Surge Parking” in 14 cities, including Boston, Wu

released a public letter

 to

local parking garage and lot owners

, warning them that if ICE were “to procure such resources, it would constitute an unprovoked and unwarranted escalation, creating potentially significant risks to public safety and halting economic activity across our entire region.”


“Today, I ask you to join us: Reject any proposition by ICE to facilitate an attack on the people of Boston,”

she wrote

. “In the face of escalating attacks on cities across the country, we have repeatedly seen that the strongest defense is solidarity.”


In the Boston suburb of Burlington, Massachusetts, Bearing Witness New England has been holding weekly protests outside ICE’s Boston Field Office, where people are

held for days

 in inhumane conditions. Activists say ICE has been keeping its vehicles in a nearby parking lot owned by local developer National Development.


According to a report by

NPR

 affiliate

WBUR

, the company sent a letter to local activists in February, stating that ICE vehicles were being “improperly parked” in its parking spaces, and that it had “reached an arrangement with ICE that they would no longer park their vehicles on our property.”


However, the company also said that the government agency, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), has

rights to use the garage

 and the company does not have authority over how the FAA parcels out parking spaces to other federal agencies, according to

WBUR

’s report.


Nathan Phillips, a Boston University professor who organizes with the Burlington-area coalition

Building Up Resilience Networks (B.U.R.N.)

, says ICE has continued to park in sections of lots National Development leases to the FAA that exceed what the lease allows.


Protests that target parking garages are “throwing sand in the gears” of ICE’s deportation and abduction machine, he says.


“So much of their operation depends on logistics of transport and travel,” Phillips told

Truthout

. “It’s human trafficking, and so if we can go after the trafficking, the means by which they’re doing this, that can have a really effective impact.”


The Appeal in Your Inbox


Subscribe to our newsletters for regular updates, analysis and context straight to your email.


          Sign Up


Fellow B.U.R.N. activist Josh Model says National Development’s recent actions contradict its public image as a

philanthropic company

 committed to improving communities.


“National Development Corporation, which, as a local developer, likes to promote that they’re cognizant of community needs and give to charity and all these nice things,” but they’re “letting ICE stage kidnappings” from their property, said Model.


While the government spending website,

usaspending.gov

, only lists 12 active contracts for parking spaces, as of September 28, the true number of parking lots that ICE uses is likely much higher, said Model. It’s difficult to untangle where ICE is parking, in part, because many of the contracts are not with ICE, but through another federal agency, the

General Services Administration

 (GSA), he said. The GSA manages government buildings and real estate, and owns or leases space in more than 8,300 buildings, according to an

explainer

 on the agency published by the Congressional Research Service.


In the case of National Development, ICE is using parking leased by the GSA for the FAA, according to Model.

PPA website

 states that, among other responsibilities, it coordinates “the efforts of public agencies concerning parking” and establishes and operates public …
