author: Brian Hioe
title: What Did China Intend to Accomplish Through Surveilling Lai Ching-te’s Son?
content:
THE FBI HAS arrested a woman, Wanying “Heather” Zhang, for acting as an unregistered foreign agent of China. In particular, Zhang’s arrest occurred because she was apparently conducting surveillance on Lai Ting-yu, the son of President Lai Ching-te.

Lai’s family generally keeps a low public profile. Lai, who is in his 30s, is thought to work for electronics manufacturer Philips and to have a young child. Zhang is accused of traveling to Seattle from Los Angeles and renting a vehicle to surveil Lai’s home along with an accomplice.

Zhang is accused of being in contact with a Chinese handler through WeChat, as well as other individuals she knew were Chinese government officials. Zhang worked as a real estate agent and was detained as she was about to board a flight for Shanghai. It is possible, then, that Zhang could be a civilian recruited by China, or that the Chinese government has continued with its practice of employing “disposable” agents.

It is unclear what China hoped to gain from surveilling Lai, who was not likely to have any sensitive government information. Nevertheless, one aim could be to threaten, by putting Lai and his family members living abroad on edge, and to warn of the potential repercussions of going against China. If China wished to broadcast that it was aware of Lai Ting-yu’s whereabouts and could potentially threaten him, this could be used for leverage over Lai, or to blackmail him. China might also seek to project power, in suggesting that it is omnipresent and all-reaching, such that it can surveil and threaten relatives of Taiwanese politicians abroad.

Otherwise, it is possible that China aimed to obtain political ammo from surveilling Lai’s son. The presence of Lai’s son in the US, for example, could be used to suggest that Lai himself may push for strengthening defense against China, but that his own children live in the US, and that Lai would potentially abandon Taiwan in wartime.

Indeed, even if the daughter of Chinese President Xi Jinping is also thought to live in the US, the presence of Lai’s children in the US has been used as a political attack for some time by the KMT. More generally, Taiwanese politicians who have children in the US, or who may have potentially held Green Cards or US passports in the past, have been used to attack them with the allegation that they plan to abandon Taiwan in wartime.

More generally, one notes that the Chinese government has been increasingly willing to target relatives of Taiwanese politicians. DPP legislator Puma Shen’s father has been sanctioned, for example, due to owning a car parts company in China. It is possible that there are other cases in which relatives of Taiwanese politicians have already been threatened, but which have not necessarily come to light.

author: John Mullen
title: France: Workers mobilise to support inspiring school student revolt
content:
There were vibrant mass demonstrations in dozens of French towns, on October 6, as five of the nation's six main trade union confederations mobilised in support of the escalating school student movement.

Entering its third week, the historic uprising against years of cuts in school budgets continues to gain momentum in the face of brutal police violence and state panic.

The movement has involved far more high schools than the last comparable movement eight years back. More than 1000 high schools (for 15 to 18-year-olds) and more than 100 middle schools (for 11 to 15-year-olds) have been blockaded.

Thirty universities have joined the movement in the past few days.

Daily student mass meetings in every establishment decide on the day’s actions. On the demonstrations you can see thousands of home-made placards with imaginative slogans. They range from quoting the 1793 Declaration of the Rights of Man (on the duty of insurrection) to quoting popular rap artists; from “Generation X, Generation Z, one struggle!” to “The 6-7 generation is aiming at 68” (referring to the uprising of May-June 1968).

Desperate to extinguish the flames of revolt, authorities resorted to mass lockouts, preemptively closing hundreds of schools and several university campuses this week.

Macron’s minority government, eager to pass its austerity budget before the end of the year, has reacted in three ways:

First, with violence and intimidation. In the hope of scaring away as many young protesters as possible, they ensured that the police repression was extreme. A couple of hundred teenagers have been injured by cops, and some of the examples are heartbreaking.

In the Paris region, an officer fired a tear gas canister point-blank into the face of a 14-year-old boy, shattering his jaw in two places and knocking out all his teeth; his family is now suing for attempted murder. In Tours, a 16-year-old lost an eye to a rubber bullet fired directly at him — on video, police can be heard boasting about blinding protesters.

Elsewhere, multiple students suffered severe eye injuries. A viral video captured an officer pinning a young girl in a violent chokehold, while in Lens, a bystander schoolchild lost a hand to an exploding crowd-dispersal grenade (he did not “pick it up” as the media have claimed).

In a further attempt to intimidate, more than 5000 young people have been arrested — only 1800 were subsequently charged with an offence. Even now, the government refuses to rein in the police thugs. Interior minister Laurent Nuñez spoke on October 6 of “supposed excesses” in police action, while former minister Bruno Retailleau demanded loudly that the age of criminal responsibility be lowered.

Secondly, the government has offered tiny concessions, which are only cosmetic. Proposals to hike some higher education tuition fees were abruptly shelved, and school student union leaders have been invited to talks with the education minister. The regime has also launched a token online portal for grievances and they have scheduled managed "consultation sessions" in all schools for the end of the week.

Finally, a propaganda offensive is trying to paint the young people as manipulated by the radical left organisation la France Insoumise (France in Revolt, FI). The old lie of “outside agitators” is being mobilised, because the FI is playing an excellent role in the movement.

Even previously sceptical far-left commentators have written that the young protestors consider the FI to be their party. Its leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon insisted that FI Members of Parliament and local elected councillors position themselves between the police and students to help protect them. All of them were present and vocal in denouncing police violence.

In parliament, Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said one could not speak of “police violence” and complained that the FI “were implying that the police forces of the Republic … were racist”!

School student leaders are not fooled by the cosmetic concessions, and are showing their confidence by announcing a new day of action, only two days after the previous one. Trade union leaders could learn from the youngsters, but are dragging their feet, suggesting a strike in November.

The establishment media are working hard at slandering the movement and twisting the truth.

Media watchdog, Acrimed, measured the time spent discussing the events on the prime-time national public news channel, France 2, this week. It found that 75% of the time …

author: Lance Selfa
title: What’s up with Jacobin’s “Working-Class Win-o-Meter”?
content:
Every few months, 

Jacobin 

magazine announces what it purports to be a secret to win working-class voters based on a finding from its associated Center for Working Class Politics (CWCP). Its 14 September editorial “

Report: The Working Class Vote is Not Lost

” was the latest in this series.

CWCP’s latest innovation is the “Working-Class Win-o-Meter”, which Jacobin describes as “a data-driven road map for winning back working-class voters”. It purports to demonstrate the optimal combination of social and political appeals to move working-class voters to vote for a hypothetical Democratic candidate.

Two points should be made at the outset. When

 Jacobin

 and CWCP talk about “winning working class voters,” they don’t mean winning the working class to socialism. They mean “winning” the working class to vote for Democrats. And they define the “working class” as non-college-educated people with family incomes of between $30,000 and $150,000.

This supposedly groundbreaking survey and analysis is an exercise in political message-testing for Democratic candidates. It uses the definition of “working-class” that is the standard in lazy polling and media commentary, and thus adds no new insights. Attaching the labels of “socialist” and “working-class” doesn’t change the fact that what

 Jacobin

 and CWCP are engaged in is a completely conventional activity that regularly earns millions for Democratic Party consultants.

Without digressing into a long discussion of the inadequacies of the study’s understanding of class, it’s worth pondering why, under its definition, a non-college educated small business owner is “working class” but a college-educated nurse or K-12 teacher who is a union activist is not considered working-class. It’s the same sort of logic that 

had Democratic Socialists of America (DSA)-adjacent consultants and 

Jacobin

 fawning over

 working-class avatar “oyster farmer” Graham Platner as a US Senate candidate in Maine before Platner’s campaign imploded.

The study’s key findings include “lead with working-class economics” and “adopt culture and climate positions that resonate with working-class voters”. These takeaways are supposed to increase the hypothetical Democratic candidate’s support over what it calls a “Kamala Harris-2024 style Democrat.”

For working-class economics or economic populist policies, the winning positions come from a list of ordinary policies from tuition-free community college to protecting Social Security from cuts to capping prescription-drug prices. There is nothing wrong with these proposals. But they are hardly bold. In fact, many of them are the same poll-tested offerings that Democratic Party politicians have included in their campaigns for years.

The fact that they are repackaged here as keys to victory should emphasise how little the Democrats have done to implement these when they have held power in the past. And it’s noteworthy that “Medicare for All,” the signature proposal that social democrats like 

Jacobin

 and DSA have championed for more than a decade, didn’t make the list.

But what really gives the game away are the “culture and climate” positions the analysis considers

losing

 messages for Democratic politicians. For anyone who is familiar with 

Jacobin’s

 antipathy to 

“subcultural leftism”

, the losing positions won’t surprise: reducing funding for police, “abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE),” and letting “trans girls play in girls’ sports.” Other so-called “social issues,” such as defence of abortion rights, don’t significantly move the needle toward the Democrats, CWCP finds.

Mainstream Democratic Party campaigns in the midterm electoral cycle are following this script without even dialling up the “Win-o-Meter”. It’s an article of faith that serious Democratic candidates run on “kitchen-table issues” like the price of groceries and gasoline, and “don’t take the bait” by engaging with Republicans over “silly culture war” issues. Or they try to get ahead of the Republican attacks by pre-emptively jumping to the conservative side. For example, Texas U.S. Senate candidate James Talarico said he too 

opposes trans girls in girls’ sports

. As the liberal journalist 

Perry Bacon

 explained:

“‘Economic issues not cultural wars’ produces a party that both loses elections and abandons moral causes and vulnerable people. That’s not a theoretical argument—it’s the story of the Democratic Party of my entire adulthood. The …

author: @ndy
title: Yeah Nah Pasaran #300 w Emma Hagberg on ‘Comrades, Not Friends’ & The Revolutionary Front : October 8, 2026
content:
This week on Yeah Nah Pasaran! we talk to Emma Hagberg. Emma is the author of Comrades, Not Friends: The Revolutionary Front, Antifascism, and Class Struggle (PM Press/Working Class History, 2026), translated by Gabriel Kuhn and with a preface by Tomas Rothaus (both of whom have been previous guests of the show).

According to Hagberg, RF had ‘a strong collective identity, the view of fascists as class traitors, and the critique of an autonomous left that often had no place for working-class people’; Comrades was originally published in Swedish as 18.6 – Kamrater, Inte Vänner (B.E.L Publishing, 2024) and is also available in a German translation.

The Revolutionary Front (RF), 2001–2015, was the most militant organization on the left in recent Swedish history. Staunchly working class, the first generation of RF members engaged in numerous street battles with Swedish fascists. When the fascists retreated from the streets, RF attacked them in their homes. The police cracked down on the organization in 2013, raiding the apartments of several alleged members at the crack of dawn. The courts handed out prison sentences of up to six and a half years. Two years later, the organization folded.

See also : Presentation on the book about Revolutionära Fronten (Revolutionary Front) (April 13, 2025).

author: AWSM
title: Why I Won’t Vote ~ A SYMPOSIUM #1
content:
Anarchy 37, March 1964, Why I Won’t Vote

Voting : “The instrument and symbol of a freeman’s power to make a fool of himself and a wreck of his country”

The saying that ” only a fool would put a loaded gun into the hands of an idiot ” is an especially apt analogy of government. An idiot (usually well-meaning) considers himself clever enough to run the affairs of a large number of people by taking a seat in parliament. A large number of people, acting like fools, vote for his party’s policy then spend the next few years grumbling about the results. The error in approach is that the voter thinks that he will get what he voted for. If he could vote for those who in fact control the country, say the Governors of the Bank of England, the directors of the industrial corporations and those behind the ministries, the illusion of democracy would be more understandable.

The real centres of power lie far beyond the people’s influence at elections. These remain constant whatever Party is ” in power “. In the terms of centralised ” democracy ” the only possible argument to justify voting is that marginal benefits may be gained. The state only incidentally attends to the well-being of its subjects. Its main concern is its power relation to other states, of which the most perfect expression is in war.

I am on the side of people anywhere who are prepared neither to live nor die for something that in the long run can only militate against survival and the conditions that make life worth living. Our immediate action must, by its nature, be to oppose that pathetic gesture, voting. It must be direct and direction. We can learn to live as free men and women only by organising against the condition we are in.

The Tenants Association, Consumers Association, and Direct Action in industry all provide opportunities for people to experience directing their own lives in positive ways towards positive ends.

Only by direct involvement in society can the individual hope to transform himself and his world. Freedom cannot be given, it must be taken; and the free society can only grow from experiments in the problems (ethical and organisational) of community.

Voting does not, and cannot, mean government by consent. By voting, one acts on the assumptions that certain men are fit to govern, and that a majority is necessarily right. Also should the state, acting in the name of a (frequently fictitious) majority, declare war, the individual loses the right to live, if he ever had it.

To me, voting is complicity with the State and a negative action, therefore I do not vote.

author: Jonathan Strauss
title: Qld NTEU members rally against wage cuts
content:
More than 500 university workers, members of the National Tertiary Education Union (NTEU), struck from 11am on October 8 before rallying at Queens Gardens in the city.

They came from Magan-djin/Brisbane’s three universities: Griffith; Queensland University of Technology (QUT); and the University of Queensland (UQ). The rally was joined by students and other unionists.

Members of the NTEU branches at all three universities are bargaining on pay and conditions with their universities’ managements. The latter have made either below-inflation pay offers or none at all. Both QUT and UQ managements are trying to have the Fair Work Commission intervene on their behalf, while Griffith’s bosses are saying they will not negotiate until next year.

NTEU members repeatedly said the workers were the ones creating the valuable things universities provide, but are being continually squeezed for money and time by management.

They contrasted this with the recent surpluses declared by UQ and QUT managements, and the spending on buildings by Griffith, including $67 million to purchase a building, opposite the rally site, that did not have the offices needed for university activities.

NTEU members said a fair pay rise would at least maintain the value of their pay against cost-of-living rises.

They are also looking to win equity in superannuation payments for casualised staff and an end to the job cuts and spiralling workloads, including among administrative, other professional and technical staff whose work underpins academics’ teaching and research.

The range of speakers from the union’s three branches — local office bearers, casually-employed activists and others — reflected the on-the-ground activism the bargaining campaigns are achieving.

This rally was larger than a similar one during bargaining four years ago, as the development of workplace organising by the union has started to take hold.

National NTEU president Alison Barnes was the lead speaker, alongside NSW Greens Senator Mehreen Faruqi and two student union representatives. Barnes noted that the cross-campus action is inspiring.

author: Yuanyi Tham
title: Mega Anthropic data centre to blight Queensland
content:
Queensland is set to become home to Australia’s largest AI data centre. Last month, Liberal National Party Premier David Crisafulli announced a landmark deal with Anthropic to develop the Western Downs Digital Park, near the town of Dalby, about 250 kilometres northwest of Brisbane. Led by Singaporean developer Zerra DC, the site will be constructed in four phases, with the first building expected to be operational next year.

The data centre will occupy 725.5 hectares, an area twice the size of New York’s Central Park. Its estimated value is $32 billion, nearly five times the 2032 Brisbane Olympics infrastructure budget.

Data centres suck up huge amounts of power, driving up energy prices and accelerating climate change. When fully constructed, electro-mechanical engineer Dr Andreas Helwig told the ABC it would use the equivalent of 25 to 30 percent of Queensland’s total energy consumption.

The data centre will run primarily on electricity generated by coal and gas, drawn from the state’s electricity grid. Greenpeace estimates that the data centre would raise the grid’s emissions by 6.6 million tonnes, the equivalent of two million extra cars on the road.

Last month, Crisafulli wrestled with the federal government and eventually won a state exemption from the requirement that data centres run on renewable energy. The exemption, Crisafulli argued, was simply “common sense”; according to him (and now the Labor cabinet), environmental protections shouldn’t get in the way of AI investment opportunities.

While workers worry about AI’s impact on their jobs, power bills and the environment, Crisafulli has never been happier. He celebrated the data centre deal as the fruits of his five-day trip to the US in early September, where he met with the CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic. On the same trip, he met with US Vice President J.D. Vance and discussed Queensland’s potential to become the next link in the American critical minerals supply chain.

Crisafulli’s MAGA meetings highlight that this data centre is a story of more than just environmental degradation and corporate greed. Attracting investment in areas like AI and critical minerals is a part of a broader mission to strengthen Australia’s alliance with the US. The data centre boom is driven in part by the AI arms race between the US and China. In this context, striking a deal with the US’s largest AI corporation is not just a step towards turning Queensland as an AI investment hub. It also further integrates the Australian and US economies, so both countries are better placed to outpace competitors in the global tech arena.

Anthropic’s new project adds to the 225 other data centres currently in development in Australia and supported by both major parties. Politicians and tech billionaires have no compunction about the impact of their actions on people or the environment, so long as they are making money and moving up the imperialist pecking order. We need a political alternative that will fight for an immediate moratorium on data centres and a socialist society where we can all have a say in the future of our lives and the planet.

author: Rachel Evans, Mark Gillespie
title: Inquest into Jesse Deacon’s shooting by NSW Police ends
content:
Jesse Deacon’s coronial inquest, which ended on October 2, heard details about the actions of NSW Police in July 2023 which led to his death.

A coronial inquest aims to establish what happened in the lead up to the death of a person, and the people involved in the incident.

Police forcibly entered the 43-year old’s home, ostensibly for a welfare check, on July 20 of that year. Jesse was kettled by three police, with one tasering him and another fatally shooting him in the back.

Judy Deacon, Jesse’s mother, represented herself and questioned the witnesses. She was supported by Leesa Topic, the mother of 22-year-old Courtney Topic, who was shot dead by police in 2015.

Deacon has led a successful campaign for health providers to supply mental health responders to replace police in mental health emergencies.

Jesse was a well-read, talented artist and musician, who struggled with “treatment resistant” schizophrenia. He had spent time in inpatient mental health facilities. A shy person, he also had an illicit drug and alcohol addiction.

In 2023, a neighbour called 000 for an ambulance after Jesse asked them for a cigarette. He had a knife and was using it to cut himself.

Three police officers, Constable Riley Avery, Sergeant Hugo James and Officer A*, arrived before the ambulance. The inquest heard that they saw blood near Jesse’s apartment, but did not discuss an approach plan. Their only attempt to communicate with Jesse was Avery asking Jesse to open the door before he kicked it in.

None of the three officers had undertaken training in how to undertake mental health call-outs.

Jesse was still holding the knife when the police intruded. Still, none of the officers attempted to deescalate the situation. Jesse became trapped between two officers.

Barrister Donna Ward, senior legal counsel assisting the coroner summarised the situation as: “Riley Avery shot a taser into Jesse’s front torso. Simultaneously, Officer A* fired into Jesse’s back, which killed him.”

It took less than eight seconds from Avery kicking Jesse’s door down, to Officer A* shooting Jesse in the back. None of the three officers took up a medical first aid kit to the unit.

Deputy state coroner David O’Neil conducted the inquest over a week in July, hearing from NDIS care workers, hospital workers and police officers, and a further week over September-October.

In the second week, the inquest heard expert medical witnesses, a General Practitioner, a boarding house manager and methadone clinic witnesses.

The Deacon family, including Jesse’s father Michael Deacon and Jesse’s sister, Lucinda Deacon, also gave testimony. An accomplished soprano singer, Lucinda had compiled photos and videos of Jesse’s life and the campaign for justice with a soundtrack “Creep” by Radiohead, covered by Avie Sheck and his mother who sang in Hindi. Lucinda finished her video statement by singing “Traum”.

Deacon and the Ward put forward their recommendations for changes to policing practices, housing and mental health to the coroner, and requested that Jesse’s case be heard in court.

If the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions and the Attorney-General agree, the case could go to trial. This has only happened twice in recent history, both times under NSW Coroner Teresa O’Sullivan.

Deacon said she wants “real changes to stop these things happening again”. She has been leading a three-year fight to replace NSW Police with trained mental health responders in cases of mental health emergencies. Some $270 million over 10 years was announced for a Virtual Mental Health Hub within NSW Ambulance and eight Mental Health Acute Assessment Teams on July 30. One hundred mental health responders will replace police in parts of NSW.

“The mental health responders program is Jesse’s legacy and will save lives,” Deacon told Green Left. “There is no justice when someone dies, but at least we have this legacy. It is only a first step and needs refining and a funding boost. We also need supported accommodation.

“Jesse’s death could have been prevented if there had been enough supported accommodation for people with schizophrenia.”

Crown counsel assisting Ward admitted to the inquiry that there was “little behind the media release” of the mental health responder program. “To date, there’s no further details of the roll-out of the new initiative to have mental health trained responders attend call outs through NSW Ambulance.”

The coroner’s report is due in the next few months …

author: Mary Ellen Murphy
title: Hospital doctors strike for wages, safe hours and public health
content:
In July, Victorian public hospital doctors voted 97 percent in favour of taking industrial action for the first time in 20 years. The reason is simple: the healthcare system is unsafe for patients and staff.

The Victorian healthcare system is in crisis. Systemic failures at every level compound one another. Limited access to primary care and community services leaves people more unwell and reliant on emergency departments for care. This results in long wait times, overcrowding and unsafe workloads.

Bed shortages, often caused by delays in discharging patients due to the lack of support services, are also an issue. For example, recent data from the Victorian Health Department shows that nineteen of 21 mental health units fail to admit acutely unwell patients from the emergency department within eight hours. This results in staff attempting to care for patients in under-resourced and unsuitable environments in which they are at greater risk of violence. The lack of suitable facilities for mental health patients and adequate staffing also contributes to the ongoing failures to meet goals for the reduction in use of restrictive interventions such as seclusion and restraint.

It is no wonder then that burnout is endemic among public hospital doctors like me working in this broken system. We are expected to be machines and cope with unsafe workloads, under-resourcing and excessive hours without complaint. The system relies on unpaid overtime, guilt and obligation to keep going.

Our industrial claims highlight the punishing hours and minimal protections Victorian doctors currently face. They include a pay rise in line with what the nurses won in 2024, better guarantees of overtime for all non-rostered hours worked, permanent employment as a default model (instead of many thousands of “junior” hospital doctors, many with over a decade of experience, being given only yearly contracts), maximum shift lengths of 12.5 hours (rather than the 14 hours commonly worked at the moment), at least four rostered days off per fortnight including two consecutive days, a maximum of four consecutive night shifts, minimum doctor-to-patient ratios for safe care and mandatory 30-minute paid rest breaks every five hours.

During the fourteen months of unsuccessful bargaining discussions, the Victorian Hospitals Industrial Association (the association of employers in the public health industry) backpedalled on its previous agreement to simplify overtime payments, arguing it would cost too much to pay doctors the hours they actually work.

It is not only at work that public hospital employees are coming under attack. Over the last few months, we have seen our regulator, AHPRA, conflate antisemitism with anti-Zionism to silence healthcare workers speaking up about Palestine, including outside of work and on social media. This violates democratic rights and sets a terrible precedent for other professions. Many healthcare workers feel particularly obliged to advocate for Palestinians based on our roles as health workers. We suffer moral injury when we are prevented from speaking out about the atrocities committed against our colleagues in Gaza and against the Palestinian people as a whole.

When confronted about the lack of a public response to this attack on our freedom of speech, the Victorian branch of the Australian Medical Association admitted it was scared to address it publicly for fear of backlash, and that the federal organisation was engaged in back-room discussions with AHPRA. This approach aligns more with a lobby organisation than a trade union.

A union’s strength comes from its members’ involvement and activity. This also protects unions when they want to speak out about political issues important to their members. There is a reason that the Australian Salaried Medical Officers Federation (the part of the Australian Medical Association that is engaged in bargaining) in New South Wales—the branch involved most recently in prolonged industrial action with an active rank and file—was the only branch of our union that put out a statement condemning the AHPRA adoption of the pro-Israel International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance definition of antisemitism.

Turning to the current campaign for a better agreement in Victoria, we have so far had multiple four-hour stop-works across different sites and services on different days. At these rallies, workers were asked to vote on whether they supported a statewide strike on 14 September. The …

author: Önder Algedik
title: COP31: A fair, not a climate summit
content:
The Pacific finally got its pre-COP meeting this week and only around 30 leaders gathered in Fiji and Tuvalu, with only five countries from outside the Pacific.

Vanuatu’s climate minister said he was hoping for more, adding that it “reflects the lack of attention and priority given to what Pacific nations consider the greatest threat to their future”.

The co-host, who did turn up, made the contradiction clear.

Australia’s energy minister Chris Bowen said in Nadi, Fiji, that “as a fossil fuel exporting nation, we can bring something different to the table”. He certainly can. Labor has approved 37 new or expanded fossil fuel projects since 2022.

The other COP31 host is preparing for Antalya in its own way. In September alone, Türkiye blocked at least 1270 X accounts, journalists and Amnesty Türkiye among them, more than in the whole of last year. Green Left itself is blocked in Türkiye: I can only read it through a virtual private network.

The COP31 host agreement, made public only last month, tells accredited participants they have a “duty” not to interfere in Türkiye’s “internal affairs”, a clause Brazil dropped for COP30.

Put the two together and the division of labour is clear. One host keeps approving the fuel. The other prepares to silence those who might object to it. This is climate politics as it actually works.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s first report in 1990 called for emissions to be cut “immediately” by more than 60%. By 2019, its sixth report found, they were 54% higher.

Last year global energy demand grew 2.7%, with oil, gas and coal all growing.

The problem, then, is not “climate change”, a phrase that turns policy into weather. The problem is a climate-changing policy — the deliberate fueling of climate change, through more and expanded coal mines, liquified natural gas terminals and 20-year gas contracts.

The system behind the deals and who pays the bill has a name — the fossil order.

COP31 is no longer a climate summit. It is a climate-changing summit and, increasingly, a climate fair. Its Action Agenda lists 10 themes, from zero waste to electrification. None names coal, oil or gas.

Its “global business partner”, Koç Holding, owns Türkiye’s oil refineries. Its “electrification partner”, Sabancı, co-owns a lignite power plant. Its “global banking partner” will run a 400-square-metre pavilion. In Antalya, the stands will be busy and the products on display will be green. An end to fossil fuels will not be up for discussion.

Asking for a “better COP” means asking for a “better fair”.

Stopping new fossil fuel projects is no longer enough; we need to start shutting down the coal, oil and gas which is being mined now.

Free public transport, the public ownership of energy and climate-friendly cities are revolutionary demands today. They do not just make new oil wells unnecessary, they empty the ones already pumping and let us begin to close mines, wells and gas lines.

The freedom to say all this out loud, in Antalya, is a challenge to the status quo.

Movements can win these demands. Australia’s High Court ruled on October 7 that the states planning bodies must consider how the burning of fossil fuels, exported from Australia, contribute to climate damage.

“We cannot dig up coal, ship it overseas, watch it drive climate change, and pretend the consequences have nothing to do with us,” said Wendy Wales, one of the retired teachers behind the campaign to get Australia to minimise all greenhouse gas emissions, including emissions produced from burning the exported coal emissions.

Wales said the court decision “has finally made a change in direction in our laws. The [planning rules] will now have to reflect the need to consider climate impacts of our scope three emissions from the coal that we export.”

The real climate summit has to be taken to the streets and wherever people dare to name the fossil order creating the climate emergency, which is devastating communities, who have had the least to do with creating problem.

[Önder Algedik is a climate researcher and activist with 350Ankara. His new book, Ya Fosil Düzen Ya Devrim (Fossil Order or Revolution), is published by İletişim this month.]

Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)

author: Vashti Fox
title: Three years of Palestine solidarity
content:
In mid-October 2023, after the first major march against Israel’s attacks on Gaza, the director of the Palestine Solidarity Campaign UK, Ben Jamal, said to his staff: “We are probably going to need to be responding to this through marches until potentially Christmas”. He was wrong. The protests did not abate. As Israel’s offensive in Gaza continued, the number of actions across the world multiplied rapidly, eventually blossoming into one of the largest and most sustained antiwar movements in generations. From the world’s largest cities to the smallest hamlets, millions of voices rose in the same chant, with the same cadence: “Free, free Palestine!” 

The numbers tell part of the story. The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data Project (ACLED), an international monitor, estimated that, in the three weeks after 7 October, some 3,700 demonstrations calling for a ceasefire and showing solidarity with Palestine took place in almost 100 countries and territories. In the first months of the genocide, most were in the Middle East and North Africa and were especially frequent in Yemen, Iran, Turkey and Morocco. In several of these countries, major government or religious institutions backed the demonstrations. 

In the West, however, governments were overwhelmingly hostile. In France, for instance, pro-Israel demonstrations were legal and encouraged. But the Macron government banned all Palestine solidarity demonstrations on 12 October, Interior Minister Gérald Darmanin determining that they were “likely to generate public disorder”. Nevertheless, on 22 October, 15,000 people took to the streets chanting “Gaza, Paris is with you!”

Two years after 7 October, ACLED provided data to SBS Australia showing 50,122 Gaza-related protests, the overwhelming majority in support of Palestinians—more than 40,000 Palestine solidarity events took place between 7 October 2023 and 5 September 2025. In contrast, just 3,120 pro-Israel demonstrations took place, more than two-thirds of them (2,159) held in Israel. 

What was striking about these actions was not simply their geographic breadth but their regularity. While the movement against the Iraq war in 2003 organised the largest single set of coordinated antiwar demonstrations in history, attracting an estimated 12 to 14 million people on 14 and 15 February, it did not sustain such mass mobilisations. The Palestine solidarity movement, by contrast, mobilised consistently over three years. London, for example, hosted the largest demonstrations in the UK, with 100,000 on 21 October, 70,000 on 28 October, 30,000 on 4 November, and 300,000 on 11 November 2003. Then, in 2024, 400,000 attended a demonstration on 9 March, followed by 200,000 again in March, April and October. 

Israel is a major participant in US-dominated imperial capitalist networks, and governments across the world (of all political colours) have been reluctant to break economically, politically or even symbolically from the Israeli-US coalition. Mass mobilisations, regardless of how mass and how determined they are, are unlikely on their own to force a government to break these relationships, especially in this new era of intensifying imperial competition. The stakes are simply too high. 

Nevertheless, the Palestine demonstrations were important for several reasons. They aimed not just to express moral outrage at Israel’s brutality but also to push their own governments for a change of policy. The demonstrations first demanded (with many local specificities) a ceasefire, and then, the longer the genocide continued, that their own governments break militarily, economically and diplomatically from Israel itself. 

Furthermore, the size and consistency of the demonstrations forced the issue of Gaza into the public debate. Governments responded differently to these protest movements, but most Western countries (with the notable exception of the USA) eventually backed the call for a ceasefire. (Of course, it was too late to stop the murder of tens of thousands of Gazans.). Some European governments, such as Spain and Ireland, moved more significantly in the direction of breaking ties with Israel, while others enacted more symbolic changes such as the recognition of Palestine and increased measures against Israeli settlements in the West Bank. None of these stances was anywhere near enough, but they likely would not have happened without the protest movement.

While protest movements’ impact on governments matters, the …

author: Pip Hinman
title: High Court’s landmark climate ruling counts true cost of coal
content:
The High Court of Australia ruled on October 7 that the New South Wales Independent Planning Commission (IPC) must consider how the burning of fossil fuels, exported from this country, contributed to climate damage.

It upheld an earlier unanimous NSW Court of Appeal ruling that the expansion approval of MACH Energy’s open-cut thermal coal at Mount Pleasant was invalid.

The Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMS HEG), from the Upper Hunter Valley, had battled for four years over the coal mine’s expansion.

Climate activists believe this is a landmark judgement. Judging from the negative responses from One Nation and NSW Labor, that would seem to be the case. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese also weighed in on the side of MACH Energy in May, telling 2HD Newcastle Radio that he supported the expansion.

The campaign group, motivated by broader notions around climate justice, is also concerned about the transition for those working in the coal industry. Tony Lonergan, from DAMS HEG told a media conference on October 7 that NSW Labor had failed to put in place, and properly fund, a fair transition plan for affected communities.

Wendy Wales, president of DAMS HEG, said: “Today the High Court has said what we have always known: We cannot dig up coal, ship it overseas, watch it drive climate change and then pretend the consequences have nothing to do with us and won’t be felt by us.

“The droughts, the bushfires, the floods — are directly connected to greenhouse gases, and massive fossil fuel projects like Mt Pleasant Optimisation simply add fuel to the fire.”

Wales and Lonergan, both retired science teachers, live on a farm in the Upper Hunter Valley adjacent to the Mount Pleasant mine.

The Hunter Valley community group has been fighting MACH Energy’s expansion plan — to double Mount Pleasant’s output to 21 million tonnes a year and extend operations until 2048.

The community group initially lost its challenge last year in the NSW Land and Environment Court, after the IPC approved the 22-year expansion. It then successfully appealed that decision, prompting Mach Energy to take the case to the High Court.

The High Court dismissed MACH Energy’s appeal, saying the IPC had not considered how pollution from its coal would affect the region, through increased bushfire risk, drought, flooding and extreme heat. MACH Energy argued that Scope 3 emissions (emissions produced from burning the exported coal) from its mine should be considered through Australia’s pre-existing obligations under the Paris Agreement.

Three of the five judges found that the NSW IPC needed to “consider imposing conditions to minimise to the greatest extent practicable all greenhouse gas emissions, including Scope 3 emissions”.

The judgement means that the Mount Pleasant coal mine expansion approval to 2048 is invalid. But MACH Energy was given approval, in August, to operate until 2032. It had sought to double the output to 21 million tonnes a year.

Wales said the court decision “has finally made a change in direction in our laws. The [planning rules] will now have to reflect the need to consider climate impacts of our scope three emissions from the coal that we export.”

Lonergan said: “This ruling is in line with the International Court of Justice ruling [in July 2025] that said countries that use fossil fuels are responsible for the mitigation of emissions.

“We cannot just say, ‘Well, 98% of emissions comes from the burning of the coal overseas — that’s somebody else’s problem. Nothing to do with us!’ That’s just not going to work any more.”

Nic Clyde, coordinator of Lock the Gate Alliance NSW, said the ruling would affect 17 coal projects currently in the state’s planning pipeline. “Today’s decision sends a strong message to the planning system: the price households and communities are paying for coal pollution must be weighed properly in the planning system,” he said. “It’s no longer okay to ignore the climate cost of coal revenues.”

“The upper hunter economy needed to be diversified away from coal mining,” Lonergan said. “The area is completely dependent on coal mining, and everyone is pretending that we are just going to carry on.

“There’s the Future Jobs and Investment Fund which has stalled in the Upper House because the Labor Party won’t pass legislation to assist in the transition of the economy, diversify the economy.

“This landmark case shows that governments have to start getting serious about emissions …

author: Charlotte Reck
title: Labour’s Byelection Candidate Stayed Quiet on Israel’s Genocide in Gaza
content:
The Labour candidate seeking to win former prime minister Keir Starmer’s seat has failed to condemn Israel’s genocide in Gaza but has criticised the recent Green party

‘Zionism is Racism’ motion

 as “divisive”. 


Sagal Abdi-Wali, a Starmer ally and leader of Camden council, is running against Green leader Zack Polanski in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection, which is widely considered to be a two-horse race between Labour and the Greens.


Abdi-Wali has not publicly spoken about Israel’s devastation of Gaza at any point between October 2023 and her selection as Labour’s byelection candidate, according to a detailed

feature in Tribune magazine.

 


Abdi-Wali also drawn criticism for

dodging questions

 about Israel’s genocide on the campaign trail. 


Camden council, led by Abdi-Wali since May after four years serving as a councillor, has seen its investments in US spytech firm Palantir, which supplies military tech to Israel, soar by over 1,200% since October 2023, according to FOI disclosures

first shared with Declassified UK

.  


The council’s overall holdings in companies complicit in Israel’s apartheid, occupation and genocide of the Palestinian people, including weapons manufacturer Elbit Systems, have increased in value by nearly 30% – worth £28m – since June 2024. 


The council has repeatedly ignored calls for divestment. 


Abdi-Wali also failed to sign the

Palestine Solidarity Campaign’s pledge

 calling on local government candidates to commit to working to end complicity in genocide. It was signed by more than 1,600 councillors from various parties – including 30 Labour party councillors in the neighbouring borough of Islington – ahead of the May local elections. 


At a Board of Deputies-organised hustings in late September, she acknowledged the “strength of feeling that the conflict in Palestine and Israel has brought to communities here” and said she wanted to “bring a sense of hope to parliament”.


When candidates were asked

“are you a Zionist, yes or no?”

, Polanski declared himself an “anti-Zionist”, while Abdi-Wali did not deliver a straight answer, instead saying: “I believe in a two-state solution.”

 


Labour’s candidate has been more vocal on the Greens’ ‘Zionism is Racism’ motion, passed just days ago with 1,022 member votes to 813 at the party’s conference.


“It has been brought up to me by people literally at the school gates this morning, of how, 


like, divisive they found that motion and how worried they are by it,” Abdi-Wali

told The Standard

. “I think it’s worrying for anyone who believes in a two-state solution,” she added.

Konto bleibt: Rote Hilfe gewinnt auch das Hauptsacheverfahren gegen Sparkasse Göttingen beim Landgericht Göttingen


„

Rote Hilfe gewinnt auch Hauptsacheverfahren gegen Sparkasse Göttingen. Das Landgericht Göttingen hat die Kündigung des Kontos für unwirksam erklärt. Ein wichtiger Erfolg gegen politisch motiviertes Debanking und für die Solidaritätsarbeit der Roten Hilfe. (…) Ein zusätzliches Risiko durch die US-Listung der sogenannten „Antifa Ost“ als Terrororganisation  konnte die Sparkasse nicht plausibel machen. Das OLG stellte zudem klar, dass die Rote Hilfe nicht eine Organisation „Antifa Ost“ finanziert, sondern gemäß ihrer Satzung Beschuldigte und Angeklagte in den entsprechenden Verfahren unterstützt. Die US-Einstufung selbst entfaltet keine unmittelbare rechtliche Wirkung in Deutschland. Dieser Beurteilung des OLG schloss sich das Landgericht heute »vollumfänglich« an.


Damit hat die Rote Hilfe nach den Erfolgen im Eilverfahren nun auch in der Hauptsache Recht bekommen. Für die Rote Hilfe geht es über den eigenen Fall hinaus auch um die Frage, wie weit politische Entscheidungen und Sanktionslisten aus Drittstaaten auf zivilgesellschaftliche Strukturen in Deutschland durchschlagen können

…“

Pressemitteilung vom 08.10.2026


 („Konto bleibt: Rote Hilfe gewinnt Hauptsacheverfahren“)


OLG Braunschweig hat die Berufung der Sparkasse Göttingen zum Konto von Rote Hilfe (und damit willkürliche Kontenkündigungen) zurückgewiesen


OLG: Sparkasse Göttingen muss Konto der Roten Hilfe fortführen

„

Das OLG Braunschweig hat die Berufung der Sparkasse Göttingen zurückgewiesen: Das Konto der Rote Hilfe e.V. muss vorerst weitergeführt werden. Für die angeführten Verdachtsmomente sah das Gericht keine ausreichende Tatsachengrundlage. Für die Rote Hilfe e.V. ist das ein wichtiges Signal gegen Debanking und gegen politischen Druck auf zivilgesellschaftliche Strukturen

.

(…)


Die Sparkasse hatte das Konto am 9. Dezember 2025 gekündigt und stützte sich dabei unter anderem auf Spendenaufrufe des Vereins mit den Verwendungszwecken „unverzagt“ und „Budapest“. Daraus leitete sie gesteigerte Prüfpflichten nach dem Geldwäschegesetz ab, die das Konto für sie unwirtschaftlich gemacht hätten.


Das Gericht hat den Verdacht als unbegründet bewertet. Er habe einer Tatsachengrundlage entbehrt. Die Sparkasse habe die Spendenaufrufe inhaltlich falsch wiedergegeben. Der Verein habe nicht zur „Unterstützung der Antifa-Ost“ aufgerufen, sondern zur „Unterstützung im Antifa-Ost-Verfahren“ und „gegen die Auslieferung und Unterstützung verfolgter Antifas in Ungarn“. Das entspreche dem satzungsgemäßen Zweck des Vereins, Beschuldigten und Angeklagten faire Verfahren zu ermöglichen. Auch eine Verschleierung sah das Gericht nicht. Kurze, prägnante Verwendungszwecke seien bei rund 2.300 Zahlungseingängen nachvollziehbar, um Spenden einzelnen Kampagnen zuordnen zu können, und der Verein habe diese Zuordnung offen vorgenommen. Dass andere Banken dem Verein nach der Kündigung kein Konto eröffnet haben, belege den Verdacht ebenfalls nicht, zumal die Gründe dafür nicht bekannt seien.


Auch die Eilbedürftigkeit hat das Gericht bestätigt. Der Anspruch des Vereins auf Fortführung des Kontos sei weitgehend eindeutig. Würde man den Verein auf das Hauptsacheverfahren verweisen, müsste er zunächst das Konto wechseln und im Erfolgsfall wieder zurückwechseln. Dieser doppelte Aufwand wäre angesichts der Vielzahl von Zahlungseingängen und Mitgliedern so erheblich, dass er faktisch einer Verweigerung von Rechtsschutz gleichkäme. Die Interessen der Sparkasse müssten demgegenüber zurücktreten

…“

Pressemitteilung vom 17.09.2026 …

author: cnt.es
title: El sindicato de inquilinas consigue una confluencia sindical histórica
content:
«

Ha sido una reunión histórica

». Así ha calificado Nieves Román, secretaria general de la CNT, la asamblea celebrada este miércoles, 7 de octubre, entre los sindicatos de toda la geografía nacional. Sindicatos como CNT, CGT, Solidaridad Obrera, LAB, CCOO, UGT, Co.bas, Confederación Intersindical, Intersindical Alternativa de Catalunya, Intersindical Valenciana, o la Unión de actores y actrices han confluido ante el llamamiento del Sindicato de Inquilinas para la organización de «una huelga general de verdad, en la que se detenga la producción y lo paremos todo».


Las reivindicaciones de la huelga general pasan por «

obtener reformas avanzadas en favor de la clase trabajadora con respecto al problema de la vivienda

» y «

abrir un nuevo período de luchas de cara a los próximos meses y años, con el sindicalismo en el centro y con capacidad de frenar a la reacción

». La decisión de la fecha para la huelga, 11 de noviembre como proponían Inquilinas, fue celebrada con aplausos por las personas asistentes. Lamentablemente, momentos después contrastó con la triste noticia del fallecimiento de Mari Carmen, apoyada por el Sindicato de Inquilinas y personalmente por algunas de las personas asistentes al acto.


«

Podríamos decir que nunca se celebró una cumbre como ésta

»- nos confirma el historiador Juan Pablo Calero. «

Podemos congratularnos de estar más cerca de conseguir una unidad más amplia del movimiento obrero. Queremos que el sindicalismo llegue a todos los sectores, incluyendo juventud, población migrante y otros que tradicionalmente han estado oprimidos.

» – ha señalado Román.


El sindicato CNT se encuentra actualmente manteniendo reuniones, tanto a nivel interno como externo, para la preparación de la huelga, y, previsiblemente, la anunciará en unos días. «

Tenemos que medir muy bien el encaje legal, contactar con otras organizaciones y, lo más importante, consultar a nuestras bases y tomar una decisión democrática, como mandan nuestros principios anarcosindicalistas

» – concluyó Román.


La entrada

El sindicato de inquilinas consigue una confluencia sindical histórica

 se publicó primero en

Confederación Nacional del Trabajo

.

title: 12 prisoners begin hunger strike at Bukan prison
content:
The Kurdistan Human Rights Network reported that at least 12 Kurdish prisoners being held at Bukan Prison for political and religious reasons began a hunger strike on October 5 to protest pressure exerted by Iranian regime forces in prisons.


The prisoners announced in a letter to Bukan Prison authorities on 5 October that they had begun a hunger strike. They are reportedly protesting restrictions on their access to leave permits and the open-prison placement program, as well as restrictions imposed on them under prison conditions.


The prisoners whose names have been identified as participating in the hunger strike are: Ardalan Mineh, Behrouz Barakhas, Esmail Atash-Mard, Kaveh Rahimi, Hamed Maroufi, Ali Mohammadi, Mahmoud Jafari, Ali Faroughi, Arsalan Minaei, Aziz Banehei, Ghader Salimi, and Mullah Davoud.


It was reported that on the second day of the hunger strike, the 12 prisoners were transferred to the quarantine section on the orders of the director of Bukan Prison. Their phone calls and family visits are reportedly still being restricted.


A Kurd detained


Meanwhile, Faramarz Seîdî, from the city of Dehgolan in Kurdistan Province, was detained by forces from the Ministry of Intelligence using violence and taken to a detention facility operated by the ministry. It was reported that Ministry of Intelligence forces arrested Seîdî on 6 October on Esteghlal Street in Dehgolan, without a court order.

author: Joseph Lee
title: From the farm to your door: How our global food system exploits workers
content:
Like many big cities, New York teems with delivery workers who bring takeout, groceries, and any number of other things to anyone with a cellphone. They work at all hours and in all conditions, often without job security, health insurance, or even

access to safe restrooms

. They are often hit by cars, assaulted, or robbed. Many of them are Indigenous people from Guatemala and Mexico who left home to escape violence and the impacts of climate change.


The worst impacts of that global crisis

add to the risks

 those

workers face

.


“When the city is hit with with massive snowstorms, floodings, or the recent smoke fires, many deliveristas are the ones who are on the front lines doing this work and responding to the climate crisis in order to take care of New Yorkers,” said Ligia Guallpa, who is Kichwa and the co-founder and executive director of the Worker’s Justice Project and Los Deliveristas Unidos. The organization organizes app-based delivery workers and advocates on their behalf. “But the reality is that often they cannot even take care of themselves.”


A report released Monday says that exploitation is deeply embedded in the global food system, leaving many of the 1.4 billion people who produce, process, distribute, and deliver food poorly paid,

inadequately protected

, and vulnerable to abuse. Climate change and a global affordability crisis are intensifying those pressures, according to the International Panel of Experts on Sustainable Food Systems, or IPES-Food, an international food policy research organization.


Although the document does not specifically focus on Indigenous peoples, it finds that many of the forces driving that exploitation have roots in the colonialism, land dispossession, forced labor, and racialized labor systems that have long harmed Indigenous communities worldwide. 


“Here we are in the United States, a country that’s founded on stealing land and the import of enslaved people to be able to make agriculture and agricultural labor possible and cheap,” said Raj Patel, an IPES-Food expert and a professor at the University of Texas at Austin. “And the legacy of that is still with us.”


The report notes that Indigenous peoples remain

particularly vulnerable to displacement

, and pressures from industrial agriculture and climate change that can undermine traditional livelihoods. For people who have been

forced off their land

 and are disconnected from those livelihoods, exploitative, low-paying work is often the only option. 


“If you put yourself in a situation of a woman who needs to feed her children, they can go to any extreme,” said Teresa Chemosop, who is Ogiek from Mount Elgon, Kenya, and the coordinator for the East Africa Indigenous Women-Led Assembly, which advocates for Indigenous women across the region. 


Read Next


The people who feed America are going hungry


Ayurella Horn-Muller


Chemosop said that Indigenous workers face severe discrimination and abuse, such as being compared to baboons and not being given utensils to eat with while working. That’s on top of low wages and long, difficult hours. 


Indigenous and intergenerational

agricultural knowledge

 is routinely minimized or dismissed as “unskilled,” the report notes, obscuring valuable expertise and helping to justify lower wages. That knowledge, which often goes back millenia, includes skills like cultivating plant medicines and drought-resistant crops. The authors call for formally recognizing that expertise alongside broader efforts to strengthen worker rights and protections.


The people who keep the global food system running do far more than grow and harvest food. They distribute it to markets and restaurants, deliver it to homes and offices, and provide care work like cooking and feeding families, often in seasonal or subcontracted jobs. Between 60 and 80 percent of food workers are informally employed — a higher share than in any other industry — and they earn about half as much as those with conventional employment. About 30 percent of food system workers, or more than 400 million people,

earn less than a living wage

.


An estimated 2.1 million people in agriculture work under forced-labor conditions, the report estimates. Migrants, who account for about a quarter of all farmworkers worldwide, are three times as likely to experience such conditions and are more likely than their peers to die on the job.

title: Palestinian Arts Workers Call for Solidarity
content:
Palestinian cultural workers living through apartheid, occupation, and genocide are

calling for solidarity

 from their counterparts abroad.


Not every artist has as large a platform as rapper Macklemore, children’s TV star Miss Rachel, or country singer Zach Bryan—who wore a “Free Palestine” shirt last weekend while playing a packed show at the same stadium where billionaire Robert Kraft had barred Macklemore for saying those words—but there’s plenty that artists and art workers can do to end complicity in Israel’s ongoing atrocities.


We as Palestinians have long decried Israel’s war crimes and crimes against humanity. Now the

Palestinian Performing Arts Network

 (PPAN), representing hundreds of Palestinian dancers, actors, musicians, playwrights, and circus performers, has

outlined

 four ways that U.S. arts unions can lend solidarity:


1. Reject the blacklisting and censorship of members who speak out on behalf of Palestinian rights.


For example, British Actors’ Equity

passed a motion in the UK’s Trade Union Congress

, representing 5 million workers, affirming the right of artists to “critique institutions and bring attention to issues through overtly political art without fear of censorship or losing their public funding.”


In the U.S., over 700 entertainment industry union members signed a 2024

open letter calling on SAG-AFTRA

 to back a ceasefire, protect members from blacklisting, and condemn the targeting of journalists.


2. Refuse to work with institutions and corporations—such as venues, festivals, publishers, broadcasters, and foundations—that are verifiably complicit in Israel’s crimes against Palestinians, and divest union funds from such corporations.


In fall 2025, over 5,500 film industry workers

signed such a pledge

. Earlier that year, Norway’s actors union Norsk Skuespillerforbund (NSF)

recommended that its members

 “reject work and collaboration with Israeli cultural institutions that operate in violation of the Palestinian cultural boycott.”


3. Exclude Israel from international labor federations

 such as the International Federation of Actors (FIA) and International Federation of Musicians (FIM).


4. Pressure governments to compel Israel to end its genocide and apartheid through lawful sanctions.


“Historically, including in the struggle that ended apartheid in South Africa, organized labor has been the working person’s leverage,” the PPAN said. “[Unions are] a powerful force for peace and justice when governments fail.”


UNION MOVES


Drawing inspiration from the global movement to end South African apartheid, Palestinian unions and workers have consistently

called on unions worldwide

 to use sanctions, boycotts, and divestment (BDS) campaigns as pressure points to end Israel’s genocide and occupation.


The United Auto Workers has

endorsed divestment

 from Israel bonds and acted on it. Since 2023, a smattering of Palestine solidarity groups across unions have pushed for pension fund divestment, joined other unions abroad to

block arms to Israel

 at international docks, and

protested complicit corporations>

.


The United Auto Workers, the United Electrical Workers (UE), National Nurses United, and the Painters have also thrown their support behind an

end to military funding

 to Israel and

divestment

. UE also became the first national union to endorse the BDS movement.


Some rank and filers have been forming loose solidarity networks like

Entertainment Labor for Palestine

,

Purple Up for Palestine

 (SEIU),

CWA4Palestine

, and

IATSE Members for Palestine

.


Union members can find resources like

Ethical Investment

 and

Ethical Procurement Policies

 to keep union pension funds and vendor contracts out of companies complicit in human rights abuses anywhere, including Palestine.


In the UK, on September 8, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband called illegal settlements in the West Bank “ethnic cleansing,” as part of the announcement of sanctions against Israel. Shortly thereafter, the UK’s Trade Union Congress, representing 5 million workers,

endorsed the Palestinian-led BDS movement

.


ATROCITIES ONGOING


The calls come as Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza reaches horrifying numbers. At least

80,000 Palestinians had been killed by Israel

author: labor4pal
title: Eyewitness report: Strikers and students rock France, Anti-fascism and Palestinian liberation mixed with anger at president Emmanuel Macron and the establishment (Socialist Worker-UK)
content:
Anti-fascism and Palestinian liberation mixed with anger at president Emmanuel Macron and the establishment

On the streets of Paris (Picture: Guy Smallman)

There were protests in 40 cities across France on Tuesday as workers and parents joined the movement of secondary school students demanding a future.

In Paris, organisers said 100,000 packed the streets. They were overwhelmingly young school and university students.

Young people chanted anti-fascist slogans. They included, “La jeunesse emmerde le Front National”—“The youth tell the Front National to fuck off” in a reference to the previous name of the fascist RN. And, “Siamo tutti antifascisti”—“We are all anti-fascist”.

They sang the Internationale and the French national anthem La Marseillaise. And there were Palestinian flags and chants of “free Palestine”. Other home made placards referenced the student and worker uprising of 1968.

When the presidential candidate for the left wing LFI party, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, arrived at the start of the march, he was mobbed by crowds of people. Both young and older protesters greeted him with chants of “president Mélenchon”.

Mélenchon called on his supporters, including many members of parliament, to join the protests. He wore a white armband on Tuesday to symbolise his support for the high school students.

As the march arrived in Place de la Nation, hundreds of riot police attacked with huge clouds of tear gas and charged at the crowd with batons. Protesters threw fireworks and set bins on fire.

Nora, Sarah and Sonia, three university students, spoke to Socialist Worker about their reasons for joining the protest.

“We protest for the rights of high school students,” they said. “All the media talks about is violence. But there are real reasons behind their protests.

“The RN is fascist. It’s homophobic and Islamophobic”.

Another student, Alice, said that young people are worried about their futures, “We are all worried about fascism, every student is worried about that. And about finding a job, everything is kind of scary.

“High school students are very stressed. We went through that so we want to be here with them.”

Trade unionists linked arms and faced up to cops with tear gas.

Pierre works in the tax office and is part of the Solidaires union federation. He told Socialist Worker, “I am on strike today, in solidarity with the students against repression and because we have the same problems with austerity.”

Clement, from the CFDT union federation, told Socialist Worker, “The demands of the school students are totally legitimate. The buildings are crumbling, there are rats in the classrooms, there are 30, 35 or even 40 people in a classroom.

“It’s a terrible period with the far right rising across Europe. We could see fascism in France for the second time in its history.”

Clement added that the current president Emmanuel Macron has “rolled out the red carpet for the RN’s Marine Le Pen”.

Another protester mentioned that there are already fascists joining the police force and that Le Pen would use them to smash the movement on the streets if she was in office.

Meet the pupils’ blockade: ‘We are young, determined and revolutionary’

Macron’s austerity measures and repression, combined with the normalisation of racism against migrants has created the conditions for the far right to rise.

Le Pen is currently leading in the polls, while Mélenchon is currently in second place.

The best hope of beating Le Pen will be if the movement stays on the streets and links the anger of the students with the power of the organised working class.

Key opportunities to deepen the movement are coming this month. Total Energy workers are set to strike Thursday—and there is a day of action on 17 October.

Anti-fascists are planning to demonstrate against the far right RN party’s conference on 24 October.

If the movement of school students and strikes deepens, it has the power to transform the political situation in France.

title: İş cinayetlerinde 2013’ten beri ilk kez beş ay üst üste 200’ün üzerinde ölüm
content:
İşçi Sağlığı ve İş Güvenliği (İSİG) Meclisi, Eylül 2026’ya ilişkin iş cinayetleri raporunu açıkladı.


Rapora göre Eylül ayında en az 226 işçi çalışırken hayatını kaybetti. Böylece 2026’nın ilk dokuz ayında iş cinayetlerinde yaşamını yitirenlerin sayısı en az 1736 oldu.


Ocak’ta 155, Şubat’ta 129, Mart’ta 151, Nisan’da 190, Mayıs’ta 214, Haziran’da 228, Temmuz’da 216 ve Ağustos’ta 227 işçi öldü.


2013’ten bu yana veri tutan İSİG Meclisi’nin raporlarda ilk kez beş ay üst üste aylık işçi ölümleri 200’ün üzerinde kaydedildi.


Ölümlerin 79’u sanayide, 54’ü inşaatta, 48’i hizmet sektöründe ve 45’i tarımda yaşandı. İşçilerin 21’i kadın, 14’ü göçmendi. Suriye, Azerbaycan, Türkmenistan, Bulgaristan, Irak, Rusya ve Ukrayna’dan gelmişlerdi.


Ayrıca Eylül ayında hayatını kaybeden işçilerin en az 7’si sendika üyesiydi. 219 işçi ise sendikasızdı. Ölen işçilerin yüzde 97’sini sendikasız çalışanlar oluşturdu.


Dokuz ayda en az 66 çocuk işçi öldü


Rapora göre bu ayda çalışırken ölen 226 kişinin 8’i çocuktu. Çocuklardan beşi 14 yaşında veya daha küçüktü; üçü ise 15-17 yaş grubundaydı.


Ölümlerin üçü tarım, diğerleri gıda, tekstil, metal, inşaat ve konaklama işkollarında meydana geldi.


2026’nın ilk dokuz ayında en az 66 çocuk işçi çalışırken hayatını kaybetti.


İSİG Meclisi, Mesleki Eğitim Merkezleri’nin (MESEM) son iki yılda çocuk işçiliğinin en görünür alanlarından biri haline geldiğini belirtti. Çocukların işyerlerinde çalışmasının MESEM modeliyle yaygınlaştırıldığı savunularak, sorunun yalnızca denetim ve iş güvenliği eksiklikleriyle sınırlı olmadığını ifade etti.


“Çocuk emeğinin düşük maliyetli hatta bedava, güvencesiz ve denetimsiz biçimde üretime dahil edilmesinin kurumsal ve yasal aracı yaratıldı. Bu noktada, MESEM’lerle ilgili tartışılması gereken şey yalnızca MESEM’lerde denetimin veya iş güvenliği önlemlerinin yetersizliği değil, çocuk emeğini işgücü piyasasının olağan ve kabul edilebilir bir unsuru haline getiren bu modelin kendisidir.” dedi.


İSİG Meclisi, MESEM dışındaki çocuk işçiliğinin özellikle tarım, küçük işletmeler, sanayi siteleri ve mevsimlik işlerde kayıt dışı biçimde sürdüğüne de dikkat çekti.


Ayrıca bu ayda ölenlerin 11'i de 65 yaş ve üstündeydi.


En fazla ölüm inşaatta


Eylül ayında en fazla iş cinayeti inşaat ve yol işkolunda meydana geldi. Bu işkolunda 50 işçi hayatını kaybetti.


Tarım ve orman işkolunda 45, taşımacılıkta 28, belediye ve genel işlerde 16, gemi, tersane, deniz ve liman işkolunda 15 işçi öldü.


Bunları 10 ölümle ticaret, büro, eğitim ve sinema; 9 ölümle konaklama ve eğlence, 7 ölümle de madencilik izledi.


İlk sırada trafik ve servis kazaları var


İş cinayetlerinin nedenlerine göre dağılımında trafik ve servis kazaları ilk sırada yer aldı. Eylül ayında 49 işçi trafik veya servis kazalarında yaşamını yitirdi.


Yüksekten düşme sonucu 41, ezilme ve göçük nedeniyle 40, kalp krizi veya beyin kanaması sonucu 30 işçi öldü.


Elektrik çarpması 15, zehirlenme ve boğulma 14, şiddet 13 işçinin ölümüne neden oldu


En fazla ölüm İstanbul’da


Eylül ayında Türkiye’nin 62 kentinde ve yurtdışında altı ülkede iş cinayeti kaydedildi.


En fazla ölüm 39 işçiyle İstanbul’da meydana geldi. İstanbul’u 9 ölümle Antep, 8’er ölümle Ankara ve Urfa, 7’şer ölümle Düzce ve Manisa, 6’şar ölümle Samsun ve Trabzon izledi.


(HA)

author: anred
title: No todo lo que brilla es un subsidio: ¿cuáles son las Zonas Frías de la política energética de Milei?
content:
Foto: Martín Álvarez Mullally


La misma semana en que el INDEC informó que la pobreza fue del 32% en el primer semestre de 2026, el Senado aprobó la modificación del régimen de Zona Fría. La decisión le quita ese subsidio en la tarifa de gas a 1,6 millones de hogares en 11 provincias y les condona 1.800 millones de dólares de deuda con el Estado a Edenor, Edesur y otras distribuidoras eléctricas. ¿Para quiénes son los salvatajes y para quiénes las deudas en la política energética de Milei?

Por Analía Zárate y Rosaura Barletta / OPSur. 


En el debate público sobre los subsidios a la energía en Argentina, gobiernos y buena parte de los medios se dedican a auditar el poder adquisitivo de las familias y la cantidad que -según ellos- le corresponde consumir a un hogar. 

“No podemos subsidiar piletas climatizadas”

, 

“el subsidio tiene que llegar a los que verdaderamente lo necesitan”

, 

“nos hicieron creer que la luz y el gas eran gratis”

, son argumentos que se amparan en la necesidad de eficiencia económica en la gestión de la energía y reducen la discusión a cómo y cuánto tiene que incidir el Estado en las tarifas que pagan los usuarios. Un abordaje que omite por qué y para qué existen los subsidios.


“Yo no uso televisión, ni microondas, ni lavarropas, ni computadora, ni pava eléctrica. Uso el cargador del celular, la heladera y las luces. También las de afuera, porque el barrio tiene muy poca iluminación y cuando llegamos de noche por la calle prendemos la linterna del celular”, dice Ana Pereyra, docente jubilada, lejos de utilizar la electricidad para climatizar una pileta como sugirió el jefe de Gabinete Diego Santilli. Vive en un barrio periférico de la ciudad de Mar del Plata, una de las ciudades que perdió la clasificación de Zona Fría, en una casa que alquila desde hace tres años y no sabe por qué no le otorgan el régimen de Subsidios Energéticos Focalizados (

ReSEF

) para la electricidad. Paga la tarifa plena, unos 200 mil pesos por mes.


El tarifazo del invierno afectó a todos los usuarios, incluso a ella, aunque dice que su consumo eléctrico no aumentó porque se calefacciona a gas. Aun cuando después de ponerse al día le quedan 50 mil pesos para vivir el resto del mes, asegura: “estoy pagando la boleta de luz completa porque aceleran los cortes por mora”. En las movilizaciones contra el tarifazo que convocaron diferentes organizaciones políticas y sociales de Mar del Plata, los usuarios presentaron boletas por montos aún mayores: 

7 millones de pesos para cuatro familias

, por ejemplo. Los damnificados por servicios impagables también se manifestaron en 

Santa Teresita

 y 

San Clemente del Tuyú

, entre otras localidades costeras de la provincia de Buenos Aires. “El invierno para mí es una situación muy delicada. Estos ajustes nos están aniquilando. Yo antes tomaba café, ahora té. Ya no uso la tarjeta de crédito para comprarme un par de zapatillas o hacer regalos, sino para ir al súper, y con cuidado”, cuenta Ana.


Foto: latecla.info


El 

Índice de Precios al Consumidor

 que elabora mensualmente el Instituto Nacional de Estadística y Censos (INDEC) es un indicador de lo que valen ciertos productos y servicios y se utiliza para seguir la evolución de la inflación. Para estimar qué rubros de la canasta pesan más sobre otros, la actualización de esos precios se combina con un ponderador elaborado en base a la Encuesta Nacional de Gastos de los Hogares (ENGHo) realizada en 2004. A comienzos de 2026 se anunció que se reemplazaría esa encuesta de 2004 por una medición de 2018. Con ese cambio, el ítem “Vivienda, agua, electricidad, gas y otros combustibles” iba a pasar de pesar el 9,4% al 14,5%. Marcela Almeyda, Coordinadora de IPC Nacional y delegada de ATE INDEC, dice sobre el episodio: “Nuestro lema siempre es que las estadísticas tienen que ser independientes de los gobiernos de turno, tienen que servir para medir lo mejor posible la realidad y hay que usar el mejor instrumento disponible”. title: AfD im Bundestag fordert Verbot von „Antifa“, indymedia.de und Roter Hilfe
content:
Die rechtsextreme AfD versucht in Deutschland auf Bundes- wie auf Länderebene Antifaschismus zu kriminalisieren, anzugreifen und zu verbieten. Wie läuft das im Bundestag und wie auf Ländereben?


In einem aktuellen Entschließungsantrag für den Deutschen Bundestag fordert die AfD im Rahmen ihrer „24 Maßnahmen gegen linksextremistische Gewalt und Terror“ unter anderem ein Verbot der „Antifa“ sowie der Roten Hilfe. Hinsichtlich der Antifa, richtet sich der AfD-Antrag exemplarisch gegen die„Antifa Süd“. Ferner wird ein Verbot und Abschaltung der Website de.indymedia.org gefordert.


Der AfD-Antrag- ein Sammelsurium an Forderungen


Erst am 06.10.2026 legte die AfD-Fraktion im Bundestag, darunter so berüchtigte Rechtsextremisten wie

Martin Hess

,

Gottfried Curio

,

Bernd Baumann

,

Maximilian Krah

, einen achtseitigen Entschließungsantrag (

als PDF

) vor, in welchem sie 24 Forderungen aufstellt.


Das Sammelsurium der Forderungen reicht von einer „erheblichen personellen Verstärkung der für die Aufklärung und Ermittlung im Bereich des Linksextremismus zuständigen Abteilungen der Sicherheitsbehörden“, über „regelmäßige Erstellung von internen Lagebildern durch das BKA zur aktuellen Gefährdungslage durch gewaltorientierte Linksextremisten mit Serien- und Musteranalyse“ bis hin zur Forderung der „dauerhafte(n) Räumungen aller besetzten Szeneobjekte, (…) wie beispielsweise der „Rigaer Straße 94“ in Berlin oder der „Roten Flora“ in Hamburg, die rechtswidrig von Linksextremisten in Besitz genommen wurden und von denen aus wiederholt Straftaten verübt worden sind oder die als Unterschlupf für linksextremistische Gewalttäter dienen“.


Aber auch ein „Verbot und Abschaltung der Website de.indymedia.org als Nachfolgeplattform von linksunten.indymedia.org“, wird gefordert, ferner die „konsequente Prüfung von Verboten nach dem Vereinsgesetz in Bezug auf linksextremistische Gruppierungen, die sich unter der Bezeichnung „Antifa“oder „Antifaschistische Aktion“ zusammengeschlossen haben“ sowie ein „Verbot der Roten Hilfe e.V. (RH), da diese bundesweit „linksextremistische und mithin verfassungsfeindliche Ziele von unterschiedlicher Intensität“ verfolgt“.


Begründung der AfD


Der Einstieg des Antrages der AfD bildet ein Verweis auf „die Vorgänge rund um die Berliner Wahlsiegerin DIE LINKE, an deren Wahlparty Vertreter aus dem Clanmilieu und Islamisten teilgenommen haben“, diese würden „dabei nur die Spitze eines Eisbergs dar(stellen), auf den Deutschland sicherheitspolitisch ungebremst zusteuert“. Anschließend geht es in einem wilden Parforceritt von einem „gezielten Brandanschlag auf das Stromnetz im Raum Berlin Steglitz-Zehlendorf zu Beginn des Jahres“, welchen der „Vulkangruppe“ zugerechnet wird, über einen weiteren „Anschlag (…) im Juni dieses Jahres in Reutlingen“ über welchen auf „der linksextremistischen Internetseite „Switch Off““ umfassend berichtet worden sei. Nicht fehlen dürfen „die konspirativ vorbereiteten Überfälle der sogenannten „Antifa-Ost“ oder auch „Hammerbande“ genannt, denn diese würden „das ganze Ausmaß der Eskalation (zeigen): Gezielte Angriffe auf Menschen, bei denen Opfer schwerste Verletzungen erlitten haben.“


Die RAF wird auch noch erwähnt, denn „bei den Hammerbandenprozessen handelt es sich (…) um die umfangreichsten Verfahren gegen Linksextremisten seit den RAF-Prozessen vor knapp 50 Jahren“, so die AfD.


Weitere Schlagworte „Missbrauch der Versammlungsfreiheit durch Linksextremisten“, Bekämpfung der „Gefahren durch linke Militanz“ vermittels der oben genannten Verbote, denn, so die AfD-Abgeordneten, „um diese Fehlentwicklungen aufzuhalten, müssen auch linksextremistische Strukturen zerschlagen werden. Vereinsrechtliche Verbotsverfahren gegen gewaltlegitimierende Strukturen der Antifa müssen vorrangig geprüft und konsequent umgesetzt werden“.


Die Rote Hilfe ist der AfD besonders ein Dorn im Auge, denn, so die Begründung des Antrags, die Rote Hilfe sei „mit rund 14.400 Mitgliedern und bundesweit rund 50 Ortsgruppen die größte und eine der wichtigsten Gruppierungen im deutschen Linksextremismus. Sie bietet nicht nur einen Legitimationsrahmen für die Begehung von Straf- und Gewalttaten“. Insbesondere befürworte und unterstütze sie „die Anwendung von Gewalt als Mittel der politischen Auseinandersetzung“.


Fazit und Ausblick

öffentlich beraten

. Vermutlich wird er im Anschluss daran an die Ausschüsse …
