content:
Bring Maja back: Antifaschist*in muss sofort aus Ungarn hierher überstellt werden!


Der Fall gehört zum sog. Budapest-Komplex: Maja und weiteren Antifaschist*innen wird vorgeworfen, sich im Februar 2023 an körperlichen Auseinandersetzungen mit Nazis am Rand des

NS

-verherrlichenden Großevents „Tag der Ehre“ in Budapest beteiligt zu haben. Seither läuft eine internationale Verfolgungsjagd gegen Antifaschist*innen, die vor allem von Ungarn und Deutschland vorangetrieben wird. Ende 2023 wurde Maja in Berlin von deutschen Ermittlungsorganen verhaftet und im Juni 2024 in einer rechtswidrigen Nacht-und-Nebel-Aktion an Ungarn ausgeliefert – nur Stunden, bevor das Bundesverfassungsgericht diesen Schritt explizit untersagte: Insbesondere für eine non-binäre antifaschistische Person ist die Situation im weiterhin rechtsautoritären und offen queerfeindlichen Ungarn lebensgefährlich. Das Gericht hatte dabei am 24. Januar 2025 nicht nur die Rechtswidrigkeit von Majas Auslieferung festgestellt, sondern auch die deutschen Behörden verpflichtet, sich für eine schnellstmögliche Rückführung einzusetzen.

Seit diesem Rechtsbruch der deutschen Behörden war Maja unter katastrophalen Haftbedingungen in Budapest eingekerkert: Schimmliges Essen, Ungeziefer in der Zelle, defizitäre Duschmöglichkeiten, ständige nächtliche Kontrollen und demütigende Nacktdurchsuchungen, Trennscheibe bei allen Besuchen – und vor allem anhaltende Isolationshaft, die nach internationalen Standards als Folter gilt. Mit einem mehrwöchigen Hungerstreik protestierte Maja im Sommer 2025 gegen diese unmenschliche Behandlung. Am 17. Juli 2026 kam es sogar zu brutaler körperlicher Gewalt durch vermummtes Wachpersonal, das Maja in der Zelle zusammenschlug, zwangsweise entkleidete, um Maja zum Tragen von nach ihrer Ansicht geschlechtsentsprechender Kleidung zu zwingen, und dann auch noch disziplinarisch verfolgte. Es war genau diese Situation, vor der im Auslieferungsverfahren immer wieder gewarnt worden war.

Für die Farce des offenkundig politischen Schauprozesses in Ungarn war keine angemessene Vorbereitung möglich: Anwaltsgespräche konnten nur beeinträchtigt stattfinden, die meisten Unterlagen lagen nur auf ungarisch vor, und Maja konnte die digitale Akte kaum sichten. Im Gerichtssaal wurde die non-binäre Person in Ketten und an einer Hundeleine vorgeführt, begleitet von medialer Stimmungsmache. Obwohl der Prozess keinerlei Hinweise erbrachte, dass Maja aktiv an den vorgeworfenen Handlungen beteiligt war, belief sich das erstinstanzliche Urteil am 4. Februar 2026 auf acht Jahre Haft unter schwersten Bedingungen. Die Berufung reduzierte dieses absurde Strafmaß am 30. September 2026 nur geringfügig auf sieben Jahre sowie eine Geldstrafe und machte damit erneut deutlich, dass in erster Linie die antifaschistische Haltung bestraft werden sollte.

Dass Maja spätestens nach dem Urteil umgehend zurück nach Deutschland überstellt wird, war ohnehin die bindende Grundvoraussetzung für die rechtswidrige Auslieferung gewesen.

„Der Fall von Maja ist ein politischer und juristischer Skandal, der von den deutschen Behörden durch die nächtliche Auslieferung offen rechtswidrig produziert und seit nunmehr weit über zwei Jahren durch Tatenlosigkeit fortgesetzt wird“, empörte sich Hartmut Brückner vom Bundesvorstand der Roten Hilfe e. V. „Wir fordern insbesondere das Bundesjustizministerium auf, endlich das Urteil des Bundesverfassungsgerichts umzusetzen und sofort die Rücküberstellung in die Wege zu leiten.“ Zudem appellierte Brückner: „Wir rufen die Öffentlichkeit dazu auf, gemeinsam politischen Druck auf die zuständigen Behörden auszuüben – durch Petitionen, öffentliche Proteste und Kampagnen. Schluss mit der Folter in Ungarn: Bring Maja back!“

content:
Lochiel, AZ – In the early hours of October 5, Border Patrol agents raided the anti-border camp called “Tierra Libre” on the U.S.-Mexico Border near Lochiel, Arizona. An estimated 200 Border Patrol Agents invaded camp — entering the tracts of private property along the border that had long-shielded land defenders from the authority of the federal agents — and cut down the ancient Grandmother tree that campers had attempted to protect. Less than 24 hours later, land defenders established a new treesit in the immediate path of construction, this time on the Mexican side of the border. 


Although Border Patrol agents were parked along the easement throughout the night, a masked land defender snuck past them and scrambled up into the 50-foot-tall Grandmother tree and into the platform already built there. “This brave warrior climbed right up there,” said Pablo, a land defender who was at camp Tuesday morning. “The new treesit is very much blocking construction, as long as someone is in that tree they will not be able to build their wall.”

Treesit Blocks US-Mexico Border Wall Construction for Six Weeks in Arizona

Agents shoved and tackled campers, pointed guns at them, stomped on their necks, and pushed several campers into the barbed wire fence that marks the private property line. One land defender who goes by the name Hoops showed wounds on her hands and wrist to members of the media that she said resulted from agents twice her size tackling her into the barbed wire fence. 


“Border Patrol has been coming onto private property since yesterday morning,” said Rachel, a land defender who spoke with Unicorn Riot about the raids. “No warrants are shown, as far as we can tell there’s no legal ground for them to come onto private property. It seems like they’re pushing through the construction process quickly and will deal with the law later.” 


Construction workers protected by Border Patrol agents used a cherrypicker to cut branches off of the 200-year-old cottonwood Grandmother tree, in which a treesit had been sustained for 71 days. Agents then removed a treesitter stationed to protect the tree from border wall construction.


Within minutes, the Grandmother tree was felled and the treesit destroyed. Ten land defenders were arrested, including the treesitter. Ten more were cited and released.

Land defenders established the new treesit in the tall cottonwood tree that land defenders had briefly occupied in August, early on in the campaign. Facing pressure from Border Patrol and Mexican State Police, the treesit had been vacated. It remained unoccupied for over six weeks – until today.

title: Far Right Gleeful Over Firing Squad Death Sentence for Muslim Fort Hood Shooter
content:
Trump has approved the killing of Muslim US soldier Nidal Malik Hasan — the first Army execution in over 60 years.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Conservative figures have reacted with glee to the Trump administration’s approval of a firing squad death sentence for Muslim Army member Nidal Malik Hasan, in what would be the first execution carried out by the U.S. military in over six decades.

Hasan was convicted of committing a mass shooting at Texas’s Fort Hood in 2009, killing 13 people, with jurors recommending a maximum sentence of death. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said in September 2025 that he was seeking President Donald Trump’s final approval for the military to execute Hasan, and the Pentagon has since laid out a plan to carry out three more executions for those who remain on the military’s death row.

Sean Parnell, the Pentagon’s spokesperson, announced on Monday that Trump has given his approval for the execution, characterizing Hasan as a “jihadist” and highlighting that he shouted “Allahu Akbar,” meaning “God is great,” during the attack.

“The Secretary of the Army will set the time and place of the execution. Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” Parnell said in a post on X.

Hasan is a U.S.-born Muslim of Palestinian descent. At the time, he admitted to committing the killings, saying that he was against his upcoming deployment to Afghanistan and opposed to the U.S. military’s biases against Muslims. His family said that he was discriminated against for being Muslim while in the military.

If Hasan’s execution is carried out, this would be the first execution done by the military since 1961, when Army private John Bennett was executed by hanging. Bennett, who was Black, was accused of raping and attempting to kill an Austrian girl, who was white, and retrospective reports said that his case was not tried properly; in the six years leading up to his execution, eight other Black soldiers on the military’s death row were executed, while six others who were white lived.

Execution by firing squad is also relatively rare in the U.S. According to the Death Penalty Information Center, only 34 out of over 8,700 executions in the U.S. between 1890 and 2010 were carried out through firing squads. This method is only legal in a handful of states, but Trump has moved to bring it back in order to ramp up the use of the death penalty.

Typically, in an execution by firing squad, the prisoner is hooded and bound to a chair. A doctor pinpoints the prisoner’s heart and puts a target on it. Between three and five shooters are in an enclosure nearby and aim at the target through a slot; in some protocols, one shooter’s gun is randomly loaded with blanks. The shooters all fire at once, and the prisoner dies via gunshot to the heart, or bleeds out.

Conservatives online were exuberant following Parnell’s announcement, which Hegseth described as “[j]ustice.”

“More of this please. This is what I voted for. More dead jihadists!” said conservative influencer and Trump confidante Laura Loomer.

Some right-wing accounts on X called for the administration to televise the execution for Americans to watch.

“I volunteer to pull the trigger,” said Carl Higbie, a former Navy SEAL and current daily host on far right outlet Newsmax.

“This is the way,” said NewsNation host Katie Pavlich.

The Trump administration’s announcement came just days after the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee. Pike, who was convicted of murdering a classmate in 1995, was hospitalized after Tennessee prison officials administered two doses of pentobarbital that were supposed to kill her, against medical recommendations. Pike’s attorney said on Sunday that she is on a ventilator and in critical condition.

title: The Marxist Roots of Spanish Fascism
content:
The political regime of General Francisco Franco, which came about following the conclusion of the Spanish Civil War, is often described as being conservative, clerical, and authoritarian. The distinctive features of the fascist rule under General Francisco Franco are revealed in a curious episode from history – on his death, the very first flowers laid at his coffin came from China, signed by Communist leader Zhou Enlai. It just happened to be about the same period of time when communist Cuba led by Fidel Castro observed three days of national mourning. It’s beyond irony for communist regimes to express such friendliness to a fascist dictator. However, rather than indicating some form of ideological sympathy, this unusual episode reveals another side of Cold War diplomacy, a possible precursor of nowadays campism.

However, looking closer, the earlier movement of the Franco regime before it suffered an internal coup had the rhetoric, symbols, and even some aspects of the organizational structure characteristic of National Syndicalism as the pre-cursor to their Spanish fascism. The earlier Spanish National Syndicalism did not emerge from the typical right-wing Spanish conservatism. Rather, the radical ideology was formed in the early 1930s and the main authors of this movement were Ramiro Ledesma Ramos and Onésimo Redondo Ortega. Being inspired by the revolutionary ideologies that dominated the European left of that period, such as Sorelian Marxism (revolutionary syndicalism), anarchism, and Marxist socialism, National Syndicalism rejected any attempts to preserve the existing capitalist or agrarian order in favor of a total revolution of the working class. Between 1936 and 1937, however, due to the physical elimination of the leadership of the movement and the purely tactical actions of Franco, who managed to seize military and political power, National Syndicalist movement in Spain was thoroughly co-opted by Franco. Having deprived the ideology of its social-revolutionary nature and keeping the symbols and slogans of the movement, Franco transformed the movement of total state transformation into a means of labor control.

In order to see how Franco managed to pervert National Syndicalism, it is necessary to take a look at the ideological origin of the movement. The main ideologist of National Syndicalism, Ramiro Ledesma Ramos, created his political newspaper "La Conquista del Estado" (The Conquest of the State) in March 1931, stating from the very beginning that his purpose was to channel the revolutionary spirit of the Spanish proletariat for the sake of the national project. His paper (The Conquest of the State) even became a subject of debate in a CNT assembly, yet, it did not have the intended impact. Ledesma was well-versed in continental philosophy and embodied what is called the greatest assimilation of Georges Sorel's revolutionary syndicalism in Spain. The syndicalism of Sorel proclaimed direct actions of workers' syndicates to crush bourgeois liberal regime. The key reference point of Ledesma on the left side of Spain was the Confederación Nacional del Trabajo (CNT), a strong anarcho-syndicalist labor union. It was obvious that Ledesma admired the fighting spirit, anti-bourgeois combativeness, and revolutionary passion of the masses of the CNT. In his opinion, anarcho-syndicalists were the best combat forces in Spain, and it was his main aim to "nationalize" the CNT, that means to redirect revolutionary power of CNT from internationalist anti-statism to the national state. It is important to note that this influence was not only theoretical. The early National Syndicalist cells included many former members of anarchist and communist organizations. One of the leaders of CNT, Alvaro de Sotomayor, became the head of National Syndicalist union of taxi drivers in Madrid. Similarly, Dr. Santiago Montero Díaz from Communist Party of Spain also joined them. Both National Syndicalists and anarchists shared the following superficial values: their common hatred of bourgeois democratic system, opposition to gradual reforms, and support of direct action through workers' unions. Similarly, the relations between National Syndicalism and Marxism were also very similar. The movement was defined by structural mimicry and fierce ideological rivalry. First of all, Ledesma admitted Karl Marx as a great philosopher and agreed with the basic ideas of his criticism of bourgeois liberal capitalist system. Even though the …

title: Women murdered in Amed: A common story of violence, complaints, and failed protection
content:
In the first eight months of 2026, 197 women were killed by men in Kurdistan and Turkey. The same period also saw suspicious deaths of women and cases in which women were driven to suicide.


In Diyarbakır (Amed), one woman has died under suspicious circumstances since June, while the body of another woman who disappeared years ago was also found. Four women were also killed by men during this period.


Similar circumstances emerged behind the suspicious deaths and femicides in the city, while the families of the women killed shared a common demand: penalties must be sufficiently deterrent.


Four women killed


Interviews with the families of the women killed during this period revealed that the women had been subjected to systematic violence and were not adequately protected despite reporting the abuse to the police.


Sultan Karadağ was killed on 10 August. Sultan Kara was killed on 26 August by Ersan Akdemir, whom she wanted to divorce. Mizgin Kılıç was killed on 18 September by her former husband, and Ayfer Çakmak was killed on 27 September by her husband Orhan Çakmak, after reportedly enduring systematic violence for years.


The names and number of the women killed are more than mere statistics. Although their stories differed, they shared a common experience: they were subjected to violence, and their requests for protection went unanswered.


Mizgin Kılıç and Sultan Kara wanted to build new lives despite the violence they had endured, but they were not protected despite filing complaints. According to information provided by her relatives, Gülistan Karadağ was killed by people who had subjected her to violence and were reportedly using drugs.


Ayfer Çakmak was shot dead by her husband Orhan Çakmak, who had reportedly prevented her from even leaving the house for years. Following the killing, Çakmak claimed that her death was a suicide, saying, “The gun suddenly went off.”


Gülistan was targeted with violence and drugs


The family of Gülistan Karadağ said their daughter had been subjected to violence and threats for a long time and demanded that those responsible be held accountable. The family said: “Gülistan suffered violence and had been beaten again before she died. Who is bringing in these drugs, and how are they getting here? She constantly wanted a new beginning, a life of her own. But they never allowed her to have one. She was constantly beaten and threatened. Whoever did this must be held accountable. Our only demand is justice. We want nothing else.”


Sultan was not protected despite requesting a restraining order


The family of Sultan Kara, who was killed in front of her three-year-old daughter, said numerous complaints had previously been filed against the perpetrator. The family said Sultan had endured threats and violence for a long time: “The state is doing nothing. We lost our sister. Sultan had been married for four years. Every morning, my sister would say, ‘He is going to kill me.’ Twice, he beat her almost to death. He threatened and assaulted her. Even when Sultan was pregnant, he grabbed her by the throat and tried to kill her. His family threatened her to prevent her from filing a complaint.


Sultan had requested a restraining order when she filed for divorce. Following the decision to divorce, the perpetrator threatened both my older sister and Sultan with death. My sister is dead, while that man is walking around freely. Women are being killed and no one is taking it seriously. I want justice. Enough is enough.”


Sultan’s family said she had been subjected to violence not only by the man she wanted to divorce but also by his mother: “Sultan suffered violence both from him and from his mother. When she went to file a complaint, they sent her away, saying, ‘They are not the kind of people who would kill someone.’ Our only demand is that he receive the harshest possible sentence.”


The electronic tag was removed after the divorce


Mizgin Kılıç, who was killed by Ömer Kırıcı a year after divorcing him, had also endured violence and threats for a long time. According to her family, Mizgin left the house several times because of the violence but was forced to return after “family elders” intervened.


Ömer Kırıcı reportedly continued to stalk and threaten Mizgin even after their divorce. Mizgin was shot dead, and Kırıcı died by suicide following the killing.

title: Projection / discussion : Jeux vidéo et politique
content:
Projection du documentaire Le jeu vidéo, une affaire d'hommes 

 

? dimanche 18/10 16h à la librairie Publico à l'invitation du Groupe libertaire d'Ivry.


Le jeu vidéo, une affaire d'hommes 

 

? Documentaire de Nostalgeek (2023, 35 min)


Je ne peux pas m'identifier au protagoniste de ce jeu car c'est une femme et je suis un homme. 

 

» Est‐ce que ce genre de déclaration ne cache pas quelque part des soucis un brin plus profonds

 

?


Le jeu vidéo — comme le cinéma, la

BD

, la littérature… — peut servir de support à des idées politiques de tous bords. Ce court métrage s'attaque plus spécifiquement au sexisme 

 

; mais, de façon plus générale, existe‐t‐il des jeux luttant contre toutes les formes de discrimination, contre le capitalisme, l'État, la religion 

 

? Des jeux vidéo anarchistes 

 

?


Le sexisme dans le milieu du jeu vidéo


Les femmes travaillant dans l'industrie vidéoludique constatent une différence de salaire (25,3 % d'écart au bénéfice des hommes). Certains rejettent les designs de personnages féminins non hyper‐sexualisés. Dans les studios de développement français, les femmes représentent 24 % des effectifs alors qu'elles n'en constituaient que 10,6 % il y a 10 ans. Depuis 2018, nous constatons toujours la même disparité selon les catégories de métier, avec une sous‐représentation des femmes dans les métiers techniques (programmation, data). La question du harcèlement au bureau est également régulièrement soulevée. D'autres formes de sexisme évoquées sont le manque de volonté d'inclure des personnages féminins bien représentés dans les jeux vidéo.


Les jeux qui cherchent à mettre en avant des personnes non hommes peuvent entraîner un harcèlement de leurs scénaristes et développeurs : c'est le cas de Amber Scott, scénariste du jeu Baldur's Gate : Siege of Dragonspear, harcelée en 2016. Elle a en effet inclus un personnage principal féminin et un personnage secondaire transgenre dans le jeu, en plus de se moquer du Gamergate

 [

1

]

 dans une réplique. En réponse à ces actions, elle est la cible d'une campagne de harcèlement et le jeu reçoit des retours négatifs en masse.


En juillet 2021, suite à son harcèlement par un manager, une employée du studio américain de jeux vidéo Activision Blizzard se suicide. Deux mille de ses collègues signent alors une pétition protestant contre des méthodes de management, et organisent un mouvement de grève. De manière plus générale, c'est la «

 

 culture Bro 

 

», culture sexiste répandue dans les milieux de la tech, qui est mise en accusation.


Sur les 152 major games publiés en 2022, 61 % des personnages sont des hommes, 39 % des femmes, et 31,7 % des jeux vidéo mettent en scène des personnages exclusivement masculins. Dans les 50 RPGs les plus joués ces 30 dernières années, les hommes parlent en moyenne 2 fois plus que les femmes.


67 % des françaises jouent aux jeux vidéo, elles ont 39 ans en moyenne et représentent 48 % des personnes qui jouent au moins une fois par semaine. Mais 40 % d'entre elles affirment avoir déjà dû se résoudre à cacher leur genre dans des parties en ligne, 46 % des gameuses jugent les contenus qu'elles voient en ligne trop sexistes ou misogynes, et elles sont aussi 40 % à avoir déjà vécu des situations de harcèlement en ligne.


Il n'y a sans doute pas plus de sexistes dans le jeu vidéo que dans le reste de la société : ce triste constat n'est que le reflet de l'état des lieux en général. Mais, comme dans la littérature ou le cinéma, changer le contenu ne devrait‐il pas participer à changer les mentalités

author: Sanya Osha
title: Art by Rock Hard African Women
content:
Oftentimes, mass acts of violent rebellion primarily driven by youths are viewed as counterproductive and nihilistic. But it is important to note that this isn’t always the case, as three major examples in African contemporary history demonstrate notably: the anti-colonial theory of violence proffered by Frantz Fanon that galvanised Algeria into civil disobedience and warfare during the colonial era; the Arab Spring that gripped North Africa and parts of the Middle East in 2011; and the #RhodesMustFall movement that rattled South Africa in 2015.  Each of these instances of mass rebellion were largely youth-driven and shook the political status quo in their respective countries, leading to sociopolitical reform and fervent collective contemplation.


In this sense, rebellion in and of itself becomes a thoroughly creative act, a measure to shake up jaded and monolithic political edifices in urgent need of transformation as atrophy and retrogression set in within the body politic. Youths often excluded or marginalised in key decision-making bodies and processes are left with no option but to revolt. And in the act of rebellion, they are not only offering their voice but also their signature as an essential component of the body politic. When dominant political structures become unresponsive to the needs and aspirations of the majority, when they become complacent and incapable of growth and innovation, then the rebellion of youth and other segments of the populace becomes not only unavoidable but also desirable. Indeed, the desirability of revolt as a creative act is the line of thinking behind this discussion. Revolt as a massive glitch in the polity can also be viewed as a rite of purification, a collective cleansing of the communal being before renewed energies are unleashed for social reconstruction.


Having established that the physical act of actual revolt could sometimes have therapeutic and reconstructive properties, it is important to note that Africa has produced many contemporary female artists whose works stand as testaments to powerful creative agency within the continent and defiant feminist sensibilities.


“Strike a woman, strike a rock” (

imbokodo

) is a Zulu proverb that became popular after the 1956 women’s march to Union Buildings in Pretoria to protest the apartheid pass laws. It is possible to explore other equally productive meanings of rock art by rock hard people and, in this instance, the San communities of Southern Africa come to mind. The San, also known as “the First People”, can be found principally in Angola, Namibia, Botswana and, of course, South Africa. Centuries ago, they mastered the art of making paintings and engravings on rock surfaces. These works of art were not merely decorative. They tell stories, communicate healing and enact rituals for communal wellness and cohesion. In spite of colonisation and various forms of oppression, these works of art have endured and this attests to the strength and resilience of the people who created them. Indeed, San communities are littered across the Southern African region despite mounting challenges, and their survival represents a broader African narrative of durability and adaptability. Their story forms the essential backdrop to this article on women who struggle against all kinds of dispossession: political, cultural, economic, and sexist, among other types of oppression.


The work of two black South African photographers, Zanele Muholi

and Ingrid Masondo, can be construed as efforts to debunk the misrepresentations of the black African woman by centuries-long colonial imagery, on the one hand, and — in spite of the constitutional recognition of gay rights — within the matrix of a largely homophobic, patriarchal, post-apartheid South Africa, on the other. Within colonial consciousness, the black female body was preposterously exoticised, anaestheticised, and hypersexualised. By being thrust into a vortex of unruly instincts, the black African female was grossly violated in more ways than one.


Sarah Bartmann was an unfortunate indigene of what eventually became South Africa who was enslaved to be paraded in the freak shows of London and Paris during the nineteenth century on account of her well-endowed posterior ( a contemporary equivalent would be the Brazilian Butt Lift – BBL). Bartmann was constantly dehumanised, abused, and subsequently left for dead for no reason other than her natural physical attributes. Judging by her …

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Leyte farmer files harassment complaint vs military
content:
By Veronika Barbosa TACLOBAN CITY – A farmer filed a complaint on September 22 with the Commission on Human Rights Regional Office 8 against the Philippine Army’s 93rd Infantry Battalion (IB) due to intimidation against her and her family.

Accompanied by the National Union of People’s Lawyers Eastern Visayas and Katungod Sinirangan Bisayas, Brenda Lagado said that the first incident happened on July 28 in their house in Jaro, Leyte. “We were visited by elements of the Armed Forces of the Philippines. At first, they were just checking in on us but they eventually pressured us to confess that we have connections with the New People’s Army even if we have none.”

In the same month, Lagado said that her 16-year-old cousin was also interrogated by soldiers and alleged military assets.

“He [my cousin] was tending to farm animal when he was approached by seven soldiers and seven other individuals. At first, he was told to wait for a certain Basas who was supposed to talk to him but the latter did not arrive. He was instead confronted by a certain Simon who later grabbed him by the collar, hit him with a piece of chopped wood, and threatened that he will be hanged or electrocuted if he does not cooperate with them.”

Lagado said that his cousin was coerced by at least 14 men to divulge information about certain individuals that the victim does not know about.

She said that in August, a certain Sgt. Andres visited their house and compelled her to go to the barangay hall to purportedly “clear her name” which she refused to do. “We already went to the barangay before but the harassment still continued.”

In the same month, Lagado said that a child development worker of the Daycare Center where her child 3-year-old child was enrolled in, also experienced interrogation. “The teacher told us that a certain Cris Edison Rivera, who we later found out was from the 93rd IB, asked for the name and even live birth of my child. He also interrogated the teacher and asked information about our family.”

On September 11, Lagado received a letter from an unknown sender via express delivery. The letter included an unknown number and contained statements maligning Brenda and her family. “The letter pressured me to cooperate and call the number written on the letter within 24 hours or else they would let my entire family and my husband know that I have a relationship with an NPA rebel.”

“I am scared for my family and worried about my children’s safety. I am scared because the military have pictures of my family and even my children,” Lagado said. In a statement, Katungod SB condemned the 93rd IB’s series of harassment targeted against the Lagado family and their intimidation tactics involving innocent children.

“Children are not the tools of war…they should never be used, threatened, or assaulted to serve the military’s agenda. The 93rd IB, the entire AFP, and the NTF-ELCAC should all be held accountable for using a child and physically assaulting a minor to force the family to surrender or report to the 93rd IB.” Katungod SB called on the Commission on Human Rights to swiftly investigate and to protect the Lagado family against further intimidation and harassment. (DAA)

author: Julius Gavroche
title: Lessons from high school students in rebellion
content:
from

lundimatin

 #536, 05/10/2026


A surprise lesson

. It was the surprise of the start of the school year, one that no one saw coming, let alone predicted. While everyone seemed resigned to waiting for the next presidential election to hope for change, high school students burst onto the scene and shook all political agendas. Starting in a few high schools in the Paris suburbs, the revolt quickly spread throughout France. Without any leading organisation, without a party or union pulling the strings; just groups of students self-organising, blocking the entrance to their schools, and spreading the word among themselves and on social media; a sign that embers were beginning to rekindle beneath the ashes, just waiting for a spark to ignite the blaze.


This has been a spontaneous, unpredictable, and sudden revolt, like all revolts. As with the emergence of the Yellow Vest movement in the fall of 2018, and so many other social uprisings before it, in the fall of 2026, all political attention seemed destined to focus, inevitably, on the upcoming presidential elections, once again reducing aspirations for change to the bleak choice of the ballot box, to delegating power over one’s own destiny to others.


Defying all predictions, and disregarding the electoral calendar with a carefree attitude, the high school students wanted to say, first and foremost, that they existed, that their present and future lives had value. Even though, as minors, they had no right to vote and no added value for political parties.


They had reasons to revolt. Those put forward, relayed by the student unions, denounced overcrowded classrooms, fragmented and restrictive schedules, unfilled teaching positions, and dilapidated and unsanitary school buildings. They also denounced the humiliation and incongruity of the cell phone ban in schools, given that their teachers, like the parliamentarians who voted for it, were constantly glued to their phones. They were treated like children who needed to be punished and disciplined, even though they were young adults who refused to resign themselves to a bleak and undesirable future.


Clearly, behind the structural reasons for the lack of resources and the state’s disinvestment in national education, lie deeper criticisms. At its core, it is a denunciation of the school system of a so-called Republic which, under the guise of formal equality, merely reproduces and perpetuates class and racial privilege and discrimination.


A lesson in sociology

. What is entirely new in the history of student revolts, from 1968 to the present day, is that the movement of autumn 2026 is not led by students from the city center, by offspring of the bourgeoisie who have (temporarily) deviated from their social class, but by high school students from working-class neighbourhoods. Moreover, those most mobilised in the struggle appear to be students from vocational high schools, already steered toward work and excluded from higher education. Furthermore, images of the blockades show that many of the rebellious high school students have Black or brown skin. These are young French people, of course, representing this new France which, while not recognised and appreciated by white supremacists (except, marginally, for the performances of PSG football players and the national football team), embodies its history and its future.


This is very likely why the State and its government decided, from the very first blockades, not to listen to the voices, the grievances, the demands of the striking high school students, but to repress them immediately and brutally. It’s unspoken, hidden, certainly not openly displayed, but how can one not suspect that behind the (completely unnecessary) decision to immediately resort to force in response to the students’ demands, there lies a deep-seated racism embodied by the Minister-Prefect of Police and so many officers under his command? That, like

Éric Zemmour

 and many other descendants of Oran settlers,

Laurent Nuñez

 is consumed by resentment and a visceral hatred towards Arabs and Muslims? That the police, accustomed to hunting down young Arabs and Black people in the housing projects under the pretext of fighting drugs, do not feel justified in beating high school students who fit the same physical profile?


A grammar lesson

. To unleash the full force of the repression, ministers, police officers, and complicit journalists set up the discrediting machine. While acknowledging …

author: groundxero
title: Jantar Mantar SIR Protests Day 2: Three Women Register Molestation Complaints Against Delhi Police Officers Including ACP, Journalists Protest Outside Police Station
content:
An independent journalist’s protest erupted outside the Parliament Street police station on 3 October 2026 after police refused to register an FIR in the case of an on duty female journalist’s complaint of molestation and assault against ACP Vivek Bhagat, only to find that several other FIRs had also not been registered. Repeated incidents of violence against women and journalists have surfaced during the protests against CEC Gyanesh Kumar. 


 


New Delhi, 3 October 2026


by

Mouli Sharma


 


After a long, spontaneous demonstration by over a hundred people, largely independent journalists, outside the Parliament Street police station between the hours of 6 PM and 11 PM, the Delhi police reluctantly accepted three complaints of molestation and assault against its officials, including ACP Vivek Bhagat.


 


The agitation began after Rosy, a journalist from News Diggy was allegedly assaulted by Bhagat while on duty covering the protests against Gyanesh Kumar in the now blockaded region of Central Delhi, following which she attempted to file an FIR against the powerful official, which the police refused to register.


 


“The Delhi Police Act entails the provision for preliminary investigation in the case of an allegation against a police officer,” said Inspector Ramesh Kumar Singh of the Parliamentary Street Police Station, who spoke to the protesting reporters after nearly five hours of continuous agitation. For these five hours, the police delayed providing even a receiving copy of the complaint or registering it in the police diary. Despite sexual assault being a cognizable offence (BNS 76), the universal provision for the immediate registry of an FIR in such a case apparently does not extend to police officers under the Delhi Police Act, 1978, said Kumar. He also mentioned that the, “Lalita Kumari judgment has been overturned, and we are no longer required to follow it,” referring to the landmark judgment which ruled out the conduct of ‘preliminary investigations’ of the kind that the police is now set to undertake in the case, which seeks to ascertain a complaint’s ‘veracity’ before the criminal investigative process (which begins with the FIR) has even begun.


 


Further, after the News Diggy team gave a call for a spontaneous protest by the city’s independent journalists in the early evening to ensure the receipt of the complaint and registry of an FIR (the former of which they succeeded in achieving after five gruelling hours outside the barricaded station), it was found that two other women had been attempting to register sexual assault complaints against police officers for their conduct during ostensible “security operations” in the region. A fourth complainant withdrew her submission upon facing familial and social pressure, while a fifth complainant, independent journalist Suhana Khan was categorically denied entry into the station.


 


“The worst part of the way these male officers conduct their so-called security operations,” Khan said, “which just means beating people, is they’ll often ask your name first. I was beaten on my privates during the July protests, I had to get stitches. My clothes were torn. And because they asked my name before doing so, I can say with certainty that they did this to me because my name is Suhana Khan.”


 


Journalists from Molitics, Khabar Lehriyan, Caravan, News Diggy, Newswine, Nation Asks, AT Live, Hind Samachaar, Online News India, and of course,

GroundXero

, were among many dozens of news platforms whose correspondents were at the scene, alongside several independent content creators, social media news-makers, and influencers like Harsh Yadav, Gajendra Singh (@desiptrakar), etc. A number of lawyers had also been called to scene after the police initially denied to accept her complaint, with Adv. Vertika Mani, Adv. Mujibur Rehman, Adv. Anupradha and Adv. Bharat Kaushik eventually made their way inside the station to represent all complainants upon pressure from protesting journalists.


 


“I was screaming myself hoarse for them to let me do my duty,” said Adv. Vertika Mani. She describes the situation as one that made her feel immensely helpless, with a group of women lawyers standing outside the jail-like barricades and a victim begging to be allowed to speak to lawyers engulfed within a sea of officers inside. She describes how the police were attempting to manipulate the victim, by asking her to point out her lawyer from among the group, knowing full …

author: rti_admin
title: Caste Denied, Gender Dismissed: Reading Literature, Love and Social Life through Selective Lenses
content:
Literature both reflects and shapes social life. This article examines how literature, people’s perspectives, and social life are deeply entangled. It asks how literary works and social relations are interpreted through selective lenses that foreground some forms of inequality while obscuring others. What readers notice in a literary work is not always separate from how they understand the social world around them. Their interpretations are shaped by what they recognise as important, what they have experienced, and what they may have learned to overlook. In this sense, reading is not simply an individual act of interpretation; it can also reveal how social inequalities are recognised, denied, or made invisible. Caste is denied in the name of progress and demanded in the name of awareness, while gender is dismissed in the name of unity. Through reflection on a poem and everyday experiences, this article shows how caste and patriarchy are intertwined rather than operating separately. Ignoring this reality reveals how easily we refuse to confront forms of inequality that do not directly affect us.

To explore this tension, we turn to the poem ଢୋଲିଆ! (Dholia/Dhulia) by the renowned poet Basudev Sunani. The poem brings together themes of love, Ganda Baja, and survival. Later circulated on social media, it offers an opportunity to consider how readers interpret literary expressions through their own social experiences and locations. The poem provides a window into how readers interpret literature through their own social locations and experiences. We should not assume that the poem has one fixed meaning. We examine how readers encounter it through their own social locations and what they see as relevant or missing. Some may respond primarily to its themes of love and connection, while others may be drawn to the social histories and inequalities that surround the lives represented in the poem. These different readings raise a question: what becomes visible when we read literature through different social experiences, and what remains invisible?

One reader asks: “Where is the caste angle?” For some readers, the question seems unnecessary: why bring caste into a poem about love and Ganda Baja? They understand the poem primarily through love, emotion, imagination, and personal expression and see these experiences as separate from social conflict. Others read the poem differently. For them, caste does not disappear simply because the poem speaks of music, intimacy, or love. Caste remains present in these experiences and shapes relationships, choices, and possibilities even when it is not explicitly named. Some feel that the poem should be read for what it expresses, without relating it to caste.

These comments therefore do more than express different opinions about the poem. They reveal how readers bring different social experiences to literature and, in doing so, make some realities visible while leaving others unseen. Reading the poem thus becomes a negotiation over not only what it means, but also whose social reality counts in making that meaning.

However, the poem can also be read through a caste angle, even though caste is not always explicitly named. The poem’s representation of intimacy makes visible the experience of being Ganda/Dom, the Dhulia’s encounter with untouchability, and the difficulty of crossing caste boundaries. The possibility of a relationship between a Dhulia and an upper-caste woman cannot be separated from these social relations. For the Dhulia, caste shapes how he is seen, approached, and touched; for the upper-caste woman, entering into an intimate relationship with him means crossing a boundary that caste has historically made difficult to cross. These realities reveal the caste dimension of the poem, even when caste itself remains unnamed.

Readers, however, respond to this poem differently. Their responses reveal the social lenses through which they approach literature. What one reader recognises as part of everyday social reality may remain invisible to another. This difference is not necessarily a limitation of the poem; it reflects the unequal social experiences that readers bring to their interpretations. Lived experience and social location shape how people understand everyday life, as caste continues to organise relationships, marriage, belonging, and social relations.

Caste shapes where people live and whom they marry. It shapes how families respond to relationships and friendships …

author: Abahlali_3
title: We Welcome the President’s Response to Femicide, but Much More Must Be Done
content:
1 October 2026 Abahlali baseMjondolo Women’s League Press Statement

We Welcome the President’s Response to Femicide, but Much More Must Be Done

On 28 September 2026, after 11 women had been murdered in Ekurhuleni since July, Abahlali baseMjondolo and other residents of Ekurhuleni marched in Kempton Park against the killing of women and the failure of the police to adequately protect women from violence. We handed a memorandum to the Kempton Park Police Station and Ekurhuleni District Management.

•⁠ ⁠A public report on the investigations into the 11 murders, presented at an open public meeting. •⁠ ⁠A well-funded and properly equipped women-led GBV task team for the townships and shack settlements of Ekurhuleni. •⁠ ⁠A 24-hour Victim Support Room at Kempton Park Police Station with properly trained female officers. •⁠ ⁠Daily visible and women-friendly policing in high-risk areas, with additional patrols at night and on weekends. •⁠ ⁠A public audit of all GBV cases reported in Ekurhuleni since July. •⁠ ⁠An open public meeting at which the police must account to the women of Ekurhuleni for failures in responding to GBV and femicide. •⁠ ⁠The election of a women’s committee to which the police must report every week on their work relating to GBV and femicide.

We therefore welcome much of what President Cyril Ramaphosa announced in his address to the nation on 29 September.

The investigation into the Ekurhuleni killings has been elevated to the national level, a specialised multidisciplinary investigation is under way and visible policing in Ekurhuleni has been increased.

The President also announced a national case-recovery operation for unresolved murders, attempted murders, rapes and serious sexual offences involving women and children. The commitment to audit unresolved cases, identify delays and establish recovery plans for stalled cases is in accordance with the demands that we made in Kempton Park.

He made a commitment to address forensic backlogs, give urgent priority to forensic evidence in cases involving the rape and murder of women and children, and report publicly on progress.

The President has also made it clear that women must not be turned away by the police, that protection orders must be enforced, that dockets must not disappear and that women reporting violence must be treated with dignity. These are all issues raised directly in our memorandum.

Along with all these measures we strongly welcome the announcement that every municipality must conduct a women’s safety audit. Broken streetlights, unsafe transport routes, abandoned buildings and neglected public spaces all place women in danger. In shack settlements a lack of lighting, unsafe or absent toilets and unsafe routes through our communities put women and girls at risk every day. We need safe and reliable public transport, including at night and early in the morning, and safe routes between our homes, transport stops, workplaces, schools and shops.

We strongly support the President’s recognition that harmful alcohol use is ‘a significant aggravating factor in interpersonal violence’, his call for the stronger enforcement of liquor laws and his instruction that a package of laws and enforcement measures to reduce alcohol-related violence be put before Cabinet within 60 days. This must include reducing the excessive concentration of alcohol outlets, restricting trading hours and enforcing clear closing times, tighter licensing controls, and much stronger regulation of alcohol advertising, promotion and sponsorship. Government must regulate the alcohol industry and resist corporate pressure to weaken, delay or block effective regulation. The long-delayed Liquor Amendment Bill should be revived and debated urgently. Serious regulation of the alcohol industry is a critical part of the struggle against violence in general.

But much more needs to be done.

Women cannot just be called to meetings to be informed about decisions that have already been taken for us without us. Women must have real power and working class and poor women, who are the majority, must have real power.

This is why our memorandum demanded an elected women’s committee to which each police station must report every week. Democratically organised women must be able to demand information about investigations, police response times, missing dockets, failures to enforce protection orders and complaints against police.

Every woman must also have the right to know who is …

content:
Komeleya Rojnamegerên Jin a Mezopotamyayê (MKG) rapora xwe ya binpêkirina mafên jinên rojnameger a meha Îlona 2026an aşkere kir.


MKGê, di raporê de bal kişand ser astengiyên li qadê, şert û mercên xebatê yên ji bo rojnamegerên jin û sansura li ser çapemeniyê.


MKGê diyar kir ku di meha Îlonê de zext bi awayên cûr bi cûr li ser rojnamegerên jin berdewam kirin û wiha got: 


“Lêpirsîn û dozên li dijî çalakiyên rojnamegeriyê, astengiyên li pêşiya nûçeyan, binçavkirin û girtin, gef û êrîş û sansura dîjîtal qada xebatê ji bo rojnamegeran teng kir. Geşedanên di tevahiya mehê de nîşan dan, raporên nûçeyan û çalakiyên rojnamegeriyê wekî bingehek ji bo tawanbarkirinê têne bikaranîn. Darizandinên bi salane berdewam dikin, dozên nû tên vekirin û berdewama biryarên girtinê nîşan dide ku zexta darazê ya li ser rojnamegeran domdar bûye. Astengiyên li qadê şert û mercên xebatê ji bo rojnamegeran jî dijwar kirin. Destwerdana li ser nûçeyan, dûrxistina rojnamegeran a ji qadê, gef û êrîşan nîşan dan ku gihiştina nûçeyan her diçe bi sînordar dibe. Di meha Îlonê de, qada dîjîtal jî yek ji wan deveran bû ku zext lê zêde bûn. Xwegihandina platformên medya dîjîtal ên gelek koman, rojnameger, sazî û dezgehên medyayê, rêxistinên jinan û parêzvanên mafên mirovan, hate astengkirin. Bi vê yekê di heman demê de xwegihandina raya giştî ya dezgehên agahdariyê jî hatin sînordarkirin.”


“Divê astengiyên li pêşiya rojnamegeran werin rakirin”


MKGê di berdewamiya raporê de bi lêv kir ku zextên li ser rojnamegeran li cihên kar jî berdewam kir. MKGê da zanîn ku ji kar derxistin, mobîng û şert û mercên bêewle zêde bûne û hebûna jinan a di qada çapemeniyê de zehmet bûye û wiha hate gotin: 


“Bûyerên meha Îlonê nîşan didin ku dema rojnameger nûçeyan çêdikin, li qadê dixebitin, di pêvajoyên darazê de û li qada dîjîtal di bin zextê de ne. Divê rojnamegerên girtî werin berdan û hemû astengiyên li pêşiya xebatên rojnamegeran werin rakirin.”

author: Marcelo Oliveira
title: Mulheres são maioria das vítimas de violência política, mesmo sendo minoria das candidatas
content:
O primeiro turno da campanha eleitoral de 2026 durou 50 dias e registrou 134 episódios de violência política contra candidatos e candidatas, além de agentes políticos.

Um aumento de 11% em relação aos 121 casos registrados no mesmo período da eleição municipal de 2022.


Os 134 episódios representam um caso de violência política a cada nove horas de campanha.

 E apesar das mulheres serem apenas 35% do total de candidatos, elas foram a maioria (52%) das vítimas do primeiro turno, segundo o levantamento.


Os dados integram a 4ª edição da pesquisa Violência Política e Eleitoral no Brasil, realizada pelas organizações de direitos humanos Terra de Direitos e Justiça Global, que pesquisa o tema desde 2016. O levantamento foi divulgado nesta quarta, dia 7 de outubro.


A porcentagem de

vítimas mulheres aumenta

 mais ainda quando a pesquisa separa apenas os casos envolvendo candidatas e candidatos. Dos 134 episódios de violência política durante o primeiro turno, 102 foram dirigidos a pessoas que disputavam o pleito. Desse total, 60 eram mulheres, quase 59% do total.


Para a coordenadora do Setor de Incidência da Terra de Direitos, Gisele Barbieri, “os dados trazem importantes achados para identificar os ambientes em que agentes políticos estão mais vulneráveis e pensar medidas de proteção. Quando eleitas, essas pessoas passam a ser vítimas de violências nos seus locais de atuação, seja no Parlamento ou no Executivo”, afirma.


Machismo e misoginia se misturam nos casos de violência política


A pesquisa mostra que a violência política é marcada pela discriminação de gênero e raça.

Quando se considera o universo completo de 70 casos de violência política contra mulheres, 45 casos envolveram machismo ou misoginia, nove envolveram racismo e cinco envolveram transfobia. Mulheres pretas foram vítimas de 25% dos casos de violência política medidos nesse primeiro turno.


A ameaça foi o tipo de violência política mais recorrente no período, com 64 casos registrados. Na sequência, aparecem 33 episódios de ofensa e 19 de agressão física. Também foram registrados 11 atentados, cinco casos de criminalização e dois assassinatos.


Mais da metade dos casos (71 ocorrências) aconteceu nas ruas, durante atividades públicas de campanha. O ambiente virtual concentrou 31,3% dos episódios.


Além disso, apenas candidatas sofreram ameaças de violência sexual. Em todos os sete casos, as vítimas eram mulheres.


“Enquanto os homens são atacados por sua atuação política, mulheres, pessoas negras e pessoas trans enfrentam também o racismo, o machismo e a transfobia que estruturam a sociedade brasileira”, afirmou em nota Glaucia Marinho, diretora-executiva da Justiça Global.


Policiais e outros agentes públicos foram a maioria dos autores


Em quase 20% dos casos o autor identificado da violência política era um agente público, incluindo parlamentares e forças de segurança.

Até o encerramento da coleta de dados pelas organizações autoras da pesquisa, nenhum dos 134 episódios havia resultado em alguma punição efetiva, limitando-se a medidas cautelares de urgência determinadas pela Justiça Eleitoral.


A região Nordeste liderou o número de casos (48), seguido pelo Sudeste (38). Entre os estados, São Paulo lidera com 16 casos, seguido por Rio Grande do Norte (13), Minas Gerais (12) e Rio Grande do Sul (10).


A presença de policiais entre os autores de violência política já havia sido detectada também em

levantamento

 realizado pela

Agência Pública

 durante o primeiro turno.

title: "We're Everywhere, My Love” “Nous sommes partout, mon amour”
content:
12-09 projection du film DIREN AYOL de Rüzgâr Buski (2016, durée 59'), suivie d'une discussion en visio avec le réalisateur et des personnes présentes dans le film (en Turquie et à Marseille) au centre LGBTQIA+.


Campagne internationale en solidarité avec la communauté LGBTQI+ en Turquie


Le 12 octobre marque le premier mois de l'opération de répression et d'intimidation « Ma famille est en sécurité », conduite par les autorités turques contre des personnes LGBTQI+ partout en Turquie. Menée à l'aube, à domicile, cette vague coordonnée de perquisitions et d'arrestations a ciblé les organisations LGBTQI+, en soutien aux personnes vivant avec le VIH, les militant·e·s, les défenseur·euse·s des droits humains. Un mois plus tard, des personnes sont toujours derrière les barreaux et la pression se poursuit. « Un mois, c'est déjà trop long ». Libération immédiate des 85 personnes détenues !


La communauté LGBTQI+ de Turquie appelle à des actions de solidarité de partout dans le monde le 12 octobre.


À Marseille, une soirée aura lieu lundi 12 octobre à partir de 18h30 au Centre LGBTQIA+ (17 rue du Chevalier Roze, 13002 ) avec la projection du film DIREN AYOL de Rüzgâr Buski (2016, durée 59'), suivie d'une discussion en visio avec le réalisateur et des personnes présentes dans le film (en Turquie et à Marseille).

author: TGEU
title: Türkiye’s crackdown on LGBTI rights – the impact on trans people in prison
content:
Since 12 September 2026, Turkish authorities have intensified a nationwide crackdown on LGBTI people, organisations and human rights defenders. At least 117 people have reportedly been detained, with at least 83 held in pre-trial detention. 


The operation, branded “My Family is Safe” has involved arrests, raids on homes and organisations, digital restrictions, and the use of ‘public-morality’ and ‘obscenity’ provisions under Turkish criminal law. 


The impact on trans people


Criminalisation, discriminatory policing and restrictive prison practices in Türkiye come together to heighten risks for trans people in detention. At least 27 of those placed in pre-trial detention are trans women, many of whom have been charged with ‘prostitution’ and/or ‘obscenity’ offences. 


Trans detainees report strip searches and humiliating treatment and placement in detention arrangements that do not match their gender identity. Prison reports describe prolonged isolation, barriers to hormone treatment and HIV medication, limits on clothing and belongings, access to drinking water, overcrowding, and difficulty reaching legal and medical support.


The wider context in Türkiye


These developments should be understood against a broader deterioration in the legal and political environment for LGBTI people in Türkiye. Since 2025, restrictions on trans-specific healthcare, public expression and LGBTI civil society have grown. Proposed legislation would further limit legal gender recognition, trans healthcare and gender expression. Some restrictions not yet in law are reportedly already applied in practice.


Our calls to action


To the Turkish government:


Unconditionally release all persons detained for their human rights work and for exercising their rights to freedom of expression, association or peaceful organising.


End the use of vague provisions on ‘obscenity’ and ‘indecent acts’ to criminalise LGBTI people, particularly trans people, and the organisations defending their rights, including through investigations and prosecutions targeting lawful expression, advocacy and community organising.


End torture and ill-treatment in police custody and prisons toward trans and LGBTI+ people in prison, including humiliating and abusive strip searches. 


Ensure that trans people in prison are placed in detention facilities and accommodation arrangements that respect their gender identity. 


Guarantee continuous access to hormone treatment, HIV medication and other essential healthcare, including during transfer between detention facilities.


To the EU, Council of Europe, United Nations, Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (OSCE)/ Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR), diplomatic missions, human rights organisations, donors and partners:


Condemn the raids and detentions directly to the Turkish authorities.


Press for safeguards against further reprisals.


Defend human rights defenders and freedom of association, publicly and in political dialogue


To the EU and European governments:


Raise the detained people’s cases, especially trans prison conditions, with Turkish authorities.


Monitor detention and court proceedings, including through diplomatic presence at hearings.


Activate legal, protection and emergency support for those affected.


To European institutional funders:


Stand by civil society partners and maintain funding.


Reject attempts to criminalise international support for human rights work.


Your support makes change possible


We work across Europe and Central Asia to advance trans rights, build strong communities, and drive change through research, advocacy, and community-building.


Your donation helps us continue this vital work — defending trans lives, amplifying trans voices, and advocating for justice every day.

author: Girard Mariano Lopez
title: Taipei Gay Bar Raid Sparks Protest, Scrutiny Of City’s Commitments to LGBTQ+ Rights
content:
A POLICE RAID on a longstanding gay bar in Taipei sparked a lightning protest and demands for independent oversight after patrons alleged humiliation and discrimination, prompting disciplinary action against officers and an apology from the mayor weeks before the city’s annual Pride celebrations.

About 100 to 200 people gathered at 1 p.m. Oct. 4 outside a police substation near Red House, a landmark in Taipei’s LGBTQ+ district. After speeches, demonstrators marched through the busy neighborhood to the Ximending Police Station which reportedly dispatched the order to raid the gay bar, demanding an explanation and apology for the previous afternoon’s operation at Commander D.

The dispute has drawn scrutiny of police treatment of sexual minorities and intensified questions about whether Taipei’s promotion of LGBTQ+ inclusion abroad is reflected in its policing at home.

Officers entered the BDSM-themed bar Oct. 3 with what police described as a court-issued search warrant obtained under prosecutors’ supervision following complaints about suspected sexual offenses. Police said the establishment had received 13 complaints this year.

Authorities said 51 people were referred for suspected violations of the Social Order Maintenance Act and the operator for a suspected criminal offense. That account differed from protest speakers’ figure of 59 people taken for questioning.

Protest organizers said the operation lasted nearly five hours. They alleged officers refused to show customers the warrant, ordered people to squat and restricted conversation and cellphone use. Patrons also reported being prevented from putting on clothing before being taken to the police station.

Organizers said officers directed derogatory comments about sex toward a wheelchair user and handcuffed the manager, who they alleged was ordered to kneel after protesting police conduct.

Police initially denied insulting disabled patrons and maintained that officers followed lawful procedures. By Oct. 5, however, authorities acknowledged inappropriate remarks by four officers after reviewing recordings. Each received two reprimands, the supervising investigation chief received a demerit, and the Wanhua precinct chief requested two reprimands for inadequate supervision.

Police maintained that the warrant had been displayed, leaving conflicting accounts about whether customers were adequately informed of the search’s basis.

The operation followed a September council exchange in which Democratic Progressive Party Councilor Hung Chien-yi raised allegations that minors were entering the establishment and being treated as sexual playthings. Mayor Chiang Wan-an subsequently ordered police to investigate.

Commander D denied the allegations, saying it checked identification and ages at entry. The bar, which said it had operated for 14 years, distinguished private interactions between adult customers from activities arranged or directed by its management and said it would cooperate with lawful investigations.

Although speculation linked the raid to drugs, police publicly described its basis as suspected sexual offenses. At Sunday’s protest, Green Party city council candidate Wang Chen-ting rejected suggestions that the operation uncovered illegal drugs.

Wang said medications examined by officers included HIV prevention drugs and produced no positive drug findings. Wang also alleged that records showed eight police inspections of the venue within 15 days the previous month.

People taken for questioning were denied food and water for hours and faced leading questions about sexual activity, Wang said.

Protest organizers also reported police visits to Hunt and Locker Room, two other gay venues, that night. They demanded an explanation of the legal justification for the operations and questioned whether queer gathering places were being subjected to discriminatory scrutiny.

Outside Ximending Police Station, demonstrators called for the police chief to come down, explain the operation and apologize. Instead, Wanhua internal affairs officer Lin Sheng-wei addressed the crowd, promising an investigation and disciplinary action where warranted, without offering an apology.

“If our colleagues are at fault, they should be disciplined,” Lin said.

Organizer Yang Kang concluded by handing Lin a copy of Taiwan’s Code of Criminal Procedure, underscoring protesters’ demand that officers follow legal safeguards when exercising police powers.

author: groundxero
title: The revolutionary act of womanly love
content:
Ashley Tellis

 thinks Karthik Subbaraj’s

Dorothy

, currently making waves in Tamil Nadu, is, like some other of his films, a feminist cult classic


 


Karthik Subbaraj’s

Dorothy

 ushers in the return of Tamil cinema but, more importantly, will go down in history as one of popular Tamil cinema’s most powerful feminist films. At the heart of it, like his earlier film

Iraivi

, and arguably many other of his films, is a critique of Tamil patriarchy from the position of the feminine, this time occupied in the world not just by women but also by certain sexual minorities. That he combines this deftly with a critique of caste and class in the Tamil heartland makes it an even more powerful exposé of Tamil patriarchy.


 


At the heart of Subbaraj’s vision is the idea of woman as goddess (

Iraivi

 means goddess), a very powerful trope in Tamil Nadu. Subbaraj’s genius is not just that he exposes the hollowness of the worship of woman as goddess in Tamil Nadu by showing how woman (and woman-identified subjects, which include

aravanis

, effeminate gay men and trans women) are actually treated but also to wield the affective power of the goddess figure in Tamil Nadu to work against sexual oppression, caste violence and class inequality, in a very grounded, material sense that actually has nothing to do with goddess worship.


 


Sexual Oppression: The feminist heart of

Dorothy


 


At the heart of the film is an

aravani

1

 who has been in denial of her

aravani

ness all her life, not least because of the terrifying violence her misogynist, classist and casteist family (comprising only of men – a father and two much older brothers) will visit upon her should she reveal it, but also because she is terrified of losing the love of her life, her childhood friend, whom she plays male buddy to all her life just to keep him close. That he, the love of her life, is of a lower caste than her (as with all Tamil cinema, actual castes are never mentioned in the film, especially when they are most at play – one of the curiosities of Tamil cinema) makes her eventual transgression even more delicious.


 


However, when things get out of hand, she explodes, becomes herself and the first words she utters while beating up her hideous brothers and father are, “Not ladyboy (what they insult her with, in her sari) but woman!


 


This identification with woman and wanting to be a woman is not the North American and Western European (including, especially, British) transgender claim to

be

 woman, with its entitlement, abuse and nastiness, increasingly visible in India too, in the fledgling transgender movement here. It is an identification

with

 women, with the position of woman in culture, woman as placeholder for different kinds of violences, all of which are contested in the film.


 


Indeed, images of dead, violated and violable women float through the film: the murdered mother, the murdered (and possibly raped) sister and the eponymous figure, who is so beautiful, she is likened to a doll (also possibly raped and definitely murdered) – all three women’s murders passed off as suicides; the lower caste woman who comes to ask for her pawned jewellery back so she can conduct her daughter’s marriage who is threatened with rape; the woman beaten by her father and mother for entertaining a boy at home. All the women in the film are under siege.


 


Yet these women, through, and perhaps because, of their oppression, identify with other figures claiming the placeholder woman. It is a precarious claim, to a very precarious position and the women see the utter bravery and the sheer madness of it. It is what they have themselves.


 


There is a very interesting verbal Freudian slip of the tongue in the film where the word the lover wants to use for women is ‘acceptance’ but he instead says the ‘arrogance’ of women. He is immediately corrected but the word is actually appropriate because Subbaraj actually believes women are arrogant, and should be arrogant, about their values of empathy, warmth, love, acceptance, anti-casteism, anti- marginalisation of any kind, anti-violence and anti-murder, even when murder seems so powerfully called for (as in a key moment in the film, and the ability to love the unlovable i.e. men.


 


Of course, the lover is using the word for the protagonist, who is not a woman but she identifies as one. She is one of the many figures that constitute the figure woman in the film and in the world. She …

author: Freya Hedley
title: One Nation doesn’t offer young or trans people a future
content:
The public’s distrust of the two parties, and the system in general, has become more pronounced over the last five years. Neither Labor or the Coalition have done anything to allay people’s fears, instead adopting some of One Nation’s (ON) policies.

Working class people’s lives have gotten harder, because wages have stagnated and the prices of basic goods and housing have continue to rise. People’s shopping baskets are lighter, but costing more.

Most young people have only experienced low wages and the loss of services.

People are scared, but also pissed off. This mood was palpable during COVID-19, but it never really went away after the pandemic restrictions lifted.

We are scared for our futures in a chaotic world, where governments wage continuous wars, and the climate emergency is getting worse.

The institutions people once believed in have betrayed them.

When people are in a state of constant anxiety, they look for the easiest answer.

That’s a factor in why ON won the by-election of the historically safe Labor seat of Secret Harbour in Western Australia.

But while ON likes to portray itself as a “protest” party — against the two major parties — its policies are just as pro-capitalist. Billionaire Gina Rinehart’s donation of a $2 million plane to Pauline Hanson and the Murdoch media’s adoration of ON makes that pretty clear.

Voting ON would be like shooting ourselves in the foot. This is because Hanson is opposed to wage rises above the rate of inflation; ON opposed the Fair Work Commission’s June decision to raise the minimum wage by 5.97%. The party will never support workers and less so unemployed workers or anyone on welfare.

Hanson subscribes to former Coalition Prime Minister Scott Morrison’s view that Australians deserve “a fair go for those who have a go”. It suggests that fairness only applies to the “deserving”.

ON has welcomed the NDIS cuts, even though they will destroy the lives of thousands. It believes that “people taking advantage of the [NDIS] system” and said “bogus therapies” must be discontinued.

ON wants Australia to withdraw from the United Nations Paris Agreement on cutting carbon pollution. It not only denies the climate science, it accuses the media of reinforcing the “illusion” of climate change by reporting on forest fires, droughts and floods.

I am a proud transgender woman and running for Socialist Alliance in the Victorian elections. Hanson’s supporters probably see me as an easy target for harassment and violence. I have already had to delete around 70 vitriolic comments from my candidate Facebook page, mostly ablest and some transphobic.

It is terrifying to know that ON, which has the backing of powerful establishment forces, is deeply against one’s fundamental right to exist.

One Nation Senator Tyron Whitten claimed that parents who support their trans kids are participating in “child abuse”. Parminder Singh, a ON candidate in Western Australia’s election last year, said that gay people are mentally ill. He apologised and Barnaby Joyce has ridiculously tried to claim that ON is one of the “gayist” political parties. But clearly, ON does not support fundamental human rights.

When you’re talking with people about who to vote for, make sure to mention that a ON is is the establishment’s “protest” party. With more power, it will make everyone’s life harder.

People are rightly fed up and there are political alternatives to the mainstream parties.

Socialist Alliance in Victoria has been at the forefront of grassroots campaigns to end Australia’s support for Israel’s genocide in Gaza, opposing the destruction of public housing, and standing up against racism.

We are helping organise the protest against Hanson on October 4 in Djilang.

Our election platform says the state must prioritise working people’s needs and direct the country’s shared wealth, created by workers, back to us first.

To quote American musician Jeff Rosenstock from my all-time favourite album Worry: “They want you to be a ghost, when they rob you of your hope, but we’ve got power when they’re not expecting anything.”

People power is the reason Coles decided not to renew its contract with AI corporation Palantir and people power is how we’ll create a more inclusive and just system for us and the planet. Join us!

[Freya Hedley is standing for Socialist Alliance in South Barwon in the Victorian elections. Get in touch to help the campaign out on geelong@socialist-alliance.org or Instagram.]

title: Los sepultureros de Gaza de Norman Finkelstein es una obra maestra
content:
Hay hechos sin consecuencias, libros sin seguimiento. ¿Qué haremos de esta monumental investigación y razonamiento que apela a nuestra conciencia y debería impulsarnos a la acción? Lo que está en juego es la esencia misma de la existencia civilizada, los valores de la Declaración Universal de los Derechos Humanos, los propósitos y principios de las Naciones Unidas. El genocidio en Gaza no es solo otro Holocausto monstruoso, es un espectáculo público.

[1]

 El fracaso de las Naciones Unidas para detenerlo y la inacción de la mayoría de los estadounidenses y europeos nos hacen a todos cómplices del crimen, porque

qui tacet consentire videtur

. Si solo somos

voyeurs

de esta masacre en curso, tenemos, como mínimo, responsabilidad moral. Por Alfred de Zayas 


En los últimos 30 años, Norman Finkelstein nos ha brindado muchos libros brillantes, entre ellos

Método y locura, Acuso, Saber demasiado,

Gaza

,

Más allá de la desfachatez

y

La industria del Holocausto.


Este libro de más de 400 páginas documenta el colapso civilizatorio de las clases dominantes en Occidente, la traición a todos los valores humanistas, el rechazo demasiado público por parte de Israel del derecho internacional y la moral, con la complicidad,

entre otros

, de Estados Unidos, Reino Unido, Francia, Alemania y la Unión Europea.


Todo esto se ve acompañado por la cacofonía de los medios de comunicación convencionales orwellianos, que difunden noticias falsas, historia falsa y leyes falsas, especialmente con respecto a los palestinos como pueblo, a quienes se les representa erróneamente como “terroristas”, cuando poseen el derecho, reconocido en el derecho internacional, a resistir la colonización y la ocupación.

[2]


Nelson Mandela también fue tildado de «terrorista», pero fue fundamental en la lucha por la liberación de su pueblo. Hoy todos reconocen que el fin del apartheid en Sudáfrica era algo que debió haberse hecho hace mucho tiempo. ¿Cuándo veremos el fin del apartheid en Israel y los Territorios Ocupados? Esto es lo que Jimmy Carter exigió en su libro

Palestina: Paz, no apartheid

.

[3]


Los políticos occidentales y los principales medios de comunicación han invertido los papeles y han culpado a la víctima de su desgracia. Israel es el terrorista que practica el terrorismo de Estado y coloca trampas explosivas en los buscapersonas, como demostró de forma obscena el primer ministro israelí Benjamin Netanyahu durante su diatriba en la Asamblea General de la ONU el 24 de septiembre de 2026.

[4]


Israel nació del terrorismo

[5]

 contra británicos y palestinos, ha sido un Estado agresor desde su creación, en un sentido muy real un

Estado fallido

, porque no ha aprendido a vivir en paz con sus vecinos.


Israel ha atacado Líbano, Siria, Irak, Irán, Egipto, etc. En una infame operación de falsa bandera, incluso atacó el buque de inteligencia de la Armada de los Estados Unidos USS

Liberty

[6]

 en junio de 1967, matando a 34 marineros estadounidenses, en un intento fallido de involucrar a los Estados Unidos en la guerra de agresión de Israel.


Israel ha sido un estado paria desde su creación en 1948, e incluso antes.


El genocidio de Gaza no es más que una continuación de la intención criminal de establecer un «Gran Israel» anacrónico e imperialista en medio del mundo árabe y musulmán.


[Fuente:

cartooningforpeace.org

]


Sin duda, los gobiernos de Israel, Estados Unidos y la UE están moralmente en bancarrota.

[7]


Lamentablemente, la

percepción

de la realidad es más determinante que la realidad misma. Dado que nuestras acciones están condicionadas por la información de la que disponemos, nuestro juicio se ve influenciado —e incluso subvertido— por las narrativas odiosas que recibimos de los principales medios de comunicación, y nuestras opiniones se distorsionan por el incesante discurso de odio y la propaganda contra los palestinos. Esto constituye una incitación al odio y a la violencia, en contravención del artículo 20 del Pacto Internacional de Derechos Civiles y Políticos.

[8]


Los principales medios de comunicación difunden la versión israelí y suprimen las opiniones disidentes. No solo nos mienten, sino que nos privan de información crucial que cambia radicalmente la situación.


El público es manipulado, pero muchos se dejan manipular. Como escribió Julio César en

De Bello Civili (II, 27, 2): «quae volumus, ea credimus libenter»

(Creemos lo que queremos creer). O peor aún, como decían los romanos …
