author: Kullathida Krajangkul & Elliot Lodge
title: Thailand’s Anti-Israeli Protest Wave Isn’t About Palestine
content:
On a hot and humid morning in early September, hundreds of people gathered outside the Israeli embassy in Bangkok. While a few carried familiar symbols of Palestinian solidarity – a flash of red, black, white and green here, a watermelon there – a far greater number came carrying Thai flags. For every placard demanding an end to the genocide, or a boycott of Israel, many more bore nationalist statements, from “Thailand is not for sale” to the openly antisemitic “You Jewish folks don’t understand Thai culture, so get out”.


Thailand has been awash with anti-Israeli sentiment over the past few weeks, resulting in unprecedented mobilisations in the capital and on the country’s largest and most touristic island, Phuket. While Palestine solidarity has played a small part in these protests, they have mostly been organised by prominent rightwing agitators calling on supporters to “take Thailand back”.


Unlike in other parts of the world, where protests condemning Israel’s ongoing genocide in Gaza and occupation of the West Bank have become a mainstay of progressive politics, until recently, few Thais seemed interested. Palestine solidarity was the quiet work of Muslim communities, a handful of student and left activists, and a small number of campaigning organisations. 


In one fortnight, the right mobilised more Thais against Israel than years of solidarity campaigning had managed.


‘My money builds your country.’


Israeli tourists, many of them recently discharged soldiers seeking a dose of tropical hedonism and escape, have long been a cause of consternation for Thai locals. In the past few years, as Israeli tourists have arrived in ever greater numbers,

reaching a record 405,000 in 2025

, hotspots such as the backpacker village of Pai in the north and the island of Koh Phangan have been visibly transformed by the influx, with entire parts of town now catering almost exclusively to the Israeli market. 


Labour, meanwhile, runs the other way.

Some 65,000 Thais are currently working in Israel

, most of them on farms,

in jobs once done by Palestinians.

 Since October 2023, when Israel suspended the permits of more than 100,000 West Bank workers, it has leaned on Thai labour harder still. “They’re trying to prevent Palestinians from getting jobs in Israel,” said Saowaluck Phothingam of Socialist Worker Thailand. “The way they do that is by importing foreign labour instead.” It’s “a problem of inequality” Saowaluck added. Thais go to Israel to do the work Palestinians are no longer permitted to do; Israelis come to Thailand to be served.


Reports of Israeli tourists behaving badly regularly surface in Thai media, with almost the entire country now seeming to have watched a video that went viral last year, of an

incensed Israeli tourist telling a worker that “my money builds your country”

, after she was asked to take her shoes off in a restaurant. 


It isn’t just Israelis upsetting the locals. Despite Thailand’s significant reliance on tourism revenue, anti-foreigner sentiment is on the rise more generally. In one of a spate of recent incidents, a group of Italian students were

forced into a public apology in late July

. Their crime? Being loud and inconsiderate on public transport. Yet Israelis have become a particularly problematic category of foreigner in the public imagination, with attention shifting from individual misbehaviour to Israeli-owned businesses.


And it’s true that something more organised than backpacking has grown alongside the Israeli influx. On Koh Phangan, for instance,

one in seven registered companies now has Israeli shareholders

. One of these businesses is a centre called David’s Circle, which had taken in more than 900 Israelis by last May, about half of them discharged soldiers. Its founder, the trauma specialist Yael Shoshani-Rom,

told the Times of Israel

 she wanted “something like a Chabad house, but therapeutic”, a reference to the Orthodox Jewish outreach centres that follow Israeli backpackers around the world. David’s Circle runs in partnership with Let’s Do Something, a nonprofit founded by friends of a young Israeli murdered at the Supernova festival, which also produces pro-Israel content and invests in what it calls “next-generation defence

s

olutions”.


For most Thais, concern about whether Israeli businesses actively support genocide is secondary to a more generalised anxiety about foreign investment and “grey” capital – the Chinese and Russian money linked …

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Festival-themed protest underscores teachers’ economic demands
content:
MANILA – On World Teachers’ Day, members of the Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) held a protest near Malacañang Palace billed as “Pistang Protesta: Dagdag Sweldo, Hindi Dagdag Trabaho.”

Teachers from different public and private schools all over Metro Manila, as well as students and supporters marched Padre Noval Street corner España Boulevard toward Mendiola, October 5, 2026.

Carrying bunting flags and surrounded by ice cream carts, protesters called for a reduced and humane workload, allocation of six percent of GDP to education, P5,000 (approximately US$79.68) economic relief allowance and P50,000 (approximately US$796.81) entry-level salary for all teachers.

The current starting basic pay of a Teacher is pegged at P31,705 (approximately US$505.26) while the economic relief allowance is only P2,000 (approximately US$31.87)

Hogier Villarias, secretary general of Alliance of Concerned Teachers NCR, said that their call for salary hike is timely considering the increase in the country’s Gross Domestic Product.

“Our primary call remains a salary increase since our GDP grew by four percent, so we are expecting that wages should also be increased,” said Villarias, who joined the protest along with his fellow teachers from Andres Bonifacio Elementary School.

According to the Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA), the GDP of the country grew by 4.4 percent in 2025. However, progressive groups argued that economic growth is meaningless if it does not translate to higher wages and better working conditions.

Katrina Ortega, president of All UP Academic Employees Union Diliman, meanwhile, pointed out wrong priorities of the Marcos Jr. administration.

“We cannot accept that funds are diverted to confidential funds and flood control projects while we lack teachers and classrooms. The children suffer — they have no learning materials, and even basic school needs like water and comfort rooms are lacking. All of these affect the children,” Ortega stated.

In the proposed P7.2-trillion (approximately US$114.74 billion) national budget for 2027, P1.326 trillion (approximately US$21.13 billion) is allotted for the education sector — P975.96 billion (approximately US$15.56 billion) for the Department of Education and P176.5 billion (approximately US$2.81 billion) for higher education. This is around 1.41 percent lower than the P1.345 trillion (approximately US$21.43 billion) allocated in 2026.

The proposed P1.467 trillion (approximately US$23.38 billion) fund for the government-wide infrastructure program is still 10.6 percent higher than the budget proposed for education. Moreover, there is also a roughly 13.8 percent increase in infrastructure budget from the P1.29 trillion (approximately US$20.56 billion) allocated in 2026.

Infrastructure projects are vulnerable to political patronage, according to the People’s Budget Coalition (PBC). In fact, the coalition identified P970 billion (approximately US$15.46 billion) worth of potential ‘pork’ from the proposed 2027 budget as they observed patterns of alleged political influence particularly in flood-control projects.

Concerns over potential misuse and abuse of these funds fueled protesters’ calls for a different direction in government spending. Progressive groups are urging the administration to stop feeding political interests and instead pour more funds toward public welfare programs.

During the protest, former ACT Teachers Party-list Representative France Castro amplified her condemnation of corruption and demand for greater funding for social services, including education.

“From the passage of the budget to its signing into law, the budget is full of corruption — this is what we are opposing. What we are demanding is funding for social services, education, housing, and others,” Castro said.

Protesters said their fight doesn’t end with the dispersal, pledging to carry the fight beyond the streets and continue pushing for urgent education reforms. (RVO)

author: Shireen Akram-Boshar
title: Thousands of Cornell Students Protest for Accountability in Rape Case
content:
In a 2025 survey, 35 percent of undergraduate women reported experiencing sexual assault during their time at Cornell.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

On Monday evening, thousands of Cornell University students protested on the university campus, demanding accountability for Cornell’s alleged mishandling of the 2024 rape case that has come under a national spotlight.

Students held signs that said “We are Jane Doe,” “Stop Protecting Rapists,” and “We Want Sentences, Not Essays.”

The demonstration was organized by Students for a Democratic Cornell alongside over 20 other student organizations at Cornell, including Gender Justice Advocacy Coalition, Planned Parenthood Generation, Cornell Grad Students United, Black Students United, and other cultural organizations on campus.

Outrage has followed the case of a sexual assault that occurred in October 2024 at Cornell’s Chi Phi fraternity house, where a victim, known as Jane Doe, says that she was drugged and raped by seven fraternity members. This anger has boiled over after Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit in mid-September, pushing the local district attorney to reopen the case.

On campus, students have highlighted the university’s failure to hold the alleged perpetrators accountable, citing the university’s decision to allow some to write essays as punishment and the university police providing the district attorney with a “summary” of Jane Doe’s complaint that omitted mentions of rape, drugging, and sexual assault, leading to the DA closing the initial case.

Students for a Democratic Cornell (SDC), which called the protest, put forward demands that include an independent judicial system to replace Cornell’s current internal judicial system; an external investigation of Cornell’s administration; mandatory sexual assault prevention trainings for students; and Cornell’s compliance with New York State’s Enough is Enough law.

They have also called for the university to expel the men accused in the Jane Doe case and to revoke the degrees of those who have already graduated. (Only two of the seven men named by Jane Doe were expelled for the assault in 2025 after the university’s Title IX investigation.)

“SDC is really focused on attacking the institutional systems that enable sexual violence to be so prevalent on campus,” Jack Huber, an activist in Students for a Democratic Cornell, told Truthout.

“Between 2018 and 2024, there were over 1,200 reported instances of sexual violence on campus. Only seven of those cases resulted in expulsion,” he said. “So when we have a statistic like that, it is clear that the administration is not interested in seeking justice for survivors, and so we must return to an independent judicial system, one where decisions about discipline are not made behind closed doors based on what looks best for the university.”

Other on-campus organizations, like Cornell Graduate Students United (CGSU), have issued additional demands.

“In coalition with Students Not Bombs, we’ve publicly demanded the resignation of [Cornell University President] Michael Kotlikoff and other administrators implicated in the mishandling of Jane Doe’s case,” Cornell graduate student Kaori Quan told Truthout, speaking for CGSU.

CGSU has also called for “the abolition of Greek Life at Cornell, and the dissolution of the Office of Student Conduct and Community Standards.”

Calls to ban fraternities, and for the university president to resign, were echoed in the chants at Monday evening’s protest, with students chanting “All the frats have got to go” and “Kotlikoff has got to go.”

“The prevalence of sexual assault on campus is due in no small part to Greek life and the way Cornell promotes it,” Quan told Truthout.

“Many of the fraternities on campus have been around for decades — wealthy donors are members of these organizations, and that stream of cash incentivizes the university to preserve their reputation over the health and safety of students,” she added. “The protection that fraternities enjoy from administration makes it easier to get away with sexual assault.”

According to a 2025 survey, 35 percent of undergraduate women at Cornell — more than one in three — reported experiencing sexual assault during their time at the university.

Campus organizations are mobilizing to continue the fight for their demands beyond Monday’s demonstration …

author: Anonym
title: In Solidarität mit Daniel Viehmann, Strom-Saboteur
content:
DANKE DANIEL


Ein paar Wochen sind vergangen, seit Öko-Saboteur Daniel bundesweit Angriffe auf das Deutsche Stromnetz durchgeführt hat. Dafür hat er selbst gebaute Raketen über Hochspannungsleitungen geschossen, eine Methode, die er selbst erfunden hat. Bei einem der Angriffe in NRW gingen infolge 5 Kraftwerksblöcke (Braunkohle) für mehrerere Tage vom Netz. Es folgte viel Medienaufmerksamkeit und nach einer bundesweiten Fahndung, wurde Daniel festgenommen. Aktuell sitzt Daniel in U-Haft und es drohen ihm bis zu 10 Jahre Knast.


SEINE WORTE


Bis jetzt, haben wir wenig – oder gar keine – öffentliche Solidarität mit Daniel gesehen. Wir fragen uns was hinter dem Schweigen steckt. Für uns gibt es keinen Grund zur Stille oder gar zur Distanzierung. Mit diesem Text wollen wir dieses Schweigen brechen und zeigen das es viele Gründe gibt anzunehmen, dass Daniels Kampf gleichermaßen auch unser Kampf ist.


Die stärkste Begründung für unsere Solidarität steckt in Daniels eigenen Worten. Aus seinen Bekennerschreiben gelangen zuerst nur wenige Sätze an die Öffentlichkeit. Die veröffentlichte erste Seite gibt mehr Aufschluss über Daniels Motivationen. Hier veröffentlichen wir diese Seite (siehe Foto) und rufen dazu auf, wer Zugang zu den fehlenden Seiten seiner Bekennerschreiben hat: Gebt Daniels Worte an die Öffentlichkeit, so dass Daniel für sich selbst sprechen kann.


Was die Presse nicht berichtete, er aber selbst als Gründe für sein Handeln beschreibt: seine Aktionen wendeten sich nicht nur gegen eine fossile Stromerzeugung sondern auch gegen die deutsche Rüstungsindustrie und vor allem deren Teilhabe am Völkermord in Palästina.


EINE ADÄQUATE ANTWORT AUF DIE FOSSILE REALITÄT


„Stromerzeugung aus fossilen Brennstoffen ist ein Verbrechen, das unsägliches Leid nach sich zieht.“


Das ist kein komplizierter Zusammenhang, nichts was nicht lange wissenschaftlich verstanden ist. Die fossile Energieerzeugung ist einer der Hauptverursacher des globalen Klimawandels – all das ist einfach zu verstehen. Genauso einfach ist es, dass um aus dem Kreislauf des Leids aus zusteigen, der Ursprung dessen zerstört werden muss. Genauso logisch ist aus unserer Sicht Daniels Reaktion.


Er hatte also gute Gründe zu tun, was getan werden muss(te). So muss auch die Klimabewegung die Tatsache anerkennen, dass CO2 Emissionen weiterhin Jahr für Jahr signifikant steigen. Nach vielen Jahren weitreichendem bürgerlichen Protest und des zivilen Ungehorsam wird klar, es ist keine realistische Lösung für das Problem. Es ist also eine logische Konsequenz für die Klimabewegung Akte der Sabotage im Kampf einzusetzen.


DIE BEWEGUNG SCHWEIGT


Viele Menschen (auch Gefährt*innen) behaupten Daniel wäre entweder verrückt oder sicherlich einer von Putins Agenten. Auch sei es unlogisch, dass er seinen Namen und Adresse veröffentlicht hat. Jede dieser Argumentation befreit uns von der Pflicht (oder Chance) seine Aktionen ernst zu nehmen. Ist es nicht das was Daniel versuchte umzusetzen genau eine heimliche Sehnsucht die in vielen von uns steckt?


UND DER STAAT WILL KRITISCHE INFRASTRUKTUR BESSER SCHÜTZEN


In Folge Daniels Aktionen stellt Staat und Presse die sogenannte kritische Infrastruktur als stark-gefährdet dar. Es werden Zählungen Sabotage-Verdachtsfällen veröffentlicht, neben Daniel ein Datenleak in Berlin, und russische Drohnenangriffe am Leipziger Flughafen. Auch soll im Zuge des im März in Kraft getretenen KRITIS Dachgesetz vermehrt KI-Überwachung der sogenannten kritischen Infrastrukur (kritsch für wen und für was?) umgesetzt werden.


Unabhängig davon wie gefährdet die sogenannte kritische Infrastruktur wirklich ist, drückt die dargestellte mediale Brisanz rund um Daniels Aktionen auch die Wirksamkeit derer aus. Gesteigerte Überwachung und Repression zeigt Un-Sicherheit & Schwachstellen des Staates. Und so denken wir, wenn die eine Aktion nicht dem Trugschluss verfällt über Forderungen an die Regierenden Zustände verändern zu wollen muss vermehrte Repression erwartet werden. Alles andere hätte keinen ausschlaggebenden Effekt auf den Status Quo. So erschreckend die Unsicherheit für manche auch klingen mag, so sehr glauben wir dass sie nötig ist um tatsächlich die Zerstörung dieser industriellen Zivilisation zu stoppen.


WAS WÄRE ALSO WENN DANIELS AKTION ZÄHLT?


Wichtiger als die ‚Macht‘ die man tatsächlich hat, ist die Macht die unsere Gegner glauben das wir sie haben. Wenn also der deutsche Staat von Unsicherheit seiner kritischen Infrastruktur …

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: RCMP arrest suspect in Pangnirtung shooting
content:
The RCMP has arrested a 21-year-old man in relation to a shooting in Pangnirtung on Tuesday afternoon.


Police received reports of gunshots at around 4:03 p.m. Tuesday. Ten minutes later, they arrested Jonah Kuniliusie, according to a news release issued by Sgt. George Henrie on Thursday.


Kuniliusie faces two counts of endangering life, two counts of pointing a firearm, two counts of aggravated assault, and the unlawful possession of a weapon in public. He also faces three counts for breach of probation.


The RCMP was not immediately available to answer questions about the incident.


Deputy mayor Markus Wilcke said the event harmed everyone in the community, either directly or indirectly, including children who were nearby

when the shooting happened

.


Kuniliusie remains in custody and will have his next court appearance on Oct. 20 in Iqaluit.

author: Harriet Williamson
title: UK Terrorism Arrests up 1,553% Since Palestine Action Ban
content:
Terror arrests in the UK have increased by 1,553% and hit a record high, with the overwhelming majority linked to support for Palestine Action, new Home Office statistics show. 


3,867 arrests were made for terrorism-related activity in the year ending June 2026, compared to 234 arrests in the year ending June 2025, according to

data released by the Home Office

 on Thursday. 


Of those arrests, a whopping 3,630 – 94% – were linked to support for Palestine Action following the group’s proscription. 


The Labour government under Keir Starmer proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist group in July 2025, making it the first direct action group to be banned under the Terrorism Act in British history.


Protests against Palestine Action’s proscription, organised by campaign group Defend Our Juries (DOJ), have seen elderly and disabled people arrested and carried away by police after holding up paper signs with the words “I oppose genocide. I support Palestine Action.” 


Since the ban, terrorism-related arrests are up 1,525% on the historical ten-year median of 238 arrests.


The Home Office’s report also confirmed that 704 arrests had so far resulted in a charge, with 634 of those charges made under Section 12 or Section 13 of the Terrorism Act 2000 and linked to supporting Palestine Action. 


A spokesperson for DOJ told Novara Media: “History shows that unjust laws become unenforceable when they are met with mass opposition, until governments are eventually forced to abandon them. The statistics released today are a clear indication of just how unpopular and unenforceable the government’s ban on Palestine Action is.


“Over a year on, and hundreds of regular people are still prepared to be arrested as ‘terrorists’ to demand that the new Labour leadership to do the only sensible thing and lift the ban on Palestine Action.”


In a statement, Amnesty International UK’s law and human rights director Tom Southernden said: “The vast majority of the enormous increase in terrorism arrests are of grandparents, teenagers and everyone in between for peacefully holding placards. 


“We are seeing a shameful attack on our right to protest. It’s past time to end the proscription of Palestine Action and with it the use of counter terrorism power to punish direct action protests.”


Dozens of peaceful protesters

opposing Israel’s genocide and the ban on Palestine Action – including

a 94-year-old Jewish human rights lawyer

 – were arrested outside the Labour party conference in Liverpool at the end of September. 


The next day, foreign secretary Ed Miliband replied to a question about the proscription

from Andrew Marr on LBC

about “all those elderly people and vicars and grannies and so on” by saying: “I don’t think anyone’s intent was to have those people criminalised.” 


Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori has been granted permission to challenge the ban in the Supreme Court.

title: Cemil Tugay paylaşımı nedeniyle gözaltına alınmıştı; Berna Laçin serbest bırakıldı
content:
Fotoğraf Berna Laçin'in kişisel Instagram hesabından alınmıştır.

author: bert
title: Konto bleibt: Rote Hilfe gewinnt Hauptsacheverfahren
content:
Konto bleibt: Rote Hilfe gewinnt Hauptsacheverfahren


Die Rote Hilfe

e. V.

 hat heute auch das Hauptsacheverfahren gegen die Sparkasse Göttingen gewonnen. Das Landgericht Göttingen hat entschieden, dass die Kündigung des Kontos der bundesweiten linken Solidaritätsorganisation vom 9. Dezember 2025 keinen Bestand hat.

Bereits im Eilverfahren war die Sparkasse gescheitert. Darin 

verpflichtete zunächst das Landgericht die Sparkasse das Konto weiterzuführen

. Im Anschluss stellte das Oberlandesgericht Braunschweig fest, dass eine öffentlich-rechtliche Sparkasse ein Konto nicht ohne sachlichen Grund kündigen darf. Die von der Sparkasse vorgebrachten Gründe, dass ein erhöhter Prüfaufwand bestehe und ein Reputationsschaden bei Führung des Kontos des antifaschistischen Vereins bestehe, überzeugten das Gericht nicht.

Ein zusätzliches Risiko durch die

US

-Listung der sogenannten „Antifa Ost“ als Terrororganisation  konnte die Sparkasse nicht plausibel machen. Das

OLG

 stellte zudem klar, dass die Rote Hilfe nicht eine Organisation „Antifa Ost“ finanziert, sondern gemäß ihrer Satzung Beschuldigte und Angeklagte in den entsprechenden Verfahren unterstützt. Die

US

-Einstufung selbst entfaltet keine unmittelbare rechtliche Wirkung in Deutschland. Dieser Beurteilung des

OLG

 schloss sich das Landgericht heute »vollumfänglich« an.

Damit hat die Rote Hilfe nach den Erfolgen im Eilverfahren nun auch in der Hauptsache Recht bekommen.

Für die Rote Hilfe geht es über den eigenen Fall hinaus auch um die Frage, wie weit politische Entscheidungen und Sanktionslisten aus Drittstaaten auf zivilgesellschaftliche Strukturen in Deutschland durchschlagen können.

Hartmut Brückner vom Bundesvorstand der Roten Hilfe

e. V.

, erklärt: „Das ist ein wichtiger Erfolg für die Rote Hilfe und für alle, die sich gegen politisch motiviertes Debanking wehren. Einer Organisation die finanzielle Infrastruktur zu entziehen kann ihre Arbeit faktisch lahmlegen. Genau deshalb war es notwendig, diese Kündigung nicht einfach hinzunehmen.«

Brückner weiter: „Besonders problematisch bleibt, dass politische Entscheidungen und Sanktionslisten aus den

USA

 überhaupt solchen Druck auf zivilgesellschaftliche Strukturen in Deutschland entfalten können. Solidaritätsarbeit für Beschuldigte und Angeklagte ist keine verdächtige oder illegale Tätigkeit. Das Recht auf Verteidigung und ein faires Verfahren muss auch und gerade dann gelten, wenn Verfahren politisch aufgeladen sind.“

Die Rote Hilfe dankt der Gesellschaft für Freiheitsrechte, den beteiligten Anwält*innen, dem Netzwerk Debanking Stoppen und allen Menschen, die den Verein seit Bekanntwerden der Kontokündigung solidarisch unterstützt haben.

author: EDRi
title: No human required: Austria’s plan for AI-only government decisions
content:
A sweeping change to Austria's administrative law would let authorities issue binding decisions using AI systems with no human ever reviewing the outcome. EDRi member epicenter.works has sent an open letter to parliament, and is looking for input from readers elsewhere in Europe about how other countries are handling, or planning to handle, the same issue.

By epicenter.works (guest author) · October 8, 2026

Austria is about to find out what happens when a member state lets large language models write legally binding government decisions, with no human required to review them.

This autumn, the Constitutional Affairs Committee of Austria’s parliament will debate a sweeping change to the country’s General Administrative Procedure Act (AVG). The AVG is the default procedural code for essentially all administrative proceedings in Austria, covering everything from social assistance and building permits to business licensing and public subsidies. A single change to the general code can therefore affect how decisions get made across almost the entire administration, not just in one sector. According to the draft law, authorities would for the first time be allowed to issue fully automated administrative decisions: legally binding rulings with direct effect on a person’s rights, comparable to what other jurisdictions might call an administrative act or order, without a human ever reviewing the specific outcome before it goes out.

Ahead of this autumn’s debate, epicenter.works has written to the Constitutional Affairs Committee, sending an open letter laying out exactly why fully automated decisions with no human review are incompatible with fundamental rights.

Let’s be precise about what’s actually being automated, because the draft treats generative AI the same way previous automation laws treated simple rule-based software.

Classic automated administrative systems are deterministic: same input, same output, traceable logic. A system built on a large language model works fundamentally differently in three ways that each map directly onto a legal guarantee:

Hallucination. LLMs generate outputs that sound plausible but can be flatly wrong or entirely invented. Even specialised legal AI systems show hallucination rates of roughly 17 to 33%, and errors are often impossible for the affected person to spot. Hallucinated facts underpinning a binding decision affect the right to a fair trial under Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights: a person can’t meaningfully exercise that right when the decision against them is built on evidence that doesn’t exist.

Black box. How the system arrived at a given output is structurally not fully explainable. This is not simply “not yet documented” but not explainable even in principle with current models. That sits uneasily with a basic rule-of-law demand: that the exercise of state power be transparent and reviewable, not just efficient.

Bias. Systematic distortions like race, income level, migration status etc. are baked into how these models are trained and can’t be engineered away by picking a “better” vendor. Left unchecked, this risks group-based unequal treatment that no one notices, because the system doesn’t expose it, touching the principle of non-discrimination, which both EU law and the Austrian constitution guarantee explicitly.

These aren’t implementation flaws. They’re inherent to how current LLMs work, and every legal objection below follows directly from this technical reality.

Weeks before this autumn’s parliamentary debate, Austria’s own state-run AI assistant “ida” supplied a preview of the problem: it falsely described a sitting vice-chancellor as a former government member and invented a government minister who doesn’t exist.

A more serious example came out of the UK in July 2026. An Upper Tribunal judge found that the Home Office had refused an asylum claim, from a woman who had fled forced child marriage and severe violence, by citing a policy document that, on inspection, appears never to have existed. The judge noted the refusal letter bore the hallmarks of AI-generated content, and suggested the reference was likely an AI hallucination, warning that this would represent an extremely serious failing on the department’s part if confirmed.

Read together, these two cases show an escalation from a chatbot inventing a minister’s name in Austria to a fabricated document underpinning an actual refusal of protection in the UK, in exactly the kind of …

author: EDRi
title: EDRi-gram, 8 October 2026
content:
What has the EDRi network been up to over the past few weeks? Find out the latest digital rights news in our regular newsletter. In this edition: Turning up the heat – Commission backs social media bans, Apple held accountable, summer to-dos, & more!

This EDRi-gram edition includes a real snapshot of the disconnect between the kind of technology and protections people and communities around the world need, and the kind that are being pushed at us by lawmakers and companies either for the sake of profits, as easy fixes to structural societal issues or more sinister reasons.

Take the EU’s recently announced KIDS ACT. We unpack the many shortcomings of the proposal which is a missed opportunity to address the root cause of why online platforms are harmful to children – and everyone else. We also look at the Cloud and AI Development (CADA) Act, a part of the EU’s Tech Sovereignty Package announced earlier this year. What was sold as a way to jumpstart the EU’s “sovereign AI” ambitions seems to be set to hurt digital rights and environmental protections instead, while also imposing an unreliable technology onto us.

Elsewhere, Austria will soon get to find out what happens when AI systems are allowed to issue legally binding government decisions without any human oversight. EDRi-member epicenter.works detail the draft proposal and all the ways it could backfire.

None of the above is without resistance from those of us working to protect your rights. Dutch EDRi-member Bits of Freedom have launched a new campaign demanding a ban on Meta’s “pervert glasses”, aka, AI glasses which can be used to film people without them knowing. Meta was clearly paying attention – their viral satirical video on these glasses was removed from Instagram.

From critical campaigns, and urging EU countries to not treat data protection and “competitiveness” as opposing goals as they discuss the Digital Omnibus, to legal action against Big Tech corporations preying on our minds – we’re fighting back.

Next week, at our flagship annual event #PrivacyCamp26, we’ll be asking the real questions – where does technology come from? Who shapes it? And what would self-determination look like if it were defined by the people, not dictated by profits or a state’s agenda? We hope to see some of you attending!

title: Yıldız Teknik Üniversitesi'nde siber saldırı duyurusu: 140 bin öğrencinin verisi çalınmış olabilir
content:
Yıldız Teknik Üniversitesi'nde (YTÜ) 1 Ekim'den bu yana yaşanan sistem aksaklıklarının arkasından siber saldırı çıktı. Kişisel Verileri Koruma Kurulu'nun (KVKK) 7 Ekim tarihli kararıyla üniversitedeki veri ihlali resmi olarak kamuoyuna duyuruldu. Yaşanan siber saldırı ve veri ihlalinden yaklaşık 140 bin öğrenci ile 4 bin 500 personelin etkilendiği belirtildi.

Yıldız Teknik Üniversitesi'nde altyapı sorunu: Öğrenciler çevrimiçi derslere erişemiyor

Üniversitenin resmi internet sitesi, Öğrenci Bilgi Sistemi (OBS), Online Yıldız ve çeşitli başvuru sistemlerine günlerce erişim sağlanamazken, üniversite yönetiminin yaşanan aksaklıklara ilişkin ilk etapta kapsamlı bir açıklama yapmadığı görüldü. Yönetim, 3 Ekim'de yaptığı ilk duyuruda süreci yalnızca "teknik çalışma" olarak nitelendirmişti. Ancak KVKK'nın devreye girmesiyle birlikte sistem kesintilerinin arkasında bir fidye yazılımı saldırısının olduğu netlik kazandı.

Kişisel Verileri Koruma Kurulu’nun yayımladığı duyuruda "Veri sorumlusu sıfatını haiz Yıldız Teknik Üniversitesi tarafından Kurula iletilen veri ihlal bildiriminde özetle; ihlalin 01.10.2026 tarihinde başladığı ve aynı gün tespit edildiği, veri sorumlusunun sanallaştırma altyapısı ve üzerinde çalışan sunucuların fidye yazılımı saldırısından etkilendiği, ihlalden etkilenen ilgili kişi grubunun öğrenci, personel ve ziyaretçiler olduğu, mevcut kayıtlara göre ihlalden etkilenmiş olabilecek ilgili kişi sayısının yaklaşık 140.000 öğrenci ve 4.500 personel olduğu, ziyaretçilere ilişkin sayının henüz belirlenemediği, ihlalden etkilenen kişisel veri kategorilerinin belirlenemediği bilgilerine yer verilmiştir" ifadeleri kullanıldı.

Öğrencilerin hangi kişisel verilerinin siber saldırıdan etkilendiği ve dışarı sızdırıldığı konusundaki belirsizlikler ise hâlâ devam ediyor.

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Mike Ludwig
title: Progressives and Republicans Introduce Competing Bills to Rein In Flock Cameras
content:
The Ban Flock Act aims to slow the rise of Flock-style cameras amid rising fears about AI mass surveillance.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Republicans and Democrats in Congress have introduced competing legislation to rein in the government’s use of Flock cameras and other automated license plate readers (ALPRs) following widespread abuses by police and intense public backlash to the powerful surveillance technology.

ALPRs allow police to track vehicles and their drivers across expansive areas by using a variety of easily searchable data points from images captured by the cameras. The Ban Flock Act, backed by some Democrats and progressives, would halt federal funding to slow the rise of AI-powered surveillance nationwide. A competing GOP bill creates legal guardrails for police when using ALPR data but would not “ban” license plate surveillance by the federal government.

Introduced on October 2 by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vermont), Sen. Jeff Merkley (D-Oregon), and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York), the Ban Flock Act would prevent federal funds from being used to purchase ALPRs, including but not limited to Flock cameras. In order to incentivize a “moratorium” on the use of ALPRs by local police, only state and local governments with laws or policies in place to prohibit the use of ALPRs could continue receiving financial assistance from several federal entities, including from the Departments of Justice, Homeland Security, Transportation, Housing and Urban Development, and Health and Human Services.

The bill would also ban the use of both ALPRs and the data gathered by them at the federal level while creating a legal avenue for lawsuits against the federal government over privacy violations.

However, the legislation would not place an outright ban on the use of Flock and similar cameras attached to license plate analytics software, nor would it ban the use of AI-powered surveillance systems by local governments and private actors. The Ban Flock Act would also allow Congress to pass legislation allowing police to use ALPRs for a specific purpose with privacy restrictions, including deleting data after 48 hours. ALPRs used to collect tolls are exempt from the bill.

Speaking at an event in Bakersfield, California, on October 5, Sanders linked Flock cameras to the controversial rapid advances in AI. While the AI systems that enhance ALPR surveillance are not the most controversial frontier models still in development, AI-powered search engines made by Flock Safety and its competitors to analyze data collected by ALPRs make the systems much more powerful.

When asked by Sanders if they had heard of AI data centers and Flock cameras, the crowd booed.

“We are looking at the possibility [of] the evisceration of privacy rights in America,” Sanders said.

Flock Safety is the leading manufacturer of ALPRs along with competitors such as Axon and Motorola Solutions, which some cities are turning to as the Flock brand becomes increasingly controversial. With an estimated 120,000 ALPRs installed nationwide, Flock’s cameras alone record and analyze about 20 billion images of vehicles each month. The anti-surveillance group DeFlock has mapped more than 143,000 ALPR cameras across the lower 48 states.

ALPRs are not new, but the technology has advanced rapidly in recent years and is often integrated with AI, allowing police to effortlessly search for vehicles and people without needing to enter a license plate number. ALPRs capture images of each passing vehicle, recording location, date, and time, as well as the vehicle’s make, model, color, and identifying features such as dents, roof racks, and bumper stickers, and then turn these into searchable data points.

For example, when police in Lenexa, Kansas, put a local activist under ALPR surveillance in 2025 after he wrote an op-ed criticizing city officials and was investigated in connection to a petty vandalism case, they were able to easily track his grocery shopping habits and even identify his shoes, according to internal records.

In a statement, Ocasio-Cortez said the widespread integration of AI-powered cameras into everyday life is “unconscionable.”

author: Isaac Nellist
title: Lizzie O’Shea: ‘Surveillance technology is a threat to democracy’
content:
Lizzie O’Shea, a writer, lawyer and founder of Digital Rights Watch, told the New South Wales Council for Civil Liberties’ (NSWCCL) annual fundraising dinner and journalism awards on October 1 that rapidly developing surveillance technology is throwing up many challenges.

Digital technology and democracy are in a “significant amount of tension”, O’Shea said. She added that defending civil liberties is not about “clever people working to impose civil liberties on everybody else”, but that campaigners “have to convince a critical mass that they have to defend their own rights”.

Referencing the origins of professional policing in London in the late 18th century, she described it as “a period of immense technological disruption”, as the Industrial Revolution was reshaping society.

The new police force, O’Shea said, was used to “monitor, enforce and impose the new conditions of social order”. Specifically, it ensured merchants’ profits and prevented dockworkers from supplementing their wages by pilfering stock. The idea was to get the state and industry to collaborate, with a “form of surveillance of everyday people”.

“Policing was talked about as a new science in the detection and prevention of crime,” she said. The spectacle of force “offered an economical and effective way of maintaining order”.

O’Shea said it helps explain the state’s decisions in the digital age. “Like their historical counterparts, modern police understand the power of surveillance in enforcing a form of discipline.

“‘Safety’ is about preserving social order, rather than reducing harm. By allowing law enforcement and intelligence agencies to tell us what is safe, we allow them to use technology in increasingly oppressive ways.

“Rapid technological advances have been accompanied by disruptive transformations in social relations, and an acceleration of policing has often been a response.”

O’Shea described advances in technology in the 21st century as being “a fundamental threat” to democracy. She said more than 100 “security” bills have been passed over the past two decades, connected to surveillance, national intelligence agencies and law enforcement, and 875 new offences have been created.

Many have sought to repurpose existing systems of corporate surveillance for state surveillance, while surveillance technology companies receive lucrative government contracts.

O’Shea also said Labor has “effectively abandoned” regulation of artificial intelligence (AI) and facial recognition technology.

“Less than 10% of Australians think it’s reasonable for a retailer to ask for your biometric information to access their services, but on an almost daily basis they will experience this.

“Everyone is telling us that AI is fundamentally important — politicians, the financial markets, a media that takes industry sources as truth — but a study by the University of Melbourne found that Australians are among the least optimistic in the world about artificial intelligence.

“More people are concerned about the negative outcomes than the benefits … 87% would be more inclined to trust and use AI products if international standards were in place to protect them.”

O’Shea pointed to the campaign to remove Palantir from Coles stores and the defeat of a data centre proposal in Lane Cove as examples of where most people’s attitudes lie.

“The hand of power is seeking to crush us, but we have the capacity to land a counterpunch,” she said. “This is the time for organisers, agitators, lawyers, ratbags and policy nerds to work together to build an alternative future where civil liberties are protected and our democracy can flourish.”

NSWCCL president Timothy Roberts told the gathering that the NSWCCL aimed to be an “ever-watchful guardian” of civil liberties, noting the huge challenges. He referenced last year’s March for Humanity, across the Sydney Harbour Bridge, when 300,000 people marched to protest Israel’s genocide in Gaza and demand that Labor act.

“It felt like the flame of liberty could not burn brighter or stronger — we must continue to celebrate that occasion as an example of the collective exercise of our human rights,” Roberts said.

The NSWCCL’s journalism awards went to Guardian journalists Ariel Bogle and Nino Bucci for uncovering the use of “less-lethal” weapons by police. Star Observer journalist Jacques Nieuwoudt won the young journalist award for his coverage of police raids of LGBTIQ spaces on Oxford Street.

author: groundxero
title: Barricades, Internet Shutdown, Mass Detentions: Delhi Police Violent Crack Down on Protest against CEC Gyanesh Kumar and SIR
content:
Thousands of protesters gathered around Delhi’s Jantar Mantar on 2 October, defying the denial of police permission and a sweeping security clampdown imposed to prevent the protests from taking place. Barricades sealed the designated protest site from all four directions, mobile internet was suspended across central Delhi, several Metro stations were shut, and riot-control forces were deployed in large numbers. What followed was a day of mass detentions, many involving the use of force against women, students, journalists and other protesters. The violent crackdown came amid a renewed call for mobilisation for a ‘Jail Bharo Andolan’ and ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ against the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and demands for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, with organisers calling the 2 October action only the beginning of a wider protest movement.


 


New Delhi, 2 October 2026


by

Mouli Sharma


 


“Thousand is a lowballed estimate,” said a lawyer’s group called

Lawyers for Detainees

, one of several such collectives formed after the historic protests that shook the national capital a mere three months ago after uproar against repeated failures and irregularities in the conduct of public examinations under the tenure of former Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Now, recent history is attempting to recreate itself as a similar uproar against the government’s Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, and the recent revelations of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s alleged role in the same has led to widespread national outrage.


 


“85 people have been detained in this station alone,” said Adv. Surya Prakash, who was present at the Badarpur police station. “We have reports that at least 20 buses filled with detainees left the protest site during the day. Many detainees were released informally at random locations far away from the centre of the city, while still more were taken to stations like this one. The actual number of detentions is much higher than whatever numbers will be produced here at the stations,” he said.


 


The figure, though, may include repeat detentions, the most prominent case being of AISA president Neha Bora herself, who was detained at least three times from the same location outside the Royal Plaza Hotel, near the East entrance of the protest site near the Kerala Bhawan canteen, first alongside psephologist and activist Yogendra Yadav, a second time with several student protesters of other parties, and a third time again with fellow AISA leader Anjali of the Delhi University. Former Delhi CM Atishi, independent journalist Harsh Yadav, and at least 700 more students were detained through the day.


 


“700 is the count we have so far from police stations taken across the city,” said Adv. Vertika Mani, also a part of the lawyers’ collective. “But that obviously cannot account for the many detainees who were released at unofficial locations.”


 


The CJP’s ultimatum to the government of witnessing a ‘Jantar Mantar 2.0’ should Gyanesh Kumar fail to resign within 48 hours (given on 25 September, the deadline for which had long since passed) kicked off with a bang on Friday, as an identical call for the police-defying protest in Shivaji Park, Mumbai was given by countless student, labour, farmer and other political organisations at the eponymous Jantar Mantar in New Delhi, led by prominent activists including Neha Bora, Yogendra Yadav, Nandita Narain, and Prashant Bhushan. Hundreds of civilians took to the streets on the morning of 2 October, on the occasion of Gandhi Jayanti, only to be met with armed state forces deployed in massive numbers and a once-designated protest site cut off from their access through curfews (Section 163 of the BNS was declared in the region, without any justification beyond prevention of a ‘crowd forming’) and police barricades blockading entrances to the site from all four directions, dispersing protesters across a wide 2km radius.


 


What followed was a circus of media, police, and protester, as for four hours following the 11 am time given for the assembly, bus after bus was filled with peaceful protesters ‘detained’ under the simple justification of following ‘orders from above’. At least one protester, a young man named Roveen from the All India Students’ Association (AISA) (of whom Neha Bora is national president), was grievously assaulted by the police and had to be taken to a …

author: Sofia Little
title: Get the Flock Out
content:
On September 23rd, the Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism held a hearing titled “Always Watching: Flock’s Nationwide AI Surveillance Network,” examining the privacy risks, data sharing, and misuse of private automated license plate reader (ALPR) networks.

The hearing was chaired by Sen. Hawley (R-MO) and featured five witnesses, including Lindsey Isaacs, a wrongfully accused driver, Alasdair Whitney from Legislative Counsel Institute for Justice, Sheriff Ross Teeple, Benn Jordan, a self-proclaimed “hacker”, and policy counsel analyst Chad Marlow from the ACLU, where they have coined a campaign called “Get the Flock Out.”

The hearing highlighted pertinent concerns about how ALPR technology can be used and shared. Public concern about Flock cameras has also grown in recent months. A September 2026 Navigator Research survey found that 62% of registered voters were concerned about Flock camera use, including 66% of Democrats, 55% of Republicans, and 70% of Independents.

Flock Safety was founded in 2017 by CEO Garrett Langley, operating as a small startup meant to provide ALPR cameras to homeowners associations and neighborhoods looking to reduce petty theft and local property crimes. Now, it has grown into something alarmingly dystopian: an AI powered network of over 120,000 cameras across 49 states that photograph, scan, tag, and log every driver that passes, whether or not they are suspected of any crime.

License plate reader technologies have existed since the 1970s, in the form of speed, toll, and red-light cameras. These are only triggered by a specific action, such as running a red-light or driving through a toll booth, and only track license plate numbers. The entry of venture capitalist funding and advanced AI technology into the mass surveillance industry has transformed these automatic traffic enforcement cameras into a complex web of invasive surveillance tools.

During the hearing, ACLU’s Mr. Chad Marlow argued that companies operating ALPR systems are profiting from the collection and sharing of information about people’s movements. The ACLU has called for greater limits on how ALPR data can be collected, accessed, and shared.

Privacy concerns extend to how ALPR data can affect people seeking reproductive health care. During the hearing, Sen. Booker (D-NJ) raised concerns that states could use ALPR technology to track people traveling to obtain reproductive care. The concern comes amid documented cases of law enforcement using vehicle surveillance systems to investigate people seeking or suspected of seeking abortion care.

Unfortunately, this ‘hypothetical’ scenario has become the reality for women across the country.

Witnesses Alaster Whitney and Sheriff Ross Teeple both testified about the overreach of Flock’s ALPRs, with Whitney highlighting jurisdiction concerns which police officers have already been accused of taking advantage of.

In Texas, a sheriff’s deputy used 83,000 Flock ALPRs to track a woman who allegedly performed a self-administered abortion, at the behest of her abusive partner. In Massachusetts, a police officer used Flock networks to stalk a former romantic partner who said she had changed her identity to escape from his abuse. In Kentucky, a police officer was accused of searching his child’s mother 1,000 times through Flock’s network, though she has a protective order. The Institute for Justice has catalogued more than 200 incidents of these ALPR abuses, including romantic stalking, wrongful stops and detentions, non-law enforcement use and other types of misconduct.

These encroachments do not just stop here, as Sen. Padilla (D-CA) spotlights the use of loopholes within Flock, which ICE officers take advantage of to track immigrant communities. While Flock has guaranteed no direct access to the Border Patrol subagency, Witness Marlow points out all it takes is one sympathetic person connected to ICE for the agency to obtain access to billions of pictures of citizens, including facial properties.

Concerns about ALPR surveillance have crossed traditional political lines. During the hearing, Sen. Hawley noted that supporters of the Second Amendment have “long feared national databases of any kind.” This has drawn criticism from across the political spectrum highlighting the bipartisan opposition.

While Flock operates as a leading company which produces ALPRs, they are not the sole producers. Companies like Axon and Motorola have slowly begun increasing …

Open Source Is Not the Same Thing as Liberation

Open Source Is a Tool, Not a Commandment

There is a peculiar form of ideological dogmatism that has emerged within parts of the FOSS movement. Even in anarchist circles, some people seem to believe that opposition to intellectual property must take precedence over virtually every other ethical consideration. After all, if copyright, patents, and other forms of intellectual property are inherently illegitimate, then any attempt to place limits on how the things we create are used or distributed must necessarily be reactionary, right? Even when those limits are intended to protect workers, creators, and wider communities from exploitation by capital?

Anarchists do not seek to abolish one particular category of property while leaving other relations of domination untouched. Nor do we advocate stripping workers of control over the fruits of their labor in the name of an ideological dogma that ultimately has little to do with fostering anarchism.

The rise of so-called “generative AI” has made this contradiction impossible to ignore. My recent essay on this technology was criticized by some open-source diehards because, in their view, no one has the right to restrict the flow of information — even when that flow gushes directly from the minds and labor of workers and creatives into the bulging bank accounts of Silicon Valley billionaires.

To be clear: I am not opposed to free and open-source software. The forum I run (Raddle.me) was built on software (Postmill) that my cofounder released into the commons from the outset under a FOSS license. Even when fascists forked her code to spread hate and harassment, and when a scummy developer violated the license and tried to pass her work off as his own for profit, we did not respond by retreating behind a closed-source license. As anti-authoritarians and anti-capitalists, we certainly could have justified doing so when her work was being used to harm marginalized communities and enrich capitalists, but the license was kept open.

The same principle applies to my own writing. I release all of my essays freely, and I give zine-makers permission to reprint them without restriction. I believe in sharing knowledge and making creative work accessible. People have the option to donate to support my work if they want to. What I oppose is capital taking that generosity, enclosing it within a for-profit ecosystem, and turning it into another mechanism for extracting wealth from the people who created it.

This is not an argument that copyright is inherently liberatory. It is an argument that the abolition of intellectual property is not, by itself, liberation.

I feel compelled to take a stand against the increasingly rigid open-source absolutism that has taken hold in parts of the milieu: against the ruling class taking our collective knowledge, privatizing it, and selling it back to us. I do not consider this a pro-IP argument, but I’m sure plenty of people will disagree. It is an argument against AI slop …

author: Slingshot robot #1
title: Live in the Real World
content:
Our dependence on our phones isn’t an accident. We depend on them logistically for our navigation, payment, and communication. But our phones and the apps they contain are also designed to build emotional dependence — there are entire teams of top-of-their-field psychologists, engineers, sociologists, and designers getting paid hundreds of thousands of dollars a year to make apps even just a little bit more addictive. The emotional and logistical dependence on our phones intertwine in a mutual feedback loop, making it difficult to reduce either.

Every interaction we have with our phones deepens opportunities for state surveillance. Our online activity creates a database of our interests, purchase history, friend networks, location, and activism that the FBI of yesteryear could only have dreamed of. But the biggest problem, as with any addiction, is how something that is fun and useful in small doses can start to take more and more of our time and attention, preventing us from doing other things that we value. So what is there to do?

For most of us, the apps that most deeply build psychological dependence on our phones are social media apps and games. These often take, in some ways, the place of cigarettes in our society today — we do them on a quick break, or when we need to ‘unwind’. But like nicotine, they mostly sate the need that they themselves create. After unwinding in this way, do you feel deeply rested and reset?

If there is an app that you feel wastes your time, or you dislike how much you use, just delete it! You can always re-download it. Note down in your organizer the date and time you deleted the app, and why. If you redownload the app, note that down too. It’s helpful to understand our own patterns of use, to help us understand where we use “tools” or “toys” out of necessity or fun, versus out of psychological dependence.

Think about other activities you can do when you would have used your phone. If you delete an app, it’s easy for some other app to quickly replace it. Be realistic about what might feel fulfilling and restful while deprogramming, in those times and in that headspace. Watching landscapes slide past, noticing the people around you, thinking about your present, past or future, having a conversation with a friend or stranger, reading: each of these might feel more wholesome or restful than your phone. Your Slingshot organizer may be able help you… Don’t you think the edges of the date pages could use additional intricate doodles? Or perhaps you can journal a bit, filling in past date entries with what you remember doing, seeing, eating, or thinking on that day? Use the blank pages in the back to write poetry or outline a manifesto or draw art. Let your boredom be a canvas, a portal to discovery, not something to avoid.

These activities won’t feel as stimulating or give you the same dopamine rush as the apps you’re used to. It’s normal to feel a sense of confusion or loss in this process. Perhaps at some deep level the bright, shifting light of the screen feels like a flickering fire: a thousand generations of finding safety and community in campfires draws us inexorably to this bright cold flame. Try changing your phone’s settings to have the display be in black and white, or switch to a dimmer, less attractive color palette.

We can also feel emotional dependence on the instant knowledge and communication phones provide. What if we can’t respond right away to a friend or loved one? It’s so easy to ask a question to AI like Siri or Google and get an affirming answer! Like puppies or young children, we become anxious without the constant presence of that communication or knowledge. Try consciously pushing your limits more often — if you don’t know something, discuss it rather than looking up ‘the answer’ right away. Delete search bars and AI assistants from your phone and download the Wikipedia app, so if you do need to look something up, you will break that instant gratification loop, finding your own answer and giving yourself context along the way. And try setting aside a specific time of the day to answer your messages. Let friends or loved ones know you might not respond quickly outside of that time.

Logistical dependence is hard in a different way. Practical uses for our phones are often the most problematic sites of government and corporate surveillance, and reinforce emotional dependence by repeatedly forcing us back to our screens.

author: Monica Atieno, Angela Chukunzira and Athandiwe Saba
title: Inside Kenya’s Hidden Deals with Big Tech
content:
When an outsourcing company working for Meta found itself being sued in Kenya, it took its problem to the President.


The dispute had begun in May 2022, when former Facebook content moderator Daniel Motaung sued Sama and Meta over working conditions. Another 43 moderators brought a case in March 2023. The workers had been employed by Sama to moderate Facebook content, work that required them to repeatedly view disturbing material. They argued that Meta, which ultimately benefited from and controlled aspects of their work, should also be held responsible.


Sama was not a minor contractor in Kenya. It was part of the labour pipeline that allowed a global technology company to outsource some of the most harmful work of the internet to Kenyan workers. Meta fought to remove itself from the litigation, arguing, among other things, that Kenyan courts did not have jurisdiction over the foreign company. But on 20 September 2024, the Court of Appeal rejected that argument.


Then on 11 November 2024, less than two months after that ruling, the Business Laws (Amendment) Bill was published. It proposed new rules for Kenya’s outsourcing industry, including provisions dealing with who should carry responsibility for workers employed by outsourcing companies.


Less than a month later, on 9 December, President William Ruto publicly said Sama had approached him about its legal troubles. “Now I can report to you that we have changed the law,” he said, adding that “nobody will take you to court again on any matter.”


But the bill was still before Parliament, where a fight was unfolding over who should be held responsible for outsourced workers. Business groups including KEPSA and the Kenya Association of Manufacturers

argued

 that responsibility should largely remain with the outsourcing company. Tech workers argued that companies that control or benefit from their work should also be held responsible. This was very important for workers trying to sue companies such as Meta rather than only their local contractors.


Figure 1: Africa Tech Workers Movement members during a joint press conference in August 2025, raising concerns about the Business Laws (Amendment) Bill, 2024.


The workers also went to court to try to stop the bill. In June 2026, the High Court

declined

 to intervene. On 19 August 2026, the National Assembly passed the amendments. It now awaits for presidential assent. 


For James Oyange, a former content moderator, Ruto’s statement sent a clear message about whose side the government was on. Workers had gone to court seeking protection from some of the world’s most powerful technology companies; instead, he said, the government appeared to be changing the rules in the companies’ favour.


“We are on our own. It is the responsibility of the government to protect us, but they are taking Big Tech’s side. It means the companies can do what they want.”


Oyange fears that if technology companies can turn to the government when workers sue them, while workers are left with fewer ways to hold those companies responsible, the balance of power shifts even further away from workers.


The Sama case is one part of a much wider relationship between Kenya’s government and global technology companies.

The Continent

 identified at least 12 publicly documented meetings, agreements, regulatory engagements and partnerships between the Kenyan government and Microsoft, Google, Amazon, TikTok and Starlink since 2023.


The investigation also found a pattern across these relationships. Major technology companies are being brought into public services, infrastructure and policymaking, often through agreements the public cannot see. At the same time, laws and policies are being developed that can make it easier for these companies to operate. What is much harder to find is who negotiated these arrangements, what Kenya agreed to in return, and who is checking whether they serve the public interest.


Agriculture is one example. In 2020, the Ministry of Agriculture signed an agreement with Microsoft to use technology to

improve farming and food security.

 Microsoft would provide cloud technology for digital tools using information about weather, pests, farming inputs and production.


The partnership expanded in 2022, when AGRA joined Microsoft on a digital agriculture programme that included Agribot known as Kuzabot, a service that sends farmers advice by SMS and WhatsApp. According to the

Community Alliance for Global Justice’s …

author: Unknown
title: Litvanya’da kitle imha silahları bulundurma yasağının kaldırılmasına ilk onay verildi
content:
Fotoğraf: Augustas Didžgalvis/Wikimedia Commons CC BY-SA 4.0

Litvanya Ulusal Radyo ve Televizyonunun (LRT) haberine göre, Litvanya topraklarında kitle imha silahlarının bulundurulmasını yasaklayan anayasa hükmünün kaldırılmasını öngören değişiklik bugün parlamentoda görüşüldü.

Parlamento Başkanı Juozas Olekas, oylama öncesinde yaptığı açıklamada, yasağın kaldırılmasının Litvanya’nın dayanıklılığını ve caydırıcılık kapasitesini güçlendireceğini söyledi. Olekas, yasağın kaldırılmasıyla Litvanya’nın kitle imha silahlarının konuşlandırılmasına ilişkin anayasal kısıtlamasının diğer AB ve NATO ülkelerindeki hukuki durumla aynı hale geleceğini vurguladı.

Litvanya Savunma Bakanı Robertas Kaunas da ülkesinin stratejik silahlara sahip ülkelerle çevrili olduğunu belirterek, Rusya’nın en batısında yer alan Kaliningrad eksklavı ile Belarus’a işaret etti. Önerilen anayasa değişikliğini Moskova’nın eylemlerine verilen bir yanıt olarak nitelendiren Kaunas, “Rusya, Ukrayna’da savaşı başlatmasaydı bugün yaptığımız tartışmaları muhtemelen yapmıyor olurduk” dedi.

Yapılan oylamada milletvekilleri değişikliğe 106 oyla destek verirken, 18 milletvekili karşı oy kullandı, 6 milletvekili ise çekimser kaldı.

Anayasa değişikliğinin kabul edilmesi için parlamentoda bir oylama daha yapılması gerekiyor. Parlamento Başkanı Olekas, kitle imha silahlarının Litvanya’da bulundurulmasını yasaklayan anayasa hükmünün kaldırılmasıyla ilgili nihai oylamanın 12 Ocak 2027’de yapılmasının planlandığını açıkladı.

Litvanya’daki tartışmalar, Fransa Cumhurbaşkanı Emmanuel Macron’un Avrupa için yeni bir nükleer caydırıcılık sistemi kurulması yönündeki önerisi ile ABD’nin bazı ilave NATO ülkelerine nükleer silah konuşlandırma seçeneğini değerlendirdiğine ilişkin haberlerin ardından yoğunlaştı.

Kremlin Sözcüsü Dmitriy Peskov, Litvanya’da nükleer silah konuşlandırılması durumunda bu ülke topraklarının Rus nükleer silahlarının hedefi olacağını belirterek, “Bu, durumu ciddi şekilde gerginleştirecek” ifadelerini kullanmıştı.

author: webdev@democracynow.org (Democracy Now!)
title: Afghanistan, 25 Years Later: Journalist Emran Feroz on the Legacy of "America's Longest War"
content:
This week marks 25 years since the U.S.-led invasion of Afghanistan, the beginning of what would become the longest war in U.S. history. After installing a pro-Western government in Kabul in December 2001, U.S. and other

NATO

 troops would remain in the country for the next two decades battling a stubborn insurgency — until a chaotic U.S. withdrawal in August 2021 that saw the Taliban return to power.


“During the 20 years of America’s longest war in Afghanistan, we could clearly see that failure was coming,” says journalist Emran Feroz, just back from a month of reporting in Afghanistan. He says the relative economic and political gains under the Western-backed government were undercut by widespread corruption and violence, particularly in rural Afghanistan. “You had torture prisons next to Burger King and

KFC

 and Starbucks.”

Angesichts wachsender internationaler Bedrohungen boomt die deutsche Rüstungsindustrie – auch in Bayern. Diese will der Autobauer Audi jetzt personell unterstützen. Auch um Perspektiven für die eigenen Mitarbeiter zu erweitern.


Die deutsche Autoindustrie steckt in der Krise, während sich viele Rüstungsunternehmen vor Aufträgen kaum retten können. Jetzt „verleiht“ Audi Beschäftigte an Rüstungsbetriebe. Wie ein Unternehmenssprecher dem BR am Dienstag auf Nachfrage bestätigt, hat der Autobauer gemeinsam mit Partnern aus der bayerischen Metall- und Elektroindustrie ein Modell für einen befristeten regionalen Personaleinsatz auf den Weg gebracht.


„Großes Interesse“, aber Teilnahme freiwillig


Im Rahmen der Arbeitnehmerüberlassung können die wechselwilligen Audianer zeitlich befristet bei den Rüstungsunternehmen Diehl, Airbus, MBDA und KNDS tätig werden. Zielgruppe sind insbesondere Ingenieure, Qualitätsingenieure, Projektmanager sowie Mitarbeitende der Werkstätten in der Technischen Entwicklung und der Qualitätssicherung.

Die Teilnahme an dem Modell erfolgt ausschließlich auf freiwilliger Basis. Die entliehenen Audianer bleiben während der gesamten Laufzeit Beschäftigte der Audi AG. Ende Oktober soll es laut Audi größere Informationsveranstaltungen geben. Doch schon jetzt stößt das Modell laut einem Audi-Sprecher „auf sehr großes Interesse innerhalb der Audi-Belegschaft“

author: Sharon Zhang
title: Trump Has Granted $6B in Contracts to Arms Makers His Sons Have Invested In
content:
Trump has previously said that his children have “inside information” about government actions.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Military contractors with investments from President Donald Trump’s sons have raked in billions of dollars in government deals and contracts since June 2025, when their venture capital company first obtained a major stake in military technology company Anduril, new reporting finds.

Last year, 1789 Capital, of which Donald Trump Jr. is a partner, invested $2.5 billion into Anduril. According to an analysis of the government’s public contracts by ABC, since then, Anduril has been awarded 135 contracts from the U.S. government, with $1.8 billion of it having been paid out thus far.

In all, military contractors with backing from Donald Trump Jr. or Eric Trump have gotten $6 billion in “active or promised government contracts,” the analysis found.

The Pentagon and a spokesperson for the two brothers denied any impropriety. “No company receives preferential treatment. The War Department always looks for solutions to benefit the warfighter, not any pre-selected entity. Outside affiliations, investors, or political connections play absolutely no role in the Department’s funding decisions,” a Pentagon official said.

However, ABC uncovered several instances in which companies were granted Pentagon contracts for the first time after Donald Trump Jr. or Eric Trump joined their teams.

A drone manufacturer named Unusual Machines was granted a contract for 3,500 motors, and potentially 20,000 more, in 2025, months after Donald Trump Jr. was named an adviser for the company. And another drone company, Powerus, got its first Pentagon contract just one month after the two brothers were listed as “notable investors” for the company in March 2026.

A Pentagon spokesperson defended the contracts, saying that “defense procurement is merit-based” and that “neither Donald Trump Jr. nor Eric Trump is an advisor to Powerus, and neither is involved in the company’s day-to-day business.”

“Their interest is indirect, held through American Ventures, an investor in the company,” the spokesperson told the outlet.

Previous reports have found instances of companies being granted large investments after receiving backing from 1789 Capital.

At an event in Maryland on Tuesday, Trump announced a new partnership with Anduril, billionaire Palmer Luckey’s autonomous military technology company, in its project to build a new shipyard called “Arsenal- 2.” The company will be providing a $3.7 billion investment into building the factory in Maryland, while the Navy will contribute $2.9 billion, he announced.

Bizarrely, Trump said that the public will be receiving “a 40 percent stake” in the shipyard, which he called “proof to our commitment to ensuring the shipyard’s enduring success.” It’s unclear what he meant by this, as the shipyard is being paid for by public money — and the $2.9 billion contributed by the Navy is actually more than 40 percent of the project’s $6.6 billion price tag.

At the event, Trump praised Luckey as a friend and a “brilliant guy.” Last week, Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth announced that Luckey will help lead a new military task force called “Project Meridian,” which is tasked with shaping the future of warfare.

Democrats have previously launched efforts to probe potentially corrupt deals involving 1789 Capital’s investments. In August, Rep. Jamie Raskin (D-Maryland), ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, opened an investigation into the firm, pointing out that it grew from managing $150 million in investment capital to over $3 billion since Donald Trump Jr. was named a partner just days after his dad was elected president.

“Whether government decisions and contracts are being manipulated to ensure that your firm and the President’s family get a cut of the action or your firm and the President’s family are being given advance insider information about those forthcoming decisions and contracts (or more likely both), these practices constitute clear violations of laws banning governmental conflicts of interest, political insider trading, exploitation of public office for financial gain and fraud,” Raskin said.

In July, Trump openly bragged that his status as the president gives his children access to “inside information.”

title: A volte ritornano. Opporsi alla ripresa del nucleare
content:
In questo mondo di ladri e ciarlatani, i governanti italiani non possono permettersi il lusso di non essere alti rappresentanti, nella prima categoria, ma anche della seconda! Così, come nei più famosi film dell’orrore, quelli che sembravano definitivamente sepolti da anni, escono dalle loro tombe con un nuovo vestito, ma con l’inconfondibile nefasto lezzo di sempre. Escono dalla tomba idee fasciste di patria e razza, e, per non sbagliarsi, riaffiorano anche tecnologie bocciate da 40 anni per mezzo di ben 2 referendum. Parlo del nucleare.


I ciarlatani parlano di crisi energetica, del petrolio che non abbiamo, per cui dobbiamo assolutamente stringere accordi con governi a dir poco criminali; parlano del gas da comprare a tutti costi, di terre rare e poi – ciliegina sulla torta – della recente guerra innescata da Stati Uniti e Israele con l’attacco all’Iran e il conseguente blocco dello stretto di Hormuz. In questo contesto, caratterizzato dalla retorica di giornalisti prezzolati e di politici, si ritira fuori il nucleare.


Queste chiacchiere nascondono una realtà ancora peggiore. Prima di tutto chiariamo che la politica energetica in Italia, ma anche le scelte politiche dei governanti italici e il posizionamento delle truppe italiane nei vari paesi del mondo, è dominata dagli interessi finanziari dell’ENI, la multinazionale nostrana, la compagnia energetica integrata in decine di paesi, che abbraccia tutti i settori, compreso quello della transizione energetica, della ricerca chimica e dello sviluppo di tecnologie innovative. Il governo italiano non fa nessuna scelta senza il suo beneplacito, in particolar modo oggi che la geografia mondiale sta cambiando radicalmente, e che le guerre sono solo l’aspetto più tremendo e spettacolare dello sfruttamento dei territori e non solo.


A questo va aggiunto che il boom dell’intelligenza artificiale, in tutti i campi, compreso quello militare, richiede molta energia. Si pensi che, secondo quanto indicano le proiezioni, entro la fine del decennio i data center per L’IA arriveranno ad assorbire circa 945 terawattora all’anno, una cifra che eguaglia l’intero fabbisogno energetico di una nazione fortemente industrializzata, come il Giappone.


In Italia le attuali forniture energetiche sono oggi appena sufficienti al fabbisogno nazionale.


Dovendo necessariamente limitare le emissioni di anidride carbonica dunque si deve eliminare o almeno diminuire l’uso di combustibile fossile, e in maniera folle ci si è rivolti al nucleare.


Questa scelta nasce da una parte dall’immenso spreco energetico in atto, imposto da questo sistema capitalista, dall’altro dal limite dettato inevitabilmente dalla strategia politica adottata anche per le rinnovabili, quella di non utilizzare le case e gli edifici esistenti, ma, per mantenere il monopolio e la proprietà dell’energia, si preferisce installare immensi campi eolici e fotovoltaici, finanziati per altro anche da chi propone il nucleare, perché il business deve essere in tutti i settori.


Ancora tu…ma non dovevamo vederci più?


Il Parlamento il 23 settembre 2026 ha approvato la legge delega al Governo in materia di energia nucleare. Tutto questo anche se c’erano già stati ben 2 referendum che avevano detto no al nucleare.


Quando in tempi non sospetti noi anarchici sostenevamo che il referendum non era la panacea di tutti i mali, che dietro questo strumento, apparentemente di democrazia diretta, si poteva effettuare una truffa, indubbiamente avevamo ragione! Vediamo perché.


Una delle cose fondamentali della Costituzione era, ed è,

 la s

ovranità del Parlamento; s

econdo il principio della democrazia parlamentare, il Parlamento mantiene il potere di legiferare su qualsiasi materia non vietata dalla Costituzione, approvando nuove norme e cornici di regole (come le recenti leggi delega sulla fissione sostenibile).


I referendum sul nucleare, in entrambe le occasioni, erano

referendum abrogativi,

regolati dall’Articolo 75 della Costituzione italiana. D’altronde in Italia i referendum possono essere solo abrogativi – qui sta l’inganno! – sono cioè uno strumento che permette ai cittadini solo di cancellare leggi esistenti, non di scriverne di nuove o di inserire divieti assoluti in Costituzione.


I tre quesiti del 1987


Nel Referendum del 1987 nessuno dei quesiti chiedeva esplicitamente “Volete vietare il nucleare?”


I cittadini furono chiamati a cancellare i meccanismi normativi che ne facilitavano lo sviluppo.
