title: Marche des Fiertés de Lyon 2026
content:
“Canicule et fascismes nous butent

 

! Pour les putes, pour les trans rentrons en résistance

 

!”


Cette année la Marche des Fiertés de Lyon aura lieu le 10 Octobre 2026. On se donne rendez-vous pour

13h à l'arrêt “Gratte-Ciel” du Métro A

 (Villeurbanne) pour revendiquer et célébrer nos luttes dans l'espace public

 

!


Les discours commenceront à

13h

 et la Marche partira à

14h

.


Le Parcours


Nous partirons de Gratte-Ciel à Villeurbanne pour suivre le Cours Emile Zola, puis le Cours Vitton et le Cours Franklin Roosevelt jusqu'à Foch. Nous remontrons ensuite le long du Rhône pour finir sur au parc de la Tête d'Or à la Porte des Enfants du Rhône.


Le parcours total fait 3.8km et se déroule sur route goudronnée tout le long. Nous avons noté très peu d'ombre jusqu'à Charpennes ainsi que peu de sanitaires publique tout le long du parcours.


Le parcours deviendra moins large après Masséna jusqu'au début du cours Franklin Roosevelt.


Un village associatif vous accueillera en fin de parcours sur la place.


Pour les participant·e·s


Accessibilité


 Un cortège Handi : revendicatif avec moins de bruit et port du masque obligatoire.

 Un cortège Calme avec peu de bruit et port du masque conseillé.

 Un véhicule accessible

PMR

 mais pas

UFR

, dans chacun de ces cortèges.

 Des casques anti-bruit, des bouchons d'oreilles et des masques

FFP2

 seront à disposition dans ces cortèges et par les bénévoles.

 Les prises de parole seront interprétées en Langue des Signes Française et un·e interprète en

LSF

 sera présent·e dans le cortège Handi durant toute la manifestation.


S'organiser


La matos classique à compléter en fonction de vos besoins

 

!


 de l'eau en bonne quantité

 

!

 de quoi grignoter.

 de quoi se protéger du soleil : chapeaux et crème solaire.

 vos meilleure tenues, maquillages et pancartes

 

!

 un masque

FFP2

 

; le

COVID

 est toujours là, prenons soin des un·e·s des autres

 

!


Sécurité


Tout au long du parcours, des personnes de l'organisation seront présentes pour encadrer la Marche. Elles seront identifiables par les manifestant.es en cas de besoin par un brassard de couleur et leur visuel.


Une vingtaine de secouristes de la Croix-Rouge française ainsi que plusieurs streets médics suivront également le parcours et seront présent.es au départ et à l'arrivée. N'hésitez pas à crier “médic

 

!” en cas de besoin d'assistance médicale immédiate pour vous ou quelqu'un d'autre.


Évitez de rester seul·e et repartez accompagné·e du rassemblement si possible.


Bienséance


 On ne touche pas une personne (ni ses cheveux, ses vêtements,ses aides à la mobilité…) sans autorisation explicite de sa part.

 Ne prenez pas en photo ou vidéo les personnes sans autorisation de leur part. A défaut, floutez les visages avant de partager des images en ligne.

 Respectez l'autodétermination des personnes qui vous entourent, n'hésitez pas à demandez les pronoms qu'une personne utilise ou de faire attention à comment elle se genre.

 La Marche n'est pas le lieu pour les questions indiscrètes sur les pratiques sexuelles, les opérations ou les handicaps des personnes.


La non-mixité


Certains cortèges dans la Marche peuvent être en “non-mixité”.


La non-mixité est une pratique couramment employée par les groupes militants

LGBTQ

+, anti-racistes, féministes ou syndicaux depuis les années 70. Elle permet de réserver ponctuellement des espaces spécifiques à des personnes concernées par un certain type d'oppression et de discrimination.


Dans le cadre de la Marche, la non-mixité sert notamment à visibiliser certaines revendications et groupes souvent invisibilisé·es.


Lorsque l'on fait partie de groupes opprimés, il peut parfois être difficile d'accéder à certains lieux et de s'y sentir à l'aise et en sécurité. De plus, Les comportements oppressifs ne sont pas forcément volontaires et conscients. Lorsque l'on est en situation de privilège, on ne perçoit pas le monde de la même manière. Il existe ainsi un besoin de la part des personnes concernées d'avoir des espaces réservés pour se sentir libres de parler, d'organiser des actions, de revendiquer des droits.


Il est donc important de savoir respecter les espaces dédiés à la non-mixité, et d'éviter d'y aller, même si vous estimez être bienveillant·e et déconstruit·e sur certains sujets. Il peut exister des exceptions, par exemple quand une personne concernée vous demande de l'accompagner pour ne pas se rendre seule dans un cortège …

author: Mandela Gapara
title: DRC: Peace in Eastern Congo Must Include the Banyamulenge
content:
Many people may have never heard of Minembwe, and those who know it may have learned about it through stories of war, displacement and hunger. For me, however, it is much more than a story. Minembwe is home to me and to many other Banyamulenge families. Generations of my family, including me, were born and raised there, built their lives there, and members of my family still live there today.


Minembwe lies in the High Plateaux of South Kivu, in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. It is a predominantly rural area where Banyamulenge and neighboring communities, including Babembe, Bafuliru, Banyindu and others, have lived for generations. Yet despite their deep roots in the region, the Banyamulenge have faced

persistent discrimination and hostility

, often centered on their identity and their belonging in Congo.


As the 81st United Nations General Assembly continues, I hope world leaders will look beyond the diplomatic halls and remember places like Minembwe. Discussions about peace, human rights, dignity and international cooperation must reach communities living through war. These leaders have an opportunity to use their diplomatic influence to help protect the fragile peace the Banyamulenge community desperately needs. In Minembwe, those principles are not abstract. They can mean the difference between a child staying in school and being forced to flee again, or between a mother safely reaching the market and having to hide from another round of fighting.


For Banyamulenge, war and insecurity are not new. Eastern Congo has experienced repeated cycles of conflict for decades, and families in the High Plateaux have endured recurring  periods of violence and displacement.

Around the beginning of 2017

, however, the violence took a systematic destructive turn.

Villages were attacked, civilians were killed, houses were burned to the ground,

families were forced to flee their homes, and cattle were looted.


In Banyamulenge culture, cattle are not just property. They are deeply connected to family life and traditions, including their role as dowry in traditional marriage. For generations, cattle have been a source of income, they helped pay school fees and served as an essential source of livelihood.


These experiences have left many Banyamulenge questioning whether their own government sees them as equal Congolese citizens entitled to the same state protection as any other citizen. FARDC, the national army, has the duty to protect them. Yet Banyamulenge have been killed, their villages attacked and their cattle looted, while FARDC have been operating alongside Wazalendo militias, and foreign forces, particularly Burundian troops known for killing Banyamulenge civilians and attacking their villages. This has deeply damaged trust in the state. For Banyamulenge, minority rights are not an abstract legal principle; they are about whether their lives and homes are protected and whether their right to belong in Congo is respected.


In recent months, FARDC and its allies were pushed out of Minembwe and several surrounding areas, creating a period of relative calm. Families who had fled began returning to their villages, markets reopened, and people regained access to different parts of Minembwe. Families were once again able to visit relatives without the constant fear of fighting. After years of violence and displacement, everyday life was slowly beginning to return.


The change was evident in their daily life. On September 1, 2026, when the new academic year began, I saw pictures from Minembwe of students in their white and blue uniforms returning to school. They looked excited to be back.To me, those pictures captured what the relative calm meant. Parents were sending their children to school knowing that they would return home safely, and families were returning to routines that years of conflict had repeatedly interrupted.


Although the calm remained fragile, it offered a glimpse of  what life could be when villages are no longer surrounded by violence.Now, that fragile calm is under threat.


In recent weeks, FARDC and its allies have launched a new military offensive toward Minembwe. The renewed fighting has included reports of heavy artillery and drone strikes, and civilians living in and around Minembwe are once again facing the fear and danger of war. For civilians, these are not simply movements on a military map. They mean renewed displacement, interrupted education, and communities that had only …

author: Unknown
title: Ticaret Bakanı Bolat'tan "Fondan 360 milyon lira kazandı" iddiasına yalanlama
content:
Gazeteci Murat Ağırel, Yeni Parti İzmir Milletvekili Ümit Özlale'nin gündeme getirdiği "babasının fon hesabına 470 milyon lira yatırıp 830 milyon lira çeken bakan"ın Ticaret Bakanı Ömer Bolat olduğunu iddia etti. Ticaret Bakanı Ömer Bolat, iddiayı yalanladı.

Yeni Parti İzmir Milletvekili Ümit Özlale, TBMM Genel Kurulu'nda Cumhurbaşkanı Yardımcısı Cevdet Yılmaz'a fon vurgununa ilişkin bir bakanın babasının hesabına 470 milyon lira yatırıp 830 milyon lirayla fondan çıkıp çıkmadığını ve Özel Kalemi Fatih Kılınç'ın kapalı fonda parası olup olmadığını sormuştu.

Yılmaz ise Özlale'nin gündeme getirdiği iddialara ilişkin, özel kalem müdürü Fatih Kılınç'ın 7 milyon lira yatırdığı fonda büyük kayıp yaşadığını belirterek, "Yatırım yapan herkes suçluysa, hepsini birden mahkemeye gönderelim. Böyle şey olmaz" yanıtını vermişti.

Cumhuriyet yazarı Murat Ağırel, Sözcü TV'de fon satın alan bakanın Ticaret Bakanı Ömer Bolat olduğunu iddia ederek "Ticaret Bakanı Ömer Bolat’ın fon satın aldığı ve kriz patlamadan önce sattığı ortaya çıktı" dedi.

Ticaret Bakanı Ömer Bolat, fon soruşturmaları başlamadan önce yatırım hesabını kapatarak parasını çektiği iddiasını reddetti ve iddiayı dile getirenler hakkında hukuki yollara başvuracağını açıkladı.

Bolat, sosyal medya açıklamasında, ailesine ait 37,8 milyon liralık tasarrufun 26 Şubat 2024’te Hedef Yatırım Portföy bünyesinde kira sertifikası niteliğindeki bir yatırım aracına yatırıldığını ve halen aynı hesapta bulunduğunu söyledi.

Sözcü TV yayınında gazeteci Murat Ağırel’in dile getirdiği iddiaları “iftira” olarak nitelendiren Bolat, 16 Eylül 2026’da başlayan soruşturmalar öncesinde veya sonrasında hesabın kapatılmadığını, hesap üzerinden hisse senedi alım satımı yapılmadığını belirtti. Bolat, yatırımın mal beyanında kayıtlı olduğunu ve yetkili kurumların denetimine açık bulunduğunu ifade etti.

Bu akşam Sözcü TV yayınında 16 Eylül’den beri yürütülen 7 kuruluşa ait fon soruşturmaları ile alakalı olarak şahsımı hedef alan ve “fonda parası olup, krizden önce çekti, hesabı kapattı”, “fona 400 koydu, krizden önce çekti, 800 aldı” şeklinde başta Murat Ağırel’in haysiyetsizce iftirasına konu olan açıklamalar konusunda, kamuoyunun doğru bilgilendirilmesi ve tümüyle mesnetsiz, yalan yanlış iddialara açıklık getirilmesi amacıyla aşağıdaki hususları ifade etmek istiyorum:

31 yıldır emeğin sesi olan Evrensel, gücünü sadece okurlarından alıyor. Emeğin sesinin daha gür çıkması için sen de güç ver.

author: Constance Sorkpor
title: Same Cocoa Crash, Opposite Answers: what Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire Reveal about Power in Global Trade
content:
The world’s two biggest cocoa producers faced the same price collapse this year and made opposite choices. The reason is not economics alone. It is who holds power in each cocoa sector — a lesson aid and trade partners keep missing.


Within three weeks of each other this September, the world’s two largest cocoa producers set farm-gate prices for the new season. They pointed in opposite directions.


On 2 September, Côte d’Ivoire confirmed that farmers would receive

1,200 CFA francs per kilo

, 57% less than the 2,800 francs they were paid at the start of last season. For more than a million Ivorian growers, that means less than half the income per ton. On 25 September, Ghana went the other way. It

raised its price slightly

, to GH¢42,400 a ton, under a new law that guarantees farmers at least 70% of the export value of their beans.


Both countries face the same market. Cocoa futures hit a record

$12,906 a ton in December 2024

, then fell below $3,000 by February 2026. Both sell much of their crop in advance. Both have been hurt. So why such different answers?


The usual explanation is money: Côte d’Ivoire had forward sold its crop at low prices, while Ghana had already taken its pain with a sharp cut in February. That is true, but it is not the whole story. My doctoral research, which compared the two countries’ cocoa sectors over several decades, points to a deeper cause. Each country’s choices reflect who holds organised power in its cocoa system. And that lesson matters well beyond cocoa.


One value chain, two paths


Together, Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire grow

over 60% of the world’s cocoa

. They sit in the same place in the same global chain, sell to the same handful of traders and grinders, and for decades received the same advice from lenders and donors. Yet they climbed that chain in different ways.


Côte d’Ivoire bet on processing. In 2020/21 it became

the world’s largest cocoa grinder

. By 2024, local plants were taking in

777,000 tons, about 44% of the harvest

, and last year the state-owned Transcao opened a new $235 million factory. But most of that grinding is done by global firms such as Cargill, Barry Callebaut and Olam, which is why the government itself now talks about reducing their dominance.


Ghana bet on the farmer and the bean. Its cocoa board, COCOBOD, kept control of quality, marketing and pricing, and Ghanaian beans have long sold at a premium for their quality. Processing lagged. Ghana has capacity to grind about 505,000 tons a year, but it has processed

only around 220,000 tons a year, less than 40% of the crop

. When beans ran short in 2024, its biggest processors including, Cargill

had to halt production at times

.


Neither path is simply ‘right’. Each has winners and losers. The question is why each country chose the path it did.


Cocoa farmer Kofi Saara on his farm in Assin district, Ghana. Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire grow more than 60% of the world’s cocoa. Photo: ESPA Directorate, CC BY-NC 2.0.


Power, not just policy


The standard answer is technical: one country had better infrastructure, the other better policies. My research found something else. Moving up a value chain is not only an economic step. It is a political bargain between farmers, processors and the state, and each group wants different things.


Farmers want a larger share of the export price, paid on time. Processors want a steady supply of cheap beans. The state wants revenue, stability and votes. Adding value at home means getting all three to cooperate, often by asking one group to give something up.


Which bargain wins depends on who is organised and who can block change. In Ghana, some 800,000 cocoa-farming families are a large, well-organised group that no government can ignore, and COCOBOD grew into a strong, fairly autonomous regulator. Institutions formed around protecting the farmer’s price and the bean’s reputation. In Côte d’Ivoire, reforms that opened up cocoa marketing gave exporters and grinders more say, and policy leaned toward their needs: more local grinding, supplied with beans at competitive prices.


Both countries went through the same structural-adjustment era and heard the same donor advice. The advice was filtered through different domestic power structures, and it produced different results.


This year’s decisions follow the same pattern. Ghana’s new

Cocoa Board Act

, passed in July, writes the farmer’s 70% share into law, adds a pension scheme for cocoa farmers and …

author: Miriam Lafontaine
title: Man injured after shooting in Pangnirtung, deputy mayor says
content:
Pangnirtung is in shock after a shooting Tuesday afternoon injured a man, says deputy Mayor Markus Wilcke.


Wilcke said he heard shots Tuesday at around 4 p.m. and that the RCMP has since made an arrest.


“A lot of people were impacted, many of them children,” the deputy mayor said in an interview. “Pretty well everybody was impacted, directly or indirectly.”


He said the shots came from near the harbour. The suspect then entered residential streets and the area near the hamlet office.


“The RCMP did a good job and everyone is safe now,” Wilcke said.


Nunatsiaq News asked the RCMP about the incident but was told information about it would be available Thursday.


Wilcke says the hamlet will update the community through public statements and that counselling services will be available.


He also said the community can expect a public meeting within the next few days to discuss what actions are needed to respond and prevent similar incidents in the future.

author: Jalal Selmi
title: The Algiers-Abu Dhabi Rupture: Redefining the Geopolitical Chessboard of the Sahel
content:
The dramatic decision by Algeria on September 10 to formally sever diplomatic

ties

 with the United Arab Emirates may have caught casual observers by surprise, but in substance, it marks the explosive culmination in a long-festering geopolitical

rivalry

. The Algerian Foreign Ministry’s official statement cryptically cited ‘hostile conduct’ by the UAE, and Algiers accordingly presented the measure as a defensive strike against Abu Dhabi’s expanding financial and military footprint in its backyard. This diplomatic divorce not only shatters decades of conventional Arab alliances but also signals a high-stakes battle for hierarchical power stretching from the Mediterranean basin to the volatile African Sahel.


The Gradual Path to Rupture and Its Main Motives


In international practice, representation is not withdrawn in a single stroke. Messages first travel through diplomatic channels, technical and then political. If they fail, the language is raised in public. If public language fails, technical cooperation is frozen in the economy, transport or the media or other.


The relationship between Algiers and Abu Dhabi degraded in an unusually public manner. Cooling set in as Abu Dhabi moved to normalise relations with Israel. That step did not operate alone. It was bound up, in the Algerian reading, with a growing Emirati role in neighbouring Libya, where Algiers has long made calls for restraint by other regional actors in line with its own

reluctance

 to intervene directly.


From early 2024 through mid-2026, Algeria sent public messages accusing Abu Dhabi of using money to sabotage the surrounding region and of spreading harm in more than one

theatre

. Then, Algiers reduced technical cooperation, and on 7 February 2026 it announced cancellation of its air-services

agreement

. Then came a complete diplomatic rupture.


Normalisation with Israel was not itself the fuse. Egypt maintains relations with Israel, and this is not a barrier to another close relationship with Algeria. The comparison suggests that Algiers objects less to the existence of those ties than to their regional uses.


Algerian president Abdelmadjid Tebboune said in 2025 that relations with all GCC countries were warm with one exception, according to Reuters.


Emirati Activity That Disturbs Algeria’s Place in the Hierarchy of Power


Since 2011, Abu Dhabi has built an anticipatory foreign policy designed to shape the regional balance of power before shocks reach the home front. That approach can be described as offensive defence: activity abroad to maximise interests and keep negative effects away from domestic order. The sequence includes support for the 2013 coup in Egypt; alignment with Khalifa Haftar after 2014; participation in Operation Decisive Storm; bridges to Somaliland; the 2017 boycott of Qatar; alignment with the Kurdish independence referendum 2017; observer status in the East Mediterranean Gas Forum while Turkey and Algeria remained outside it; and cooperation with Russia in backing Mali’s military council against northern movements, especially the Azawad movement, bringing the risk of war closer to the Algerian

border

.


These moves exceed the UAE’s rank as a small power by conventional measures of population, industrial base and autonomous military capacity. Independent action is also constrained by the search for influence through alignment with American and Israeli orientations, as in the Emirati stance toward Hamas and in Western Sahara.


A small state that wants more influence looks for a functional role that can raise its rank. Abu Dhabi has pursued that role through ports, alliances and hard methods: support for secessionist tracks in Yemen and Somalia; control of selected raw materials, especially

gold

, in Mali and Sudan; containment of regional rivals; and the sharing of geopolitical space with major or regional powers, visible in ties with Israel, India and Ethiopia in the Red Sea basin and Somalia.


From Algeria’s standpoint, the problem is not activity as such. It is the transfer of this activity from West Asia into the Mediterranean basin and the African Sahel. A space Algiers wanted as a zone of understanding becomes a theatre of confrontation in which Algerian military intervention had been rare. Algeria has also maintained courteous working relations with external powers in this region such as Russia and France, but there is a fear that the UAE may now usurp this role, especially in the relationship …

author: The Canadian Press
title: Denied Indigenous rights, NunatuKavut council fighting Canada in Federal Court
content:
The NunatuKavut Community Council in Labrador is fighting Canada’s decision to deny the group Indigenous rights under Section 35 of the Constitution.


In a Federal Court application, the council says the Canadian government ignored historical and genealogical evidence when it ended Indigenous rights talks with the group last month.


Dated late last week, the application seeks to quash the government’s decision to abandon talks with the council.


The NunatuKavut Community Council says it represents about 6,000 Inuit in southern and central Labrador, though it is not recognized by other Inuit groups, including the Inuit Nunatsiavut government in northern Labrador.


Last month, Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada said information provided by the council did not meet established tests for rights under Section 35 of the Constitution.


Section 35 of the Constitution Act recognizes and affirms Indigenous and treaty rights.


In a news release Monday, the community council said it received “affirming messages and feedback” from Crown-Indigenous Relations and Northern Affairs Canada about its claim for rights. The department told the council it had met a test to proceed to land claim negotiations,

 the release said.


Read More: 


Ottawa ends NunatuKavut process for recognition of Indigenous rights 


The council accused the federal government of bowing to pressure from other Indigenous groups and ignoring evidence in favour of internal advice.


“The Government of Canada has breached the honour of the Crown time and again in their dealings with us,” said Todd Russell, president of the NunatuKavut Community Council, in the release.


“NCC has been to various levels of the courts over the last 30 years and has, many times, found a fair hearing and much success,” he added. “We are very confident in the legal process.”

Denied Indigenous rights, NunatuKavut council fighting Canada in Federal Court

APTN News

author: Unknown
title: AKP, Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya’ya kapıyı gösterdi
content:
AKP, fon soruşturmasında adı gündeme geldikten sonra Genel Başkan Yardımcılığı görevinden ayrılan eski Aile ve Sosyal Politikalar Bakanı Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya’yı partiden uzaklaştırdığını açıkladı. 


AKP Genel Sekreteri Eyyüp Kadir İnan, Kaya’nın artık parti üyesi ve mensubu olmadığını açıkladı. İnan, kararın parti yönetiminin iradesiyle alındığını da açıkça ortaya koydu:


“AK Parti olarak Cumhurbaşkanımızın talimatları doğrultusunda, yetkili kurullarımızın tespiti doğrultusunda zaten gereken işlemleri yaptık. Bugün Fatma Betül Hanım partimizin üyesi değildir, partimizin mensubu da değildir.”


İnan’ın açıklaması, Kaya’nın eşi İlyas Kaya ile birlikte aynı gün İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı’nda “şüpheli” sıfatıyla ifade vermesinden birkaç saat sonra geldi.


İhraç mı, zorunlu istifa mı?


AKP yönetimi, Kaya’nın parti üyeliğinin hangi usulle sona erdiğini açıklamadı.


İnan’ın “Cumhurbaşkanımızın talimatları” ve “gereken işlemleri yaptık” sözleri, ayrılığın Kaya’nın kendi tercihiyle gerçekleşmediğini gösteriyor. Ancak Kaya hakkında disiplin kurulu tarafından kesin çıkarma kararı verilip verilmediği ya da kendisinden üyelikten istifa etmesinin istenip istenmediği de kamuoyuna açıklanmadı. 


AKP’ye yakın Star gazetesi dahil çok sayıda yayın, gelişmeyi “Kaya AKP’den ihraç edildi” diye duyurdu. Star da haberini İnan’ın aynı açıklamasına dayandırdı; ayrıca bir disiplin kurulu kararına göndermede bulunmadı. 


Kaya’nın AKP üyeliğinin parti yönetiminin müdahalesinden sonra sona erdiği yönetim açısından netleşmiş görünse de, bunun AKP tüzüğünün ve disiplin yönetmeliğinin hangi hükmünün ihlali nedeniyle gerçekleştirildiği açık değil. 


11 gün önce yalnızca görevlerinden ayrılmıştı


Kaya 26 Eylül’de AKP’de yürüttüğü görevlerden “affını” istemişti.


Kaya açıklamasında, hakkındaki iddiaların araştırılması sırasında bulunduğu makamın tartışmaya konu edilmemesi gerektiğini söylemiş ve “yürütmekte olduğum tüm görevlerimden affımı Sayın Genel Başkanımızdan istedim” demişti. AA ve TRT de gelişmeyi “partideki tüm görevlerinden affını istedi” şeklinde duyurmuştu.


Böylece Kaya, 26 Eylül’de AKP yönetimindeki görevlerini bırakmasına rağmen parti üyesi olarak kalmıştı.


AKP Genel Sekreteri’nin 7 Ekim’deki açıklaması bu statünün de sona erdiği anlamına geliyor.


Önce TMSF’ye ödeme, ardından savcılık


Partinin Kaya’ya kapıyı göstermesine giden süreç son üç günde hızlandı.


Fatma Betül Sayan Kaya ile eşi İlyas Kaya’nın dondurulan hesaplarındaki yatırımlarının anapara dışındaki bölümünü, 5 Ekim’de Tasarruf Mevduatı Sigorta Fonu’nun (TMSF) “isteğe bağlı iade hesabına” gönderdikleri açıklandı.


İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı, SPK’nın “gönüllü ödeme” yöntemi kapsamında Kaya çiftinin yaptığı başvuru üzerine transferin gerçekleştirilmesine izin verdi. Kamuoyuna açıklanan bilgilerde ne kadar para iade edildiği belirtilmedi.


İki gün sonra Kaya ve eşi İstanbul Adliyesi’ne çağrıldı.


İstanbul Cumhuriyet Başsavcılığı Terörizmin Finansmanı ve Aklama Suçları Soruşturma Bürosu tarafından yürütülen sermaye piyasası soruşturması kapsamında Betül Kayan Saya ve eşi savcıya “şüpheli” sıfatıyla ifade verdi. Yaklaşık bir saat süren işlemlerin ardından Kaya çifti adliyeden ayrıldı.


Reuters da Adalet Bakanlığı kaynaklarına dayanarak Kaya ile eşinin soruşturmada şüpheli olarak yer aldığını ve Sermaye Piyasası Kurulu’nun (SPK) haklarında Sermaye Piyasası Kanunu kapsamında suç duyurusunda bulunmasının beklendiğini bildirdi.


AKP’nin siyasi mesafesi büyüdü


AKP Genel Sekreteri, Kaya’nın artık parti mensubu olmadığını duyurduktan sonra soruşturmayla ilgili siyasi değerlendirme yapmaktan da kaçındı:


“Geri kalan konu hukuki bir konudur, ona da yargı karar verir.”


(AEK)

author: Lilli Akpaleeapik
title: Boil water advisory issued for Taloyoak
content:
Nunavut’s Health Department issued a boil water advisory for Taloyoak due to the mechanical failure of a pump at the water treatment plant.


Any water used for consumption must be brought to a rolling boil for a minimum of one minute, either on the stove or with a kettle that does not have an automatic shut off, according to the advisory.


The advisory applies to water for drinking, preparing infant formulas, making juice or ice cubes, washing produce, cooking and brushing teeth.


Residents are also reminded that a camp stove should be used outdoors to avoid the risk of carbon monoxide poisoning.


The Health Department will notify community members when the boil advisory has been lifted.

author: Rizomatica
title: Escuela Popular Campesina José Bengoa Cabello: Diez años sembrando educación popular desde Curaco de Vélez
content:
La Escuela Popular Campesina José Bengoa Cabello de Curaco de Vélez, Chiloé, celebró sus diez años de vida con dos jornadas que reunieron a estudiantes, profesoras y profesores, organizaciones sociales, artistas, artesanas y artesanos, voluntariado y comunidad, marcando además la inauguración oficial de esta nueva etapa que lleva el nombre de José Bengoa Cabello, manteniendo viva una memoria que no queremos solamente recordar, sino proyectar desde nuestros territorios.


El encuentro comenzó reuniendo a estudiantes y profesorado de la Escuela Popular Campesina José Bengoa Cabello de Curaco de Vélez (Chiloé) y de la Escuela Ismenia Ortiz Lizama de Palquibudis (Curicó), compartiendo una asamblea entre ambas experiencias campesinas, para continuar con Saberes del Mar, junto al profesor Constantino Contreras, y el conversatorio de Género y Ruralidad con Ximena Valdés, «porque hablar del mundo rural es también reconocer a las mujeres, sus trabajos, aquello que históricamente ha permanecido invisibilizado y las transformaciones que aún necesitamos impulsar», destacaron en la presentación.


Seguidamente, el 29 de agosto, el Gimnasio Bordemar de la Población Vista Hermosa de Curaco de Vélez acogió una extensa jornada. Desde la organización, se señaló: «Quisimos expresar aquello que somos y en lo que creemos, uniendo cultura, formación, organización y autogestión, con puestos de artesanía de nuestras ferias, organizaciones sociales, estudiantes, voluntariado y productos de ambas escuelas, haciendo posible que una parte importante de la actividad se financiara desde nuestro propio trabajo colectivo».


La organización del festival de la Escuela, también resaltó:

«Para nosotros la autonomía y la autogestión no son solamente principios escritos, son prácticas que se aprenden haciendo, compartiendo responsabilidades y poniendo cada cual algo de sí para sostener lo que hemos decidido construir en común».


Como señala Janett Cárdenas, esta trayectoria también nos invita a preguntarnos para qué educamos y desde dónde lo hacemos:


«Seguimos apostando a que la educación es una acción transformadora y una herramienta política que ponemos a disposición de quienes queremos transformar este modelo de injusticia, porque educarnos es también organizarnos, recuperar nuestra memoria y reconocernos en nuestros propios saberes, comprendiendo que desde el campo, el mar, las semillas, la artesanía, la cultura y la experiencia de quienes nos antecedieron se construye conocimiento para transformar nuestra realidad.»


La jornada permitió también reconocer a personas que han acompañado ese andar: Ximena Valdés, en memoria de José Bengoa; Sergio Faumangaun, director de la Escuela Campesina Águila Sur; la familia Gamin, en memoria de don Enrique Gamin; Mirian Alarcón, voluntaria y profesora de Agricultura Campesina desde el comienzo de este camino en 2016; y Patricio Larco, profesor de Acuicultura.


La cultura, inseparable de la manera de comprender la formación y la vida comunitaria, estuvo presente con Patricio Guerrero, Raíces Curacanas, Amaranto, Maribel Manquecoy, Javier Chandía, el bloque infantil integrado por Luis Soussi y Natali, Daniela Reyes, Aliwen, Nancy San Martín y su banda, Los Pirulonkos, Almas Chilotas y Rancheritos Vientos del Sur, quienes generosamente acompañaron esta celebración con música, voces y expresiones nacidas también desde nuestros territorios.


«Mirar estos diez años es reconocer que la Escuela ha podido sostenerse gracias a estudiantes, profesoras y profesores voluntarios, campesinas y campesinos, artistas, organizaciones y familias que han compartido conocimientos, trabajo, semillas, alimentos, música, tiempo y afectos, haciendo posible una experiencia que no pretende enseñar desde arriba, sino construir conocimiento desde aquello que cada una y cada uno sabe y aporta»

, señaló la declaración de la Escuela.


Agregan en su declaratoria:

«Cumplir una década no significa cerrar una historia, sino mirar lo caminado para continuar, ahora llevando el nombre de José Bengoa Cabello y recogiendo esa invitación a SER, HACER y PENSAR, desde Chiloé, desde nuestras insularidades y desde el mundo campesino, convencidos de que mientras existan saberes que compartir y comunidades dispuestas a organizarse, existirán también posibilidades de transformación»

author: Tareq S. Hajjaj
title: Children Born in Gaza Over Last 3 Years Have No Memory of World Before Genocide
content:
Israel’s genocide has narrowed Palestinian children’s expectations of life’s possibilities.

Truthout is a vital news source and a living history of political struggle. If you think our work is valuable, support us with a donation of any size.

When I left Gaza in 2024, after six months of living through genocide, I wanted one thing above all else: to spare my only child a life spent permanently at war. I did not want him to grow up believing that the whole world looked like Gaza.

But I left more than fifteen nieces and nephews behind. Many were still too young to understand the world they had been born into. They were learning what a home was, what a school was, what it meant to be alive, at the very moment those things were being destroyed around them.

I spent the next year and a half in Cairo. It took me a long time to learn how to inhabit ordinary life again. Whenever I saw a garden, a playground, a school, or children playing freely and safely in the street, I could not simply enjoy the sight. Gaza was always there, beneath it.

A garden brought back the rubble. A school brought back the children who no longer had one. Even safety became a reminder of those still denied it.

There was a comparison I could not stop making: why could children elsewhere grow up among their families and the people who loved them, while Gaza’s children remained trapped in this unending cycle of occupation, bombardment, destruction, genocide, and hunger? How could a child starve to death in a world with so much food?

I kept thinking about the children whose first understanding of life was taking shape inside the genocide. My niece, Elaf, was a year and a half old when I left. She was still at the beginning of everything.

Then her life changed entirely. A tent became her home. Missiles and bombs became the sounds she fell asleep to. Rubble shaped the landscape through which she was learning to see the world, and daily death shaped her first knowledge of life.

What could she know of the world beyond Gaza’s walls? What reason did she have to imagine that elsewhere, children slept without bombardment, lived in homes that stood, and went to schools built to shelter them?

I feared she would grow up believing that life in Gaza was simply life.

At first, I thought this was a danger facing mainly the youngest children: those born during the genocide, or too young to remember anything before it. But children who were two or three when it began, and are now five or six, are also learning to see the world as rubble upon rubble.

During a video call with my brother Osama, who has eight children, his six-year-old son, Muhammad, saw me sitting on a sofa in a brightly lit room.

“Uncle, how did your tent fit that sofa?” He asked. I did not know how to answer.

His question took me far from the room where I was sitting. Muhammad had lived in a beautiful home before the genocide. But now, when he looked at his uncle’s home, he was left wondering how such lavish furniture could fit into the only kind of home he had come to expect.

He had more questions. “Is your tent made of fabric pieces, or is it ready-made? Do you have a community kitchen that gives you food?”

These were simply the only frames of reference he had to try to understand my life, asking whether the arrangements that governed his own survival also governed mine. Shelter meant a tent. Food meant waiting for a meal to be distributed.

There was nothing strange about his questions. What was unbearable was how much sense they made within the life imposed on him.

The change reaches older children, too. My nieces, Amira and Heba, respectively 12 and 10, remember life before. Yet I can hear their expectations for ordinary life shrinking.

They no longer ask for much from a school. They hope it might be something more than tents pressed against one another: perhaps a wooden structure with a roof of corrugated steel sheets.

During one call with my brother, Amira sat beside him as we discussed my son starting school.

“Are your schools tents, or are they wooden?” she asked. Those were the possibilities she offered me. I asked what she liked about her own school.

“We leave our cramped tent and go to a bigger one,” she said. “We can play more freely. There is a little space where we can play.”

Her answer stayed with me. Even that small difference — being able to move from one cramped space to another slightly less cramped one — mattered.

Then I asked what she wished her school could …

author: infolibre
title: Υποχρεωτική η καθαρογραφή αθωωτικών αποφάσεων από το Εφετείο Αθηνών
content:
Όπως αναφέρει στο Δελτίο Τύπου που ακολουθεί ο Κώστας Παπαδάκης, μέλος του Δ.Σ. του Δ.Σ.Α. και εισηγητής του σχετικού αιτήματος, στην υποστήριξή του ενώπιον της Ολομέλειας του Εφετείου Αθηνών: “

Το επόμενο βήμα είναι να μην περιοριστεί μόνο στο Εφετείο Αθηνών αλλά να επεκταθεί σε όλα τα δικαστήρια και εν τέλει να νομοθετηθεί με ανάλογη τροποποίηση του άρθρου 142 παρ. 4 Κ.Ποιν.Δ, ώστε να είναι υποχρεωτική παντού η καθαρογραφή όλων των αθωωτικών αποφάσεων χωρίς καμμία προϋπόθεση..”

ου Υπουργού Δικαιοσύνης (επισυνάπτεται) έγινε δεκτή η γνώμη που περιλαμβάνεται στην υπ αριθμ. 1/2026 απόφαση της Ολομέλειας του Εφετείου Αθηνών σχετικά με την καθαρογραφή των αθωωτικών αποφάσεων.


Με την υπ. αριθμ. 61301οικ/30.9.2026 Απόφαση του Υπουργού Δικαιοσύνης (επισυνάπτεται) έγινε δεκτή η γνώμη που περιλαμβάνεται στην υπ αριθμ. 1/2026 απόφαση της Ολομέλειας του Εφετείου Αθηνών σχετικά με την καθαρογραφή των αθωωτικών αποφάσεων.


Η απόφαση είχε ληφθεί από την Ολομέλεια του Εφετείου Αθηνών στις 19.2.2026, όπου είχε κληθεί και παρέστη η αντιπροσωπεία του Δ.Σ. του Δ.Σ.Α. αποτελούμενη από τον πρόεδρό του κ. Ανδρέα Κουτσόλαμπρο και μέλη του Δ.Σ,. του, μεταξύ των οποίων και ο υπογράφων ως εισηγητής που ανέπτυξε τα σχετικά αιτήματα. Ενώ είχε προηγηθεί η διοργάνωση εκδήλωσης στις 11.2.2026 στα γραφεία του Δ.Σ.Α. στις για την προβολή του αιτήματος.


Το αίτημα είχε στηριχθεί πάνδημα από όλους τους δικηγορικούς φορείς και από τις Ενώσεις Ποινικολόγων και πολλά νομικά περιοδικά. Όχι ωστόσο από τις δικαστικές και εισαγγελικές ενώσεις.


Σύμφωνα με την παραπάνω Υ.Α. η καθαρογραφή των αθωωτικών αποφάσεων του Εφετείου Αθηνών καθίσταται η υποχρεωτική εφόσον το ζητήσει ο κατηγορούμενος εντός 6 μηνών από την έκδοση τους χωρίς να απαιτείται η επίκληση εννόμου συμφέροντος.


Ανεξάρτητα από την καθυστέρηση έκδοσής της Υ.Α. πρόκειται για μία μεγάλη νίκη που πιστώνεται σε όσους συνέβαλαν με κάθε τρόπο διότι άρχισε να αποκαθίσταται μια μεγάλη αδικία, της οποίας οι πτυχές έχουν αναλυθεί λεπτομερώς, αλλά και ένα έλλειμα δικαίου που είχε οδηγήσει στην εξαφάνιση της επιτυχούς υπερασπιστικής νομολογίας.


Το επόμενο βήμα είναι να μην περιοριστεί μόνο στο Εφετείο Αθηνών αλλά να επεκταθεί σε όλα τα δικαστήρια και εν τέλει να νομοθετηθεί με ανάλογη τροποποίηση του άρθρου 142 παρ. 4 Κ.Ποιν.Δ, ώστε να είναι υποχρεωτική παντού η καθαρογραφή όλων των αθωωτικών αποφάσεων χωρίς καμμία προϋπόθεση.


Με θερμές ευχαριστίες προς όσους/ες συνέβαλαν.


Αθήνα, 7.10.2026


Κώστας Παπαδάκης


Δικηγόρος, Μέλος του Δ.Σ. του Δ.Σ.Α.

author: Emran Feroz
title: The War on Afghanistan Was Launched 25 Years Ago. It Still Hasn’t Ended.
content:
The war inaugurated a terrible new global order in which armed drones kill civilians who are neither named nor counted.

Support justice-driven, accurate and transparent news — make a quick donation to Truthout today!

“There were nights full of terror. Our village was bombed constantly,” says Zalmay Khan. Afterward, he goes to pray. Because of his wounds, he cannot kneel, so he prays sitting down.

Khan is in his early twenties and now works as a Taliban intelligence officer. As a boy, he says, he learned to read the sky before he learned to read words. His village in Wardak province, near Kabul, was bombed, then bombed again. First came American planes, then NATO’s, then those of the Afghan army the West had built. By night it got worse, when jets and armed foreign contractors hit villages and killed civilians seemingly at random.

“I became a Mujahed [a Taliban fighter] naturally,” Khan tells me.

He is not an outlier. In village after village on my most recent trip to Afghanistan a few weeks ago, I met men who grew up as the so-called war on terror’s raw material. Some wear the Taliban’s turbans, and some do not. Almost all of them say the same thing, with remarkable calm: The American narrative of this war belongs to the past. After two decades of war and destruction, it is their turn to control narratives and to rule the country.

October 7, 2026, marks exactly 25 years since the United States began bombing Afghanistan. The anniversary will pass in Washington with little reflection. In Afghanistan, the reality of it is lived daily.

The war on terror made history in a way few people remember. In its opening weeks, the United States used an armed drone against a target in Afghanistan, one of the first such attacks ever, in an attempt to kill the Taliban’s founder, Mullah Mohammad Omar, in Kandahar. Omar was not hit on October 7, 2001. He survived and reportedly died of natural causes a decade later, which the Taliban kept secret for years.

Who died instead? The record offers almost nothing: no definitive or officially confirmed names, ages, villages. One news report cites unnamed Kandahar residents suggesting the raid killed Omar’s 10-year-old son and the child’s stepfather, but the Taliban’s ambassador to Pakistan declined to confirm or deny this report.

In other words, the first known attempt to kill a man with an armed drone killed people no one has ever definitively identified, and it set the template for the type of warfare that would dominate over the next decades. No one can say who the victims were. But if the pattern of the following years is any guide, many were likely civilians, like the thousands of victims who came after them. During the Obama years, Afghanistan officially became the world’s most drone-bombed country.

That template repeated itself so often that Afghans developed names for the many men who were declared dead after supposed “surgical strikes,” but who then reappeared alive: mord-e zinda (the living dead) in Farsi and khyali marr (the not truly dead) in Pashto. I call them “Taliban ghosts.”

It continued across successive U.S. administrations, even across the bureaucratic, supposedly methodical “kill lists” infamously used by the Obama administration used to mark people for death from the skies.

The first known attempt to kill a man with an armed drone killed people no one has ever definitively identified, and it set the template for the type of warfare that would dominate over the next decades.

The obvious question was almost never asked: If Omar was not the victim, who was killed instead? In the logic of the drone war, a body is a statistic, and a body in a targeted area becomes a militant by default. The dead were not counted, and the stories of their families, who were left to count for themselves, largely continued to go unknown.

Strikes did not only create ghosts. They also created recruits. Researchers, journalists, and Afghan elders have long described the same pattern: A village is hit, a family is destroyed, and the Taliban offer the survivors the only form of justice made available to them. By the end of the war, entire districts had made that choice, not out of ideological conviction but out of grief.

One of the people I talked to on my recent trip was a Taliban official who had been held at Bagram, the American prison north of Kabul, for several years. He told me what the Americans wanted from him. “Accept our democracy or get tortured and rot here. That’s what …

author: Charlotte Rene Woods
title: VA Ballot Measure Would Restore Formerly Incarcerated People’s Voting Rights
content:
The state permanently disenfranchises people with felony convictions unless pardoned or successfully petition one.

Did you know that Truthout is a nonprofit and independently funded by readers like you? If you value what we do, please support our work with a donation.

Quadaire Patterson will vote for the first time this fall, a fact that brought a smile to his face on a recent afternoon as his 1-year-old daughter Trinity frolicked around the living room of the Henrico County home he shares with his wife.

He said he has been thinking about how future elections can shape Trinity’s future. But presently, he is eager to vote for a proposed amendment that could cement voting rights for formerly incarcerated people, like himself, into Virginia’s constitution.

Patterson, who was incarcerated at 19 years old after committing an armed robbery, served 16 years of a 20 year sentence before being released early in 2024 through a good behavior program.

He and wife Santia Nance joined other formerly incarcerated people and their families to advocate for the law change that allowed his early release. He has frequented the state capitol in the years since to lend insight to criminal justice legislation, despite being unable to vote for lawmakers himself.

That changed this summer when Gov. Abigail Spanberger restored his voting rights along with more than 60,000 formerly incarcerated Virginians. But the restoration process remains subjective; the amendment aims to make it a certainty.

“Voting rights have been deduced down to a privilege that can be handed out and restricted,” Patterson said. “This amendment restores it back to the people.”

Virginia’s current constitution permanently disenfranchises people with all felony convictions unless they are pardoned by a governor or successfully petition one.

Restorations trended downwards under former Gov. Glenn Youngkin. For years, it had been unclear which formerly incarcerated people would get their voting rights back, and the criteria guiding that decision was murky.

After trying unsuccessfully to pass the restoration amendment, lawmakers saw a new opportunity when Democrats gained majorities in the legislature in 2023 and tried again.

The current amendment had to pass the General Assembly two years in a row and will appear on statewide ballots this fall, where voters will approve or reject it.

Most Republican state lawmakers have consistently blocked the restoration amendment. Del. Mike Cherry, R-Colonial Heights, is an exception.

Cherry sponsored an earlier version of the amendment in 2022, which failed. And when the latest attempt advanced earlier this year, he joined his Democratic colleagues in voting for it.

He first offered adjustments that would have limited the measure’s scope: one to exclude people with violent offenses, and another mandating formerly incarcerated people pay restitution in full before getting their voting rights back.

Those efforts were unsuccessful.

In an interview with The Mercury, Cherry described his tweaks as a way “to bring some of my other colleagues along with me.”

This was in reference to GOP lawmakers who staunchly opposed restoring rights to people convicted of murder or manslaughter.

“That’s where (some of my Republican colleagues) fall on it. They want the victims to be restored,” Cherry explained. “They don’t like the fact that someone can get their rights back if they’ve disenfranchised someone else permanently.”

He said he understood their perspective but still supported the amendment, even without his proposed changes.

“If a judge didn’t give you a life sentence, we shouldn’t give you a life sentence as a society,” he said. “Once you’ve been adjudicated for your crime and you’ve served your time, then your right should be restored.”

Similarly, Patterson likened the state’s disenfranchisement to “this extra sentence that carries on.”

Other formerly incarcerated people released as part of the good behavior law have gone onto serve local government commissions, become peer recovery specialists, launch nonprofit organizations, or join lobbying and advocacy groups.

Nance, Patterson’s wife, said it’s important for those experiences to gain visibility, especially for those behind bars.

“I’m big on having our story reflect what potential there is for incarcerated people currently,” she said.

Patterson said the time he spent separated from society made him eager to not just rejoin it, but help shape it.

title: Infotour de Bure à Marseille 15-17 octobre
content:
Il y aura 3 temps d'informations sur la lutte antinucléaire de Bure à Marseille du jeudi 15 au samedi 17 !


Pourquoi un infotour sur Bure ?


Bure est un des points importants de la lutte antinucléaire en France. En effet, le projet CIGEO d'enfouissement de déchets nucléaires à Bure est central pour la continuation de l'industrie nucléaire tant les déchets sont nombreux et volumineux. L'industrie a également besoin de prétendre avoir trouvé une solution aux problèmes des déchets pour redorer son image et justifier de son caractère « écologique ». Afin de stopper l'industrie nucléaire dans son entier, de protéger le territoire meusien de la pollution radioactive et d'empêcher un projet délirant menaçant la survie des écosystèmes sur des centaines de milliers d'années, des militant.es luttent contre le projet CIGEO en Meuse depuis plusieurs dizaines d'années.


Les soirées d'information ont pour objectif de faire connaître la lutte antinucléaire, de faire connaître un des plus grands – et néfaste – projet industriel européen (plus de 30 milliards d'euros étalés sur un chantier prévu pour 150 ans) et de se rencontrer.


La lutte à Bure arrive à un tournant dans les prochaines années. Les travaux directement liés au projet CIGEO vont prochainement commencer. L'opposition va devoir alors, en plus de continuer les recours juridiques et administratifs, se confronter au début d'immenses travaux qui vont complètement transformer le territoire meusien (routes, voies ferrées, forages, déboisement de forêts, etc.). L'année 2026 a déjà été marquante pour la lutte avec l'expulsion de l'ancienne gare de Luméville l'un des 4 lieux collectifs qui ont été achetés par les militant.es anti-CIGEO.


Description des temps à Marseille


On prévoit des soirées assez similaires à la base et au Dar. L'après midi à la Camaraderie sera sur un thème différent pour permettre de venir à la camaraderie et à une des deux soirées :)


Jeudi 15 octobre à la Base

Adresse : La base, 3, rue Pierre Roche

Programme : accueil à 18h avec infokiosques, gâteaux et soft, présentation à 18h30, projection à 19h30, fin vers 20h30

Projection de "2015-2025 : dix ans de lutte à Bure".


Vendredi 16 octobre à la Camaraderie

Adresse : 78 rue de la Belle de Mai 13003 Marseille

Programme : Accueil et infokiosques à 14h, début de la discussion à 14h30. La discussion se centrera plus sur la vie dans les lieux collectifs et dans le milieu autonome. On ne dira pas les mêmes choses pendant ce temps que lors des deux autres soirées.


Samedi 17 octobre à Marseille (13)

Adresse : 127 rue d'Aubagne, 13006 Marseille

Programme : accueil et infokiosques à 18h30, discussion à 19h et projection à 20h de Vivre à Bure en 2025 suivi de Après les nuages.


Programme des soirées d'information


Le discours dominant présente aujourd'hui le nucléaire comme faisant partie de la solution pour lutter contre le réchauffement climatique. Évidemment, nous sommes en désaccord avec cela et nous expliquerons pourquoi il est important de continuer la lutte antinucléaire. Si vous ne pouvez pas venir aux soirées d'informations, de nombreuses brochures présentent différents arguments antinucléaire sur notre site internet. On présentera également les actualités de la lutte de Bure, ces dernières années ayant été particulièrement chargée : grande manifestation en Septembre 2025, occupation d'un terrain – l'ancienne gare de Luméville – en 2025-2026 et expulsion de cette dernière en avril 2026. L'année 2027 s'annonce également charnière avec le début des travaux du projet CIGEO.


La discussion à la Camaraderie le 16 après-midi se concentrera sur le thème de la vie dans des lieux collectifs autonomes, que cela soit à Bure ou ailleurs (ZADs, squats, etc.). Venez avec vos questions et vos expériences :)


Les projections


On prévoit de projeter des courts-métrages du collectif des Scotcheuses, un collectif de cinéma militant en Super 8, ainsi que des vidéos réalisées par l'Automédia de Bure. On variera selon les villes les courts-métrages projetés. À Marseille, on projettera Vivre à Bure en 2025, 2015-2025 : dix ans de lutte à Bure et Après les nuages. author: Rizomatica
title: 2do Koneltun de diversidades travestis trans Mapuche en Fiske menuko – Río Negro Puelmapu
content:
El viernes 09 de Octubre comienza el 2do koneltun de diversidades travesti trans Mapuche en una inmersión lingüística del Mapuzungun, que incluye diferentes niveles de idioma. Este fütxa txawün, gran encuentro, es parte del fortalecimiento de la memoria y existencia de identidades sexuales y espíritus diversos pertenecientes y caminantes del mapuche ngen. El koneltun, que tuvo su primera versión en Txaytxayko/Nueva imperial, Gulumapu/Araucanía, se dará lugar en Füshke menoko/Gral. Roca, Puelmapu, provincia de Rio Negro. Durante la jornada, habrá además, talleres de cartografía travesti de tiempo y espacio guiado por Pewmayen Figueroa, un nütxamkawün/conversatorio sobre la identidad afro kurüche por Tiwa Curiqueo finalizando con un taller de Pintura y cosmovisión guiado por las artistas visuales Poleo Painemal y Shakin Huaiquil.


La fecha elegida corresponde a la conmemoración y práctica de memoria al cumplirse 534 años desde la invasión colonizadora que hasta hoy intenta arrasar los territorios y vidas preexistentes.


No es casual que el 2do koneltun se decida realizar en Fiske menuko. En este lugar Geo Colicheo de ATTS, histórica travesti mapuche, ngen ruka, junto con su comunidad trans diversa del Alto Valle de Neuquén, han luchado años para nombrar a Roca como un agente que lideró el genocidio en la Patagonia del lado argentino.


“En medio de los continuos desalojos y del plan de exterminio que están llevando los gobiernos de chile y argentina contra el pueblo nación Mapuche, sumado a los continuos recortes en derechos del colectivo travesti trans, urge reencontrarnos y articularnos sin fronteras en una fuerza potenciadora y diversa para decir basta de militarización, de extranjerización de tierras ancestrales y del transodio que sostienen líderes de ultraderecha y sionistas”.

Añade Pewmayen Figueroa, Araucanía andina, una de las organizadoras desde el Gülumapu.


“Entendemos profundamente que en el marco del genocidio liderado por Roca también existió un etnotravesticidio y un generocidio. Un atentado y eliminación de nuestras formas de vivir como comunidades diversas».

 Comparte Ayla Rúa travesti Mapuche Tewelche de waqül Güyew – ingeniero Jacobacci.


El encuentro incluirá el día domingo 11 de octubre una jornada de varieté plurisexual abierta a todo público desde las 17:00 en el predio de ATE, barrio Mosconi Fiske menoko/ Gral Roca. Esta actividad contará con la presencia de distintos artistas, música en vivo, venta de comida (plato único), además de micrófono abierto para quienes deseen compartir pensamientos y sentires.


Relevamos la imagen gráfica de Flor de Jarilla en nuestro encuentro como forma de hacer memoria de nuestra ancestra travesti mapuche arrestada injustamente en Viedma a principios del siglo XX. Aquella gran bordadora de tejidos, fue muy querida por las comunidades aledañas de lo que hoy se conoce como General Conesa. Honramos su memoria y valentía, tras ser detenida por ser una persona trans indígena habitando la Patagonia en plena campaña del desierto.


Esta información se publicó en

Radio Kurruf

title: Humanitarian Workers Keep at “Noble Mission” Despite Risks, Gaza Journalist Says
content:
“Every single aspect of the life of the people of Gaza has changed once and forever,” says Akram al-Satarri.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

In Gaza, October 7, 2023, is viewed as the beginning of the genocide. Over the past three years, Israel killed over 74,000 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry, but many believe that number is a vast undercount. The killing continues despite a so-called ceasefire that took effect about a year ago.

“Every single aspect of the life of the people of Gaza has changed once and forever,” since October 7, says Akram al-Satarri, a Gaza-based journalist. He points out that a large majority of structures in the Gaza Strip have been reduced to rubble and that Israel controls around 70% of Gaza. “The Israeli Air Force is still hovering all around different parts of the Gaza Strip, and the IDF is still hunting Gazans, disturbing the already disturbed life, spreading death and displacement once and once again.”

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now!, democracynow.org. I’m Amy Goodman.

We end today’s show in Gaza, where today’s date, October 7th, is seen as the beginning of Israel’s genocide. In the three years since the Hamas attack on Israel that killed nearly 1,200 people, Israeli forces have killed over 74,000 Palestinians. Many believe the death toll is a vast undercount. This is a displaced Palestinian from Beit Hanoun speaking today in Gaza City.

AKRAM ABU JARAD: [translated] The worst three years that have passed in our lives. There is no life, no living, no food, no basic necessities of life. We wait for water from 5:00 to 10:00. And we are living in the streets, homeless, tired, worn out. I mean, a life worse than this? We are not living, my friend. We are dead in Gaza.

AMY GOODMAN: We go now to Gaza City, where we’re joined by journalist Akram al-Satarri.

I want to thank you so much for being with us. We spoke to you a few years ago as a journalist. You then went on to work with a humanitarian aid organization for several years. Now we’re back, being able to speak to you in Gaza City. Can you describe what’s happening on the ground? We just reported that as Israelis mourn the dead at the music site in southern Israel, they could hear the booms of Israeli airstrikes on the Gaza Strip right nearby. Tell us what’s happening where you are, Akram.

AKRAM AL-SATARRI: Well, October 7th was a day when Gaza changed once and forever. The way Palestinians have been living has changed. The way Palestinians have been managing their life has changed, as well. The way Palestinians were defining their life has changed. The Palestinians now are living in a de facto that has redefined everything — their understanding of life, their way of running and managing that life, their way to access things, their way to live, their way to stay in homes, their way to live in tents. Every single aspect of the life of the people of Gaza has changed once and forever.

Around 85% of the built environment in Gaza is already destroyed. Around 74% of the land of the Gaza Strip is also controlled by Israel and the IDF. Gazans have been struggling to access water and to access food. They have been facing significant public health hazards because of the fact that they were consuming water that was not properly treated. Organizations have been struggling for the sake of helping the people of Gaza. Statements were made by international and U.N. figures, diplomats all over the world, condemning the situation that has been going on, calling for Gazans to live and lead a normal life.

Unfortunately, for the third year now, and on October 7th, Gazans are reminded by the fact that they have been living in death and fear, destruction and displacement. The people who are living in the tents, with no even minimum standard for living, are living in exacerbating safety and security risks. author: Sharon Zhang
title: Democrat Opens Probe Into Kushner’s Firm’s Stake in Israeli Military
content:
Kushner’s role as a “special envoy” allows him to dodge financial reporting requirements, the Democrat pointed out.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

The top Democrat on the powerful House Oversight Committee has opened a probe into Jared Kushner and his private equity firm’s stake in Israeli military suppliers, raising concerns over “significant conflicts of interest” as Kushner serves as a top Middle East negotiator for the Trump administration.

In an inquiry addressed to Kushner sent Monday, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-California) demanded that Kushner disclose all of Affinity Partners’s foreign investments related to Middle East countries that the U.S. has dealings with, including in Israel, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and elsewhere.

Garcia also asks for accounting of Affinity Partners’s financial links to Israeli military suppliers, as well as details on meetings with or visits to Israel since the beginning of President Donald Trump’s second term in office.

“Your dual role as your father-in-law’s Middle East and Gaza negotiator while investing in a company that makes profits investing in arms manufacturing presents significant conflicts of interest, all while you avoid disclosing your financial entanglements to Congress or the American people,” Garcia wrote.

He notes that Kushner’s role as a “special envoy” for the Trump administration allows him to dodge financial disclosure requirements otherwise required from those in high positions within the federal government.

“Without oversight, the American people will continue to have serious questions about your motives and decision-making for as long as you profit from extensive business dealings,” Garcia went on. “The foreseeable and catastrophic failure of President Trump’s Middle East policy, including the disastrous Iran war, only deepens doubts about whether this Administration is acting in the public’s interest.”

Garcia’s letter follows a CNN report last week revealing that Affinity Partners holds the largest stake in a Tel Aviv-based firm, Phoenix Financial, that has at least $450 million in shares across nine companies that supply the Israeli military. This includes numerous Israeli military contractors, like Elbit Systems.

Kushner and the White House denied that his dealings with Israel and Middle East leaders benefit him personally. In posts on X, Kushner said CNN’s reporting was “misleading.”

CNN’s reporting compounded on a prior revelation that Kushner has also apparently tried to raise $5 billion or more from Middle East governments for Affinity Partners while simultaneously conducting deals for the Trump administration. Affinity’s biggest clients are the sovereign wealth funds of the Gulf states, and as of 2024, Kushner had already raised $4.8 billion in investments with major contributions from Saudi Arabia and Qatar.

Forbes estimates that Kushner is worth $1 billion — and that he first attained his status as a billionaire in September 2025. At the time, Kushner told Forbes that his “best investment” was increasing his stake in Phoenix.

author: Daron Letts
title: Nunavut duo wins at Pan-Arctic Vision
content:
A duo from Nunavut earned one of three honours at the fourth-annual Pan-Arctic Vision competition in Denmark on Oct. 2.


Christine Piunguałaq Tootoo

 of Rankin Inlet and

Tooma Laisa

 of Iqaluit shared the award for “most feeling of community and togetherness.”


The event, billed as the Arctic’s answer to the Eurovision Song Contest, took place at the Nordic House in Tórshavn, Faroe Islands.


“I love experiencing new cultures and languages,” Tootoo said in a preprepared video broadcast before her performance alongside Laisa. “Travelling gives me a zest for life.”


Travel was the theme of their traditional drum song,

Kiviuq

.


Kiviuq is the name of a

legendary Inuk

 who travelled across “the imaginary borders” of Inuit Nunangat, Tootoo said as she introduced the song from the stage.


Laisa softly drummed and hummed beside Tootoo, who recorded and looped Laisa’s voice. Then they sang their rendition of the legend.


When the performance ended, the audience broke the silence with a roar of applause.


Icelandic rock band Falinn gjóður won “most revolutionary song” and Nuunu, a Greenlandic singer-songwriter who goes by one name, won “most Arctic song.”


The 400-member audience cast votes, which were combined with online votes logged in realtime on the organization’s website, to pick the winners. Voters also selected Iceland as next year’s host.


All of the performers packed the stage and chanted, “This is Arctic land — we will always stand” and “

the Arctic is not for sale” during the finale. S

everal artists also fired ticker-tape cannons into the air.

author: Unknown
title: Гениальность Ленина
content:
Название

: Гениальность Ленина

Дата

: 1926

Источник

: Текст из журнала «Голос труженика», выпуск №19

(1926 год)


 «Наш гениальный Ильич»... «гениальный тактик»... «Гениальный аналитик?... «глубокий мыслитель»... «Наш гениальный учитель»... «Гениальный строитель»...


 Вот эпитеты, без которых ленинские «дурачки» и большевистские нахлебники никогда не говорили и не говорят о жестоком диктаторе, перед которым бледнеют тени Нерона и Торквемады.


 Мы, лично, никогда не были склонны рассматривать этого маниакального человека не только гениальным, но даже глубоко одаренным человеком.


 Изучая писания Ленина, мы убеждаемся, что он не мыслитель, а простой популяризатор марксизма. Вся его оригинальность сводится к Марксовой «Гражданской войне во Франции», которую он пережёвывает на все манеры.


 Как аналитик, дающий прогнозы он гениален, но... задним умом. В самом деле, вот посмотрите. На третьем всероссийском съезде советов, в январе 1918 года, «гениальный» Ленин заявлял: «понятия об анархизме принимают, наконец, жизненные очертания» (собр. соч. т. 15 стр. 90). Что означало, употребляя ленинскую терминологию, что мы не только на пути, но уже в пределах коммунизма, в его низшей стадии — социализма. Прошло три года и «гениальный» Ленин, в полемике со своими «левыми дурачками», признает себя круглым дураком: «Только дурак мог думать, писал он в одной из статей 1921 г. что в России возможно осуществление социализма». — И «гениальный» капитан направил корабль в море «нэпа».


 Возьмём другой пример: польскую войну. Известно, что ни один крупный вопрос советской политики не решался без Ленина. Вопрос о движении красной армии в Варшаву, как один из крупнейших вопросов внешней политики, был решён с согласия Ленина. И что же, на 10 съезде партии «гениальный аналитик и тактик» заявляет: «при нашем слишком быстром продвижении почти что до Варшавы, несомненно, была сделана ошибка»... «Ошибка налицо, и эта ошибка вызвана тем, что перевес наших сил был переоценён нами». Я мог бы привести бесконечное множество таких примеров, указывающих на сколько Ленин был «гениален» в политике. Но это для нас ненужно. Однако, я не могу не привести ещё одного примера «гениальности Ленина». В речи о роспуске учредительного собрания, произнесённой Лениным 6-го января 1918 г. на заседании ВЦИК, он говорил: «Существование Советов несовместимо с процветанием буржуазного строя»... (собр. соч. т. 15, стр. 59); прошло три года и Ленин ввёл «нэп», а всех, повторявших его мысль, назвал «дурачками»...


 Но в чем действительно Ленин проявил свою гениальность, так это в терроре. Здесь мы не можем отнять от него «творческой гениальности». Только в одних «Чека», «ревтрибуналах», и пр. милых учреждениях было размозжено сотни тысяч человеческих черепов! Это не сказка; нет, это — грубая действительность.


 «Мы должны предоставить полную свободу творчества народным массам» (собр. Соч. т. 15, стр. 20) — писал Ленин в 1917 году, а в 1918 предоставил эту «свободу творчества»… Чека. Все мероприятия внутренней политики и социалистического творчества не только не гениальны, но даже не разумны. Ибо, если бы эти меры были разумны, то мы спросим большевиков словами самого Ленина: «Где и когда погромы и анархия вызывались бы разумными мерами? Если бы правительство поступало разумно и если бы его мера шли навстречу нуждам крестьянской бедноты, то разве крестьянская масса стала бы волноваться?» (Собр. соч. т. 15, стр. 15). Этот вопрос Ленина мы можем теперь задать его партии, и ответить на него его же словами: «Вызвав восстание, оно (правительство) стало кричать о погромах и анархии, которые само же вызвало». (Тамже). И после этого во вею развернулась ленинская гениальность: «организовать насилие во имя интересов трудящихся». С этих пор насилие легло в основу всей деятельности большевиков; сначала оно служило для организации «военного коммунизма», а теперь для проведения нэпа. Всюду, где не хватало ума и творческой энергии, посылали «чеку»... Господствовал один принцип: «зажать, стеснить, заставить, принудить» и т. д. Идёт ли речь об организации промышленности или о постановке образования, о производстве сапог или о кооперации — всегда возлагается надежда на «свободное творчество» Чека. Вы не верите? Напрасно. Впрочем, сам Ленин подтвердит мою мысль. «...В кооперации сидит целый ряд контр-революционеров... Тут справедливо сказали о Ч. К. Если благодаря своей близорукости — говорит Ленин — вы не можете изобличить отдельных вожаков кооперации, то посадите туда одного …

content:

Εμείς όσο μπορούμε θα ενημερώνουμε, ενισχύουμε και στηρίζουμε τις υποθέσεις τους, αλλά και την συνέχιση των ζωών τους.


Με τους πρόσφυγες!

author: Chris Walker
title: Paxton Audio Reveals He Thinks Trump’s Policies Are “Dragging” Down His Campaign
content:
“I don’t know what’s behind some of the decisions” Trump is making, Paxton says in the audio recording.

Truthout is an indispensable resource for activists, movement leaders and workers everywhere. Please make this work possible with a quick donation.

Newly unearthed audio of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton (R) reveals his frustration with President Donald Trump and his policies, which he views as dragging down his own campaign for U.S. senator.

The leaked audio, obtained by Axios, was recorded at a closed-door fundraising event in Washington, D.C.

In the recording, Paxton complained that he doesn’t “make the decisions” that impact his campaign, citing Trump policies that have been detrimental to the economy and likely resulted in voters shifting toward Democrats — including his opponent, state Rep. James Talarico (D).

When asked what’s “dragging” his campaign, Paxton responded, “It’s the war, it’s gas prices, it’s diesel.”

The Republican Senate nominee also recognized that “people are feeling the pinch,” with rising fuel prices “driv[ing] up food prices and everything else.” Affordability is “by far our biggest problem,” Paxton added, and “why we’re having a hard time with [polling] numbers.”

Paxton then expressed doubts over Trump’s actions.

“So many factors in this federal race are uncontrollable. I don’t make the decisions, and I don’t … know what’s behind some of the decisions,” he said.

The revelation of this recording comes a week after other leaked audio from Paxton also made headlines. In that conversation, Paxton expressed similar misgivings over Trump, specifically faulting the president’s decision to have a “midterm convention.”

“To be honest with you, the numbers — when we did that convention — it dropped our numbers,” Paxton said in that conversation. “Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.”

The reporting on these conversations comes as the president is scheduled to speak at a rally for Paxton in the Lone Star State on Wednesday evening.

Multiple polls show that Talarico is ahead of Paxton in the Texas race. In a recent YouGov poll of likely voters, Paxton garnered only 44 percent support, whereas Talarico secured 50 percent. The Democrat is also ahead of the Republican candidate in a New York Times/Siena poll, which shows a 51-45 margin favoring Talarico.

Trump is unlikely to see it Paxton’s way if he and other Republicans lose their midterm races. In an interview in August, Trump claimed that voters are “angry at Republicans,” but “not angry at me.”

Despite Trump’s claims, a recent NPR/PBS NewsHour/Marist poll showed that 45 percent of voters said their preferences in the midterms should be viewed as a “vote against President Trump,” versus just 24 percent who said their preferences should be viewed as a vote for him.

The president currently has a net -27 point approval rating, according to an aggregate of polls compiled by FiftyPlusOne. Voters also prefer Democrats over Republicans in the midterm congressional races by eight points.

author: Amna Ahmed Dmeida
title: 3 Years Ago My Family Harvested Olives, Not Knowing It Would Be the Last Time
content:
Two of my family’s olive groves fell under Israeli control and got bulldozed. The third is damaged beyond recognition.

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

Every year, there were seasons and occasions that brought families together: holidays, Ramadan iftar meals, the end of the school year, and other gatherings. But for us, there was another season we looked forward to every year: olive-picking season.

Before the war, we always looked forward to the month of October. As the weather changed and the olives ripened, families prepared to spend long days in the fields. We would start before sunrise. It was still dark when we got ready to leave for our land.

My twin sister Alaa and I would go with our parents, grandparents, uncles, aunts, and cousins. The night before, we would prepare the baskets and large pieces of cloth that we would spread under the trees. Someone would bring tea, while someone else would bring bread, olive oil, olives, and za’atar. Somehow, we always forgot something. For us, olive picking was part of the rhythm of our lives and family memories, a time we knew would return every year.

The last time my family picked olives together was October 6, 2023. That day, there was nothing to suggest that the season would be different. We went to our land as we did every year and spent long hours among the trees. Some of us collected olives, while others spread the cloths or gathered fruit from the ground. Then we put the harvest into bags. My grandfather was there with us, as he had been during previous seasons. We worked, talked, and ate together as the cloths slowly filled with olives. We did not think this day would become a memory. We thought the olive season would come again the following year. But the next day, the war began, and the olive season was no longer the same.

Olive picking was one of the few times each year when our extended family came together for a day. The work was tiring, but the day was filled with conversation and laughter. The men climbed the trees and used sticks to reach the branches, while the women spread cloths underneath and gathered the olives. During breaks, we sat under the trees, drank tea, and ate together.

For Alaa and me, October had another meaning. It was our birthday month. On October 30, 2022, we celebrated our birthday on the land where we picked olives. Our mother made a cake, and we all sat together and spent the day there, surrounded by our family and the olive trees. It was a simple birthday, but having everyone together made it special. It was my last birthday on that land before the war.

My family had three plots of land planted with olive trees. Two of them are now under Israeli control and have been bulldozed, so we can no longer reach them. We can still access the third, but it no longer looks like the place where we used to spend our autumns. The trees that once brought us together have been damaged, and the land around them has changed. The land is there, but our life there has been uprooted.

The destruction of olive trees in Gaza means more than losing a harvest. It means losing a season, a tradition, memories, and a place where generations of my family used to come together.

The destruction of olive trees in Gaza means more than losing a harvest. It means losing a season, a tradition, memories, and a place where generations of my family used to come together.

What happened to my family’s land is not an isolated experience. Across Gaza, agricultural land has been damaged or has become impossible to access. Wells, greenhouses, irrigation systems and other infrastructure that farmers depend on have also been decimated.

According to an August 2026 assessment by the UN Satellite Centre and UN Food and Agriculture Organization, only 448 hectares, or 3 percent of Gaza’s farmland, were both accessible and undamaged as of June 24, 2026. Much of the accessible land had been damaged and could no longer be farmed without repairs.

A UN assessment published in late 2025 found that 89 percent of orchard trees had been damaged. Olive orchards were among the most affected, with 90 percent of their area damaged.

These numbers show the scale of the destruction, but they cannot show what it means for a family to lose trees that were part of its life and memories.
